News.title: How October 7 massacre was the day Britain became mired in antisemitic hate and turned so many in this country insane
News.content:
Next

EVEN on October 7, 2023, as Hamas terrorists rampaged through Southern Israel, murdering, raping and taking hostage every man, woman and child they could lay their hands on, it was clear this was an event which would change Britain too.

That night, while most people in this country were shaken with revulsion about the unfolding massacre, there were people across our country who were celebrating.



They were lighting fireworks and they were dancing.

Jewish TV presenter Rachel Riley was among the first to document this astonishing behaviour.



Tweeting a video of apparently rapturous people near her home in West London, she wrote on X: “People have been brutally murdered, kidnapped, and there are people in London dancing. Make no mistake, this is a dangerous and terrifying time for all Jews around the world.”

The spike in antisemitism — on social media, in the street — started that day too.

Novelist Howard Jacobson has described it as a “bloodlust” — the idea that seeing Jews being hurt encourages other people to want to hurt more Jews.

The pattern has continued in the three years since, from the terrorist attack on Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester a year ago, to the stabbings and firebombs in Golders Green, North West London earlier this year.

Every time a Jew is hurt, for most people the response is sympathy.

But for some people, it elicits excitement. They want to hurt more Jews.



It tells us something about antisemitism but also the society that houses it, that allows it to flourish.

Just in the past few days, as we hear about a pilot trying to crash a plane-load of Israelis, British police arrest Iranians allegedly plotting a terrorist attack and the Green Party passes a Jew-hating motion.

The temperature for British Jews like me feels as though it keeps getting hotter.

As I write this, I am waiting for a call from the Metropolitan Police after I was assaulted while being called “Zionist scum” and a “Zionist fascist”, threatened and hemmed in by a giant banner held by a mob at a supposed anti-racism demonstration on Sunday.

The irony was that this was an event celebrating the 90th anniversary of the Battle of Cable Street when the working class helped defend their Jewish neighbours from Oswald Mosley’s fascists.



But the mob turned on me when they heard I was a Zionist — someone who believes in a Jewish state on our ancestral homeland.

For me, there is little difference between the people in keffiyehs who dress up as Islamist terrorists and the fascist Blackshirts who also used to want to hurt Jews and march through where we live.

And we have allowed them to run rampant for three years now.



It was just after midday on October 7, 2023, that the Palestine Solidarity Campaign applied for its first demonstration for Gaza.

Hamas — a proscribed terrorist group — was still killing Israelis, yet these people wanted to march in favour of the other side.

From October 7, 2023, to the end of that year, there were 900 protests in favour of Gaza.

From the start, they were steeped in antisemitism, waving placards with the Jewish Star of David entwined with a swastika or thrown in a bin.

And protesters dressed as terrorists with images of the paragliders who had invaded Israel.



Cries of “baby killer” and “genocide” started on October 7 as Israel was fighting for its life.

Those demonstrations have continued.

Successive governments have struggled to know how to deal with them, even as they have led to entire parts of our cities being closed every weekend for months.

While right-wing protests against immigrants are quickly shut down, the pro-Gaza crowd have been given practically free rein.

How have we got to the point where all the Metropolitan Police can do about a planned pro-Gaza demonstration by London university students today — on the anniversary of Hamas’s attack on Israel — is to ask them to change the date?



How are we so toothless against what is essentially the celebration of terrorism?

Against a terrorism that isn’t just about Jews but about the West and the freedoms we all take for granted.

That free rein on our streets has given the green light to hatred in this country, which I could never have envisaged.



From classrooms where children are bullied for saying they are Jewish to university students who have been shunned by housemates, to the NHS where a doctor was suspended for a rant about “Jewish supremacy”.

While one Jewish man — in the middle of an operation — had to suffer a doctor telling him about how much Jews liked to hurt children.

There’s the overt hatred, the violence and the terrorist attacks.

And then there are the quieter, silent attacks — the Jewish comics or musicians banned from appearing on stage, the Israeli restaurants that have had to rebrand as “Mediterranean”.

The mob that comes after them also comes after everyone who dares to show sympathy with Jews.



Boy George could no longer perform in a musical because he had written a song with the lyrics “I stand with the Jews”.

Ed Sheeran, for daring even to say that he didn’t want to be political, faced death threats and mass cancellation.

In the meantime, a terrorist group called Palestine Action smashes up British military equipment and violently assaults police officers and guards, yet thousands stand up for them.

This is pro-terror radicalisation happening with Israel as an excuse.

October 7 was a catalyst, showing something has broken in our country.



How else to explain that we have four MPs voted into Parliament “for Gaza”, a war more than 2,000 miles away over which we have no influence?

Or that a political party, the Greens, should be so overrun by obsessive Jew haters that anyone who believes in the right of Jews to have their own state in their ancestral homeland — that is most of us — are now deemed officially racist by them.

Or that Labour, so determined to win the same antisemitic voters who have abandoned them for the Greens, have blown up our relationship with Israel, an ally that has prevented multiple terrorist attacks in this country.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It is important today to remember the terrorism of October 7, those who died on that awful day and in the war that inevitably followed it.

And to wonder how it ended up turning so many in this country insane.

News.title: Insane cost of executing death row inmates vs life in prison – & that’s before Christa Pike’s life-saving medical bills
News.content:
Next

THE staggering price of putting a killer to death is often millions more than keeping them locked up for life.

Now the cost of capital punishment is under renewed scrutiny after murderer Christa Pike was left critically ill when Tennessee’s attempt to execute her failed.



Pike, 50, survived two doses of lethal drugs after spending three decades on death row for the brutal 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, with her case estimated to have already cost taxpayers more than $3 million.

Her legal team said on Tuesday that Pike is now “conscious, speaking” but remains under critical medical care.



Her lawyers claim botched IV lines caused the drugs to leak into tissue, leaving both arms “swollen, burned and blistered.”

And the taxpayer bill is still mounting, with the state now facing the cost of Pike’s hospital treatment, an investigation into the failed execution and potentially further legal proceedings.



Six days of intensive care and ventilation alone could carry charges of around $26,000 based on published Nashville hospital rates, before other treatment is factored in.

Stacy Rector, executive director of Tennesseans for Alternatives to the Death Penalty, told The U.S. Sun, “I would guess her case has exceeded $3 million, before this botched execution attempt.

“I can’t even begin to guess what her hospital bill will be once this is all over – a hundred thousand plus?

“All is being paid by TN taxpayers.”



Pike had been held at Nashville’s Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, formerly the Tennessee Prison for Women, since March 1996 before being transferred to Riverbend Maximum Security Institution for her attempted execution.

She was then taken from Riverbend to an off-site medical facility after the lethal injection failed.

Rector based her estimate for Pike on a detailed Maryland study of 1,136 death-eligible murder cases from 1978 to 1999, covering the period in which Pike was convicted.



Cases where prosecutors did not seek the death penalty cost around $1.1 million over their lifetime.

That rose to around $1.8 million when prosecutors sought death but a death sentence was not imposed.

Cases resulting in a death sentence cost around $3 million, almost $2 million more than those where death was not sought.

The $3 million included the trial, penalty phase, state and federal appeals and prison costs.

Prosecutors decide before trial whether to pursue death.



If they do not, there is no separate capital sentencing hearing after conviction, explaining the $0 penalty phase cost.

When death was sought, that extra phase cost an average $71,000 when no death sentence was imposed and $263,000 when it was.

Newer studies have also found a major gap between the cost of death penalty and non-capital cases.

A 2021 review by the Ohio Legislative Service Commission looked at studies from several states and found death penalty cases cost between 2.5 and five times as much as non-capital cases, with some studies putting the additional bill at between $1 million and $3 million per case.



A 2025 Indiana analysis found an even bigger difference at the trial stage, with an average death penalty trial costing $290,022 compared with $36,173 for one seeking life without parole.

That works out at around eight times as much at the trial stage alone.

Tennessee’s own research found death penalty trials cost taxpayers an average of 48 percent more than cases where prosecutors seek life imprisonment, while state estimates have put the added cost of capital trials and appeals at more than $750,000 per case.

Rector said, “I think the cost is a colossal waste of tax dollars spent pursuing death for a handful of people who are already incarcerated.”



She questioned the spending when Tennessee “solves only about half its homicides” and said the state’s victims’ compensation fund was difficult for those impacted by violence to access.

She added, “Too many Tennesseans lack access to mental health care, and our Department of Children’s Services continues to struggle to serve children like Christa Pike, who have experienced terrible trauma and violence.”

Rector said many Tennesseans remain unaware of how much is being spent in her state.

She said, “Our organization, TADP, continues to educate people about these costs, but too many Tennesseans don’t know how expensive it is.

“Our state has no centralized mechanism to track these costs so taxpayers are in the dark.”



Rector feels the money spent pursuing executions could instead be used on victims, unsolved murders and crime prevention.

She said, “We are paying for a system that does not achieve anything for us. It does not make us safer.

“It traps surviving families of murder victims in decades of trauma without the resources and space they need to begin their healing process.

“It is not applied fairly. It diverts an inordinate amount from investments in real crime prevention and solving unsolved crimes.”

She added, “And it sometimes gets it wrong: over 200 people sentenced to death in the US since 1973 have later been exonerated and released from death row.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We don’t know the number of innocent people we have executed.”

She added, “The bottom line is that the death penalty system is a costly government program that is totally unnecessary and distracts us from investing in real solutions.”

News.title: Christa Pike is now AWAKE & speaking 6 days after botched execution – but is still in ‘critical’ care & shackled to bed
News.content:
Next

CONVICTED murderer Christa Pike is awake and speaking nearly a week after she was injected with two doses of a lethal drug.

Pike, 50, remains in critical medical care and handcuffed to a hospital bed despite having endured severe damage to her arms, her attorneys fumed.



“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” Pike’s attorneys, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in an email statement on Tuesday, six days after the state of Tennessee failed to execute her.

“Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed.



“Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”

Pike’s defense attorneys praised the convicted murderer as a survivor and again called on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Read more in The U.S. Sun FOOT THE BILL Insane cost of executing death row inmates like Christa Pike vs life sentence

The statement was the first indication disclosed by Pike’s legal team that her condition had improved since she was rushed to an off-site hospital after receiving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Since Wednesday’s failed execution, Pike had remained unconscious and on a ventilator as her defense attorneys feared she might have suffered brain damage.

Dr. Joel Zivot, who consulted as an expert to Pike’s legal team, told the Associated Press that the latest development “bodes well for a good recovery.”

“She’s still in the ICU. She has recovered to a certain degree that she’s able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk,” Dr. Zivot told the outlet.



The medical expert said that Pike has a long road ahead of her to make any sort of recovery.

“There’s still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well,” he added.

The update comes after a horrifying picture leaked online showing the extended damage to Pike’s arm, which her attorneys said were “swollen, burned, and blistered.”

News.title: Doctor ‘murdered at home while hosting kids’ sleepover’ was GP for Royal Family ‘who treated Camilla’ as husband charged
News.content:
Next

A DOCTOR murdered at home while hosting a children’s sleepover was a GP for the Royal Family.

Mum-of-three Hannah Terry, 45, was found dead on Sunday at her property on the edge of the Sandringham Estate, Norfolk. Tonight husband Mark Cain, 45, was charged with murder.



The doctor seemed “stressed” in the days before her suspected murder, pals said.

Friends, colleagues and neighbours have been left in shock after Hannah was found dead at her home in the early hours of Sunday.



Cain is due to appear at Norwich magistrates’ court tomorrow morning.

The Sun can reveal Dr Terry, who lived with her husband and three sons in a £830,000 property near the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk, was a GP for the Royal Family. Sources said King Charles and Queen Camilla had been informed of her death.

Tonight, a friend said that in the days before she died Dr Terry had seemed “stressed” and “distracted” on the school run, which was “out of character”.

Police scrambled to the family home in Dersingham, just over a mile from Sandringham, at around 2.20am on Sunday after being alerted by paramedics.

Dr Terry was pronounced dead at the scene.

The detached property was sealed off on Monday, with police arriving in forensic suits.



The friend added: “They lived on one of the poshest streets in the village — and that’s saying something in an area as well-heeled as North Norfolk.”

A hugely experienced and much-loved GP, Dr Terry served in a pool of doctors who were regularly on call for members of the Royal Family nearby.

She was believed to have treated senior royals, including Queen Camilla, while they stayed at the Sandringham Estate.



Dr Terry had worked at the Heacham GP surgery in West Norfolk for nine years but left last summer to “spend more time with her young family”.

She later took up a role at the Grimston Medical Centre, in King’s Lynn, a practice which has served the royals for years.

In an announcement at the time, the surgery said that she would be working three days a week, and they were “excited to have her on board”.



It was closed on Monday “due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team”.

Patients, colleagues and locals left flowers on Monday, and paid tribute to the “kindest” and “wonderful” medic.

Clinical administrator Julie-Ann Rayner said: “I had the pleasure of working with her for a few years.



“She was an amazing doctor and an amazing person, really wonderful, really warm-hearted, she really cared about her family.

“It’s incredibly sad what’s happened, everybody’s completely shocked. I can’t stop thinking about her boys and what they must be going through.”

GP Pallavi Devulapalli, a local councillor, posted online: “Dr Hannah worked briefly with me at my former practice — intelligent, really pleasant, a lovely colleague. I am genuinely struggling to understand what happened.”



Local resident Charisma-Mai Ellis said: “She was my GP when I was younger and my mum’s GP for a long time.

“She was very softly-spoken and I remember her being so understanding and empathetic. She had all the time for you.”

“She shouldn’t be remembered for this – she should be remembered for being the kind, caring, powerful, bright woman she was.”

A poignant note left at the surgery by a patient read:

“Dr Hannah Terry our GP, we are all thinking of your family, your children, your friends and even more for all staff and colleagues at Grimston Medical Practice.



“You were the kindest doctor to Alan and I.

“You never rushed us and you listened to both of us, nobody else will ever be able to replace a beautiful GP and person like you.

“Fly high Dr Terry, sleep well, Heaven has certainly gained an angel.”



Dr Terry also co-owned Norfolk Sky Aesthetics, a cosmetic treatment company which was set up in November 2024.

A neighbour said: “She was just a lovely human being with three gorgeous young children. Something’s obviously gone very badly wrong.

“I’m just out of words, we all are.”

Another who lived next door said: “I didn’t know anything until the police came. I very rarely saw them.

“The children were lovely.



“They used to kick their football into my garden and I’d throw it back to them, or they’d come and ask me if they could come in and look for it.”

Others said they could not comprehend something so shocking happening in their village. A local told The Sun: “You read about things like this happening in other places.

“But nothing like it ever happens this close to home.”

Another said: “Dersingham is the sort of place where if you forget to lock your car and leave it out all night, nothing will happen to it.”

Norfolk Police said: “Police were called to a house in Fern Hill shortly after 2.20am on Sunday by the ambulance service.



“Sadly, a woman in her 40s was pronounced dead at the scene.

“A man in his 40s was arrested on suspicion of murder and taken to King’s Lynn Police Investigation Centre. A cordon is still in place at the address while we continue to carry out enquiries.”

A post-mortem took place on Monday but the cause of death had yet to be established.

Specialist officers were supporting Dr Terry’s family, while investigators appealed for help.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Det Insp Alix Wright, from Norfolk and Suffolk Major Investigation Team, said: “We are in the very early stages of this investigation working to establish the exact circumstances surrounding the woman’s death.



“I’d ask anyone who believes they may have information that could help our investigation to please share this with us.”

News.title: Thieves steal 500kg of grapes from family-run vineyard as distraught owner loses an entire year’s worth of wine
News.content:
POUR CHOICES Thieves steal 500kg of grapes from family-run vineyard as distraught owner loses an entire year’s worth of wine







Next

THIEVES have made off with 500kg of grapes from a family-run vineyard, as the owner loses a year’s worth of wine.

Lee Dyer, owner of Winbirri Vineyard in Surlingham, Norfolk, said the stolen Bacchus grapes were enough to make 400 bottles of vino.



Mr Dyer said that while the grapes were worth around £1,000, their value as wine would be about £8,000.

He added that on September 20 the fruit were on the vine, but on September 22 it was noticed that two rows in the field had been “completely stripped bare”.



“We’re a family-run business, we all work seven days a week and this is a year’s worth of work that we’ve had to do to get these grapes over the line,” said Mr Dyer.

“They’re not an easy crop to grow full stop, no matter what country you’re in.

“You do have to put a lot of work into them and someone then comes along and feels it’s ok to come on your property and just take it for themselves.”

He said that “we’re going to have to change things”.

“We’re now going to have to up the security on the vineyards,” he said.

He suggested this could include “motion-activated cameras and we’ll have to get some form of Sim card wi-fi set-up in the vineyard”.



“This is all expense that you really shouldn’t have to be going to just because someone feels it’s acceptable to come into your property and just take your crop,” he said.

Mr Dyer said that “to take that much fruit I don’t think it was a single individual”.

He said that grapes had gone missing “on a much smaller scale” in previous years, and that last year a volunteer picker “actually caught a few gentlemen red-handed with electric bikes and modified trailers and secateurs in hand”.

“This year we had a couple of visits from people asking questions about buying grapes and that they make wine themselves and they would come and pick them,” he said.

“It might just be a coincidence but then a few days later after these visits we noticed a couple of the rows had been completely stripped bare.”



He added: “My main hope from this is the individuals that did it will see this publicity and then suddenly go ‘actually it’d probably be a wise idea not to repeat that’ because of the attention it’s brought.”

A Norfolk Police spokesperson said the force received a report on October 2 regarding the theft of grapes from a site in Surlingham, believed to have happened between September 20 and 22.

The spokesperson said an officer is due to speak with the person who reported the incident.

News.title: Couple stole £5m of parents’ school fees from top private school and used it as their own ‘piggy bank’, court hears
News.content:
'LAVISH LIFESTYLE' Couple stole £5m of parents’ school fees from top private school and used it as their own ‘piggy bank’, court hears







Next

A COUPLE who founded one of Britain’s top private sixth-form colleges stole more than £5 million from parents’ school fees to use it as their own “piggy bank”, a court heard.

Yasmin Sarwar, 48, and her husband Nadeem, 50, were said to have used the registered charity to fund their own “lavish lifestyles”, allegedly raiding its accounts to purchase properties and line their own pockets.



Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court was told that Mr Sarwar has already admitted stealing £5 million from Cardiff Sixth Form College between February 2008 and October 2016.

But his wife denies nine counts of theft and fraud over the same period.



Prosecutor Mark Cotter KC said the pair were paid “handsomely” for their roles at the top-performing institution, which charges up to £30,000 a year for day pupils and £75,000 for boarders.

“The defendant and her then husband treated the college as their own personal piggy bank,” Mr Cotter told the jury.



“They raided the funds to fund their own lavish lifestyles.”

The prosecutor said their assault on the school’s finances was “so relentless and widespread” that it left their accountant unable to produce proper audited accounts.

To cover their tracks, the couple hired 41-year-old Ragu Sivapalan as a “new, less rigorous accountant” who accepted their statements at “face value” to file false figures.

Sivapalan has since admitted causing an auditor’s report to include misleading, false, or deceptive information.



The college grew from a small A-level tutoring group founded in 2004 by Mrs Sarwar, a self-styled “tiger mum”, into a world-renowned institution that topped national league tables by 2010.

By 2009, the school had begun successfully marketing overseas, attracting more than 300 pupils from countries including Albania and China.

“It became one of the top performing sixth form colleges in the country with international recognition,” Mr Cotter said.



The court heard that the Malaysian-born couple recruited relatives to sit on the board alongside well-meaning trustees, including respected teacher John Price-Thomas, his wife Carol, and their son Huw.

Four other trustees were family members, including Mr Sarwar’s sister and cousins, alongside Mrs Sarwar’s sister.

Mr Cotter told the court that financial decisions, including the setting of the couple’s “very substantial salaries”, were dictated entirely by the Sarwars rather than the trustees.



When the Sarwars announced plans in 2013 to convert the charity into a private business, the Price-Thomas family resigned.

Although the commercial conversion never took place, new trustees were brought in – including parent Nabeela Sheik, who was appointed despite having poor spoken and written English.

Describing Mrs Sarwar as a “wilful, intelligent and manipulative woman”, Mr Cotter told the court she was a willing participant in the fraud who took money that did not belong to her and tried to cover it up.

He added that she even set up “sham companies” to “divert huge sums of money away from her husband after their relationship went sour, and to overseas”.

Investigators later discovered Mrs Sarwar had transferred more than £1.1 million of college funds to her mother’s bank account in Malaysia and bought a £1.1 million property in Cardiff.



The college was bought by multinational firm Dukes Education in 2018.

All charges predate the takeover.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mrs Sarwar, of Cyncoed, Cardiff, denies all charges.

The trial continues.

News.title: Soaring sex attacks in primary schools are direct result of porn industry warping boys’ minds – we must fix it
News.content:
Next

A STUDENT at New York’s supposedly elite Cornell University wrote “free pussy” on a 50-strong Snapchat group of mates when the girl he’d just had sex with was virtually comatose from alcohol and ketamine.

Consequently, of the seven who allegedly sexually assaulted her, just two were expelled, one was barred from campus but had already left, two others were temporarily suspended, and the remaining two were reportedly asked to write “reflection” essays.





No charges were brought against the alleged perpetrators, who deny wrong- doing, and the case was only reopened when the woman — known as Jane Doe — filed a civil lawsuit.

Now the university’s president has described this sordid behaviour as a “defining moment” for fraternity culture.

Is it though? Or will the university’s promised “review” simply kick concerns in to the long grass with the age-old assurance that “lessons have been learned” blah blah blah. This particular scandal belongs to America, but we have our own shameful behaviour to deal with, too.

The Children’s Commissioner for England says that child-on-child sexual abuse in our schools is “widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet”.

Shockingly, around five primary-age children report being sexually assaulted on or near school premises. Every. Single. Day.

And nearly two-thirds of the sexual crimes against under-13s were committed against girls.

These statistics were obtained by The Guardian newspaper via Freedom of Information requests to 43 police forces across England and Wales. Shamefully, ten of them didn’t bother to respond.

Women and girls live with the threat of sexual violence every day.





So, as the mother of daughters, I dished out the depressingly familiar advice when they were in their teens. Walk under the street lights, have a key in your hand, run to a house with lights on if you’re being followed, carry an alarm, don’t leave your drink unattended, stick together, keep your wits about you, etc.

Yesterday, the actor Stephen Graham said of his daughter: “Now maybe people will say this is wrong, but from a young age I’ve always wanted our Gracie to throw a great right hook, just in case. I teach her kicking the shins, kicking the balls.”

Sounds eminently sensible to me, particularly now that younger girls aren’t even safe from being sexually assaulted in primary school.

Every time I write about male violence, I get the predictable “not all men” response from certain quarters. Yes, we know. But that’s not the point.

Of course, the majority of them will be kind and caring young men who are taught to call out bad behaviour among their peers — but they can’t do it alone.

They need parents to relentlessly instil the “respect women” message but, equally, they need back-up support from those in authority.

And that means tackling the relentless march of easily available, hardcore pornography that has warped young boys’ attitude to sex with images of choking and other submissive and debasing acts.

We spend millions teaching boys and girls in class that no means no, that they have agency over their own bodies and that they deserve respect — while simultaneously allowing the porn industry to present women as objects and teach them something entirely different.



On paper, women have more rights than ever.

In practice, misogyny has been given a smartphone, unlimited data and a global distribution network.

And scandals like the Cornell Seven and the deeply shocking sexual assault statistics in UK primary schools are surely a direct result of that.

Daley divas headfirst into drag

THIS, believe it or not, is Olympic diver Tom Daley in drag.

Following the full makeover by Drag Race star Plastique Tiara, Tom’s husband Dustin Lance Black said: “Oh my God, I’m straight now.”

Indeed. He makes a very convincing beauty thanks to false eyelashes, foundation, contouring, lip plumper and eyebrow lamination – all topped off with an impressively realistic wig.

It reveals the tricks we women have at our disposal to look glam on a night out.



And explains why, when we take it all off, the man we’ve started seeing looks slightly baffled when he wakes up next to someone who looks more like regular Tom Daley after he’s just plummeted off the high board.

SU WILL LEARN A LOT

KATIE Price has been handcuffed to former Home Secretary Suella Braverman for the Channel 4 TV show Celebrity Handcuffed: Last Pair Standing.

The idea is that people with diverse perspectives on life spend 24/7 together until one of the pair can’t bear it any longer.

I spent Friday night with Katie at Tulley’s Farm Shocktober Fest in West Sussex and, during an excellently spooky tractor ride, we had a long chat about life, love and the universe.

Her son Harvey, who has complex medical needs, was with her and the way she communicates with him and delights in his company was wonderful to see.

Katie’s mum Amy is seriously ill, and her latest disastrous marriage has hit the rocks in spectacular fashion.

But every day, she picks herself up and gets on with life in a disarmingly matter-of- fact way.

Many will think that Katie will learn a few things from Suella – but, trust me, it will be the other way round.

ANDY’S INVITED TO TEA



WHEN you’ve been sent to Coventry, how long do you stay there?

Not long, it seems, if you’re the King’s brother.

Rumour has it that the pariah formerly known as Prince Andrew is now out of social Siberia and back on the dinner party circuit in the grand homes surrounding Sandringham in Norfolk.

It has been suggested that the Earl and Countess of Leicester, Tom and Polly Coke, have already had him round to their, gulp, 25,000-acre pile and that other posh types in the area are now likely to do the same.

How charitable of them.

Or, far more likely, the recent return of Harry and Meghan and the need for someone from the inner circle to dish the tea has forced a rethink.

KEMI’S WAY IS RIGHT

HAVING referred to Reform leader Nigel Farage as a grumpy grandpa, and PM Andy Burnham as a cheesy uncle, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch described herself as a “no nonsense mum”.

It struck me as just what we need after far too many years of “gentle parenting” by the likes of Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Rishi Sunak, Sir Keir Starmer and, now, the self-styled King of the North.

In other words, supposed leaders who led the country without authority and created an unholy mess where every decision is renegotiable, every rule needs justification and every “no” can be pushed back on by the errant toddlers on the backbenches.



Children need boundaries, rules and structure to make them feel safe – and so does the electorate.

Bring it on.

A SIGNED copy of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex’s children’s book The Bench has popped up on eBay for £20k.

It appears to be dedicated to Princess Eugenie, and her husband Jack Brooksbank, along with a heartfelt, handwritten message about the book “celebrating the special bond between father and son”.

Oh dear. If genuine, how could this precious gift have fallen into the hands of the London-based book dealer who listed it? We demand to be told.

Meanwhile, the search for an extremely rare, unsigned copy continues . . .

RICH’S FATE AWAITS

THE gloriously watchable Richard E Grant broke every rule in the Traitors playbook before the end of the first episode.



Stay beneath the radar. Make friends with everyone. And don’t show anything that could be interpreted as traitorous behaviour.

Instead, just a few minutes after the holy hand of High Priestess Claudia Winkleman anointed him with an AAA pass to the turret of treachery, comedian Joe Lycett asked him what role he’d been given and he answered: “Traitor” with a big grin.

Cue gasps in living rooms across the country and head slaps in the director’s gallery where the production team had never seen the like.

We’ll find out tomorrow whether his manic backtracking has worked, but you never know.

After all, when previous Traitor Alan Carr was asked his role and said “Faithful” before bursting out laughing, he still went on to win whole series.

News.title: Three arrested after raid on gang accused of helping migrants pretend to be gay to get asylum
News.content:
Two people were arrested at addresses in London this morning on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, with Home Office officers also seizing phones, jewellery and thousands of pounds in cash. A third person was arrested on suspicion of being in the country illegally.

Chris Foster, a regional lead for criminal investigations at the Home Office, said the fake claims were connected to a Bangladeshi community LGBT organisation called Apanjon, which is based in Whitechapel, east London.

He said asylum caseworkers had initially spotted patterns in suspicious claims, which raised concerns about the group, and that immigration officers had been investigating for several months.

"We've got some intelligence that they can provide fake letters and documents, and they could charge anywhere between Â£1,000 and Â£4,500," Foster said.

"It could be letters of support from Apanjon, it could be staged photographs, suggesting that these people are gay, it could be letters from people claiming to be in a friendship or a sexual relationship - [a] same-sex relationship - as the claimants."

More than 100 asylum claims linked to the criminal network are being reviewed by the Home Office. Foster said some of the fake asylum applications would have "undoubtedly" been granted.

Immigration judges have previously criticised evidence from Apanjon as unreliable or not credible and found that an applicant who claimed to have attended the group's events had submitted staged photographs.

The Home Office said the group would often vouch for men who claimed asylum on the basis they were gay only after having initially been refused on political grounds. In one case, a man didn't raise his sexuality until nine years after his original claim.

The group is accused of using the same tactics as those pushed by advisers exposed in the BBC's investigation earlier this year.

A Home Office spokesperson said it was continuing to review asylum claims linked to that reporting, which led to two arrests in May.

In the BBC report, published in April, an adviser called Tanisa Khan told an undercover reporter she could provide a "comprehensive package", including photographs at gay clubs and other supporting evidence.

She was linked to a community group called Worcester LGBT, which she told the reporter they should attend in order to add to evidence for his fake claim.

Men attending one of the group's events at a community centre in Beckton, east London, claimed they were not really gay. One said: "Nobody is a gay here. Not even 1% are gay. Not even 0.01% are gay."

The investigation also revealed how bogus medical conditions and fake news websites were being used to bolster fraudulent asylum claims.

Worcester LGBT has since closed. Its founder previously said the group did not create or support fabricated evidence in asylum claims and it was not up to the organisation to determine whether any individual was actually gay.

Khan blamed communication difficulties for a "misunderstanding" and denied advising the reporter to make a false claim or offering to create fabricated evidence.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said "those faking persecution are beneath contempt and mock real victims who need protection".

"To the gangs profiting from this disgraceful fraud: you will be prosecuted, stripped of your dirty money and shut down," she said.

"And to those cheating the system, your claim will be thrown out, and you will be removed from this country."

A conviction for asylum fraud carries a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison.

News.title: Watch: Police raid on gang behind fake gay asylum claims
News.content:
Three people have been arrested after a raid on a suspected criminal network believed to be behind dozens of fake asylum claims from people pretending to be gay.

It follows a BBC investigation earlier this year which revealed that law firms and advisers were helping migrants pose as gay in an effort to get asylum.

The BBC's Politics Investigations Correspondent, Billy Kenber, joined members of the Home Office Immigration Enforcement team as they looked to arrest the group's suspected ringleaders on Tuesday morning.

News.title: British national arrested in connection with RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
A 22-year-old British national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident close to RAF Fairford, counter-terror police said.

He was arrested in Westminster, London, on Tuesday as part of the investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire on 27 September.

It is the seventh arrest in connection to the incident but no one has been charged.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

Senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said it "remains a live investigation" and police are continuing to "pursue multiple lines of enquiry".

Five men were arrested on 27 September near the base in connection with the incident and were subsequently released on police bail.

The men, aged between 23 and 25, were detained in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual Iranian-British national, was arrested on 1 October in Westminster and was also later released on bail.

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

On Sunday, it emerged the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

While speaking to a group of reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.

He replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.

"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy.

"But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."

Earlier, US Vice-President JD Vance said the bombers were moved "out of an abundance of caution".

The comments came after US media reports suggested the decision was made after intelligence suggested Iran was plotting a drone attack. The BBC has not verified those reports.

On Tuesday, a spokesperson for US European Command, which coordinated American military activity in Europe, said it would be "inappropriate to discuss matters of intelligence" but that the US would "continue to assess the threat environment" at bases.

The spokesperson added the US remains at the "highest state of readiness" and would take "appropriate actions to protect our people, our platforms, and the bases where our forces operate".

Prior to Trump's intervention on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to his previous comments, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

News.title: Asos confirms hackers sent 'unauthorised' notification to app users
News.content:
Asos says it is investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms it uses after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers.

Dozens of people told the BBC they received the strange "ASOS HACKED" message from the clothing and beauty store's app on Tuesday morning - with some saying it left them "scared" to open the app.

The notification was addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams in what cyber security experts said looked like a "brazen" extortion attempt.

Asos acknowledged the "unauthorised customer notification" on Tuesday afternoon, saying some "basic personal information" may have been accessed.

In an email to customers on Tuesday night, the company apologised and urged customers not to engage with the notification. And it said the website and app are "operating as usual" promising customers they can "shop with confidence" while it investigates the incident.

The company has not as of yet informed the UK's data watchdog, the Information Commission's Office (ICO), about any breach.

Exactly how many Asos customers received the notification on Tuesday remains unclear, but Google's Play store says the ASOS app has been downloaded to android devices more than 10 million times.

The British retailer has a substantial global footprint - serving around 17 million customers each year across more than 150 markets.

Some Asos app users in Australia, France, Sweden and the Republic of Ireland had also received the notification, according to local reports on Tuesday.

Hackers seeking to pile pressure on potential victims by informing their customers is rare, as most extortions happen in private, so this incident may go down as a significant moment in cyber-attack history.

Shares in the company fell by around a tenth on Tuesday.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, called it a "deeply serious" and "brazen" attack whereby the hackers had apparently "turned Asos' own app into their ransom note".

But she told the BBC that Asos customers should not be "scared and frightened" - encouraging those worried to change their passwords, avoid clicking on the notification's link and be cautious about possible scam emails or texts.

News.title: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK, says Badenoch
News.content:
Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election.

The Conservative Party leader told the BBC that Nigel Farage's Reform are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another".

Polling suggests there would be a hung parliament at the next election, with Labour currently expected to be the largest party followed by Reform and the Tories.

As the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham nears its end, Badenoch has also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24-year-olds by halving the rate of employer national insurance (NI) contributions.

Badenoch has been trying to position the Conservatives as a party that is different to the one that suffered an historic defeat in the 2024 general election.

She told BBC Political Editor Chris Mason "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved" after she published a 100-page document, called The Right Way, setting out the party's principles, external.

Badenoch added "politics is volatile", as she tried to talk up the party's chances despite the polls suggesting only one-in-five voters would back them.

She said: "We're in a different political world, and it is within that context that we know that we can win. I'm not saying that we would win.

"The current polling shows a hung parliament, no party getting an overall majority.

"My prediction is that there would be another election immediately after. But we're the only credible alternative to Labour, the only ones with a plan."

A scenario was put to Badenoch in which the Conservatives would be the largest party and Reform have a significant presence in a hung parliament after the next election.

Asked if she would work with Reform in government, Badenoch replied: "If you want Conservative, you have to vote Conservative. I have said we'd have another election if there was no overall majority."

Badenoch added she wants Reform voters to "come back" to the Conservatives, saying people in Farage's party are "neck deep in scandal, it'd just be one problem after another".

She pointed to the arrest of Dan Thomas, who quit last month as Reform's leader in Wales after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour. Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong".

Badenoch also highlighted the case of Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform in Wales who was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after admitting taking bribes for pro-Russia interviews and speeches.

Farage has faced intense scrutiny over financial support he has received, including a Â£5m gift he received from a billionaire Reform donor before he became an MP. He has insisted he has done nothing wrong.

Badenoch added: "I want to get this economy growing, I want to make the country richer, I want to stop the boats, we've got a plan on borders, we've got a plan on welfare, we've got a plan on defence and bringing energy costs down.

"That's what we're about."

Privately, senior Conservatives talk of what they see as the importance of a potential 'tipping point' in support for the Conservatives and support for Reform UK.

Tories hope that if they can draw level and then establish a small lead over Reform in opinion polls, they can begin to make the case that they are the only viable alternative to Labour winning the next general election, potentially then attracting more support.

Badenoch has long said she wouldn't do a deal with Reform before the election, as it was a party trying to destroy the Conservatives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he was not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". The next one must be held by August 2029.

Farage has previously said Reform have "replaced the old fuddy-duddy existing Conservative Party".

News.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
News.content:
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (Â£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.

The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.

Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.

Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.

News.title: Watch: How Russia responded to US after plague researcher death
News.content:
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has urged people not to "listen to various rumours" after a Russian lab technician died at a plague research centre in Siberia.

Peskov called for people to follow only information from Russia's public health watchdog, which named the official cause of death of the lab technician as pneumonia of unknown origin.

BBC Russia editor Steve Rosenberg also asked Peskov about US President Donald Trump's offer of support to Russia.

News.title: PCs who used Taser and baton on amputee, 92, sacked
News.content:
Two police officers who pepper-sprayed and Tasered a 92-year-old amputee at a care home have been sacked for gross misconduct.

PC Stephen Smith and PC Rachel Comotto, who were both acquitted of assault occasioning actual bodily harm in May 2025, had been called to Park Beck care home in St Leonards-on-Sea after resident Donald Burgess threatened carers with a dinner knife.

Burgess, who had dementia, was hit with a baton, pepper sprayed and Tasered as he sat in his wheelchair in his bedroom in June 2022.

At Sussex Police headquarters in Lewes earlier, a disciplinary panel decided there had been "unjustified and excessive use of force" and dismissed both officers without notice.

Burgess was taken to hospital after the incident, where he contracted Covid and died 22 days later, but the officers were not held responsible for his death.

The misconduct panel found Comotto and Smith did not attempt to de-escalate the situation before using force and had breached standards of professional behaviour.

Both have been placed on the College of Policing's barred list.

News.title: Rise in babies in care proceedings raises fears of unnecessary adoptions, experts tell BBC
News.content:
Broadhurst acknowledges that term is "politically loaded" and the modern care system is very different from the coercive practices that took place mainly between 1949 and 1976 - and for which the government recently apologised for cases in England.

But she says it "is actually what's happening because parents do not agree".

"They want to continue to be in contact with a child," she says. "Even parents who feel they couldn't look after a child at that point find it particularly brutal that they're going to have no contact, or very little contact, with that child until they're 18."

One birth mother, Jean, tells us she never wanted to give up her daughter, Tye, for adoption - and describes it as "forced". Her local council says it followed a lawful process.

Jean was separated from her daughter for 16 years, after Tye was taken into care at 11 weeks' old and then adopted at the age of two.

Now, with Tye an adult, they are reunited. When she turned 18, having struggled with adoption and questions about her identity, Tye looked for her mother on social media.

"I knew I had a mum somewhere and it wasn't the people I was growing up with," she says - describing her adoption as something that had left her "completely alone" without a "whole chunk of heritage".

When Jean became pregnant, she was looking forward to being a mother. But she had concerns too: "The only thing I knew for certain was that I was disabled, I couldn't look after myself properly, so I wasn't sure how I was going to be able to look after a baby, so I needed help."

Her local authority at the time, Newham Council in east London, told her such help was not available, she says. Tye was put into foster care, but Jean was able to see her often.

There had been multiple assessments and residential placements as Jean tried to keep Tye. But professionals, including doctors and social workers, ultimately advised the court that Tye needed a stable, permanent family and that Jean could not provide it.

Jean says she fought and "gave it my all" through years of court proceedings. She even asked if she could have visiting rights, in a similar way to a parent in a divorce. "I was told that was an unrealistic expectation," she says.

News.title: Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect
News.content:
A Dunfermline childminder has admitted leaving more than 20 children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home.

Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court to neglect and abandoning children in her care.

Her offending took place at a number of locations in Dunfermline and elsewhere in Fife.

The court heard Mathewson had 27 children in her home, 19 more than she was licensed to look after.

Mathewson, who has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, was arrested by police following allegations of cruelty towards children.

The court heard she had provided childcare services at her home in Dunfermline for children under the age of 16.

At the time of her arrest she had 15 children aged under 12, 10 children under primary school age, and two children under the age of one in her care.

News.title: One million UK people who have never smoked are now vaping
News.content:
More than a million people who say they have never smoked are now vapers, latest data for 2025 reveals, external - up from around 940,000 in 2024.

People aged 25-34 are vaping more than any others, overtaking 16 to 24-year-olds, with 16.4% using e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.

For the second year in a row, more over-16s in Great Britain are using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

Meanwhile, the number of smokers in the UK continues to fall to nearly one in 10 adults, or 4.9 million people, down from 5.3 million in 2024, with more over-16s now vaping than smoking at 5.4 million.

News.title: Man charged with GP's murder
News.content:
A man has been charged with the murder of a GP who was found dead at her home.

The man was arrested after the body of 45-year-old Dr Hannah Terry, also known as Hannah Cain, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday.

Norfolk Police said 45-year old Mark Cain, of Fern Hill, Dersingham, has been charged with her murder.

He has been remanded in custody until a court appearance on Wednesday.

A notice on the website of Grimston Medical Centre, where Dr Terry is listed as a member of the practice team, said it was "temporarily closed due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team".

Tributes have been left outside the centre, including a teddy bear and flowers on a bench. A card from two patients reads: "Dear Dr Hannah Terry. We are so shocked and saddened to hear such tragic news."

News.title: Roll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates
News.content:
Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the government has announced.

On Tuesday, East Midlands Airport became the first airport to offer the new technology before it is rolled out to all UK airports by early 2027, the Home Office said.

The system uses facial technology so as passengers approach the e-gate, their photo is taken and then checked against immigration, travel and passport information and, if verfied, the barrier opens automatically.

Testing showed the new contactless system was up to 25% faster than using a passport, according to officials.

If further checks are needed, travellers will need to put their passport on the reader or may be directed to a Border Force officer.

Officers will continue to monitor all e-gates and offer assistance, while passengers should keep their passport with them at all times, the Home Office said.

News.title: Queen pays tribute to 'irrepressible' Jeffrey Archer
News.content:
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news".

"We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday.

Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently."

Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world."

Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed â and long remembered".

Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday.

Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form.

"He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience."

Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him."

Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer".

James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer.

Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company."

News.title: Iranian men accused of spying targeted journalists for 'serious violence', court hears
News.content:
Three Iranian men have gone on trial in London accused of spying for Iran on UK-based journalists, who were being targeted so "serious violence" could be inflicted on them.

The prosecution said Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, was to carry out the attack, with Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, doing the surveillance and reconnaissance. All three were born in Iran but were living in London.

The jury at Woolwich Crown Court heard that Sepahvand does not deny his involvement but said he did it out of fear of the consequences of refusing.

The prosecution said that is "an entirely bogus claim", adding that he did it for money and to have a criminal conviction for theft in Iran "fixed".

Sepahvand was in contact with two men with Iranian telephone numbers.

According to the prosecution, Manesh and Noori are expected to say they did not know they were carrying out surveillance on behalf of Iran.

All three face charges under the National Security Act, including "assisting a foreign intelligence service".

Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC said the men's targets were journalists working for Iran International - a Persian-language satellite channel that is critical of the Tehran regime and has its headquarters in London.

Jones said at least two journalists linked to Iran International were targeted in the surveillance.

He said at least one of them was to be "subjected to serious violence" as retribution and "to try to silence and deter others who might dare to voice their criticism".

Iran International, which broadcasts into Iran, has been declared as a "terrorist organisation" by Tehran.

"The evidence we will call illustrates that these three defendants carried out surveillance and reconnaissance, visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos, taking videos, doing online research about them," Jones said.

"The defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying," he added.

The men also allegedly had a "briefing sheet" on a barrister, Jonathan Turner, who was a founding member of a group called UK Lawyers for Israel.

One Iran International journalist who was allegedly targeted was Mojtaba Pourmohsen.

Images of him, his workplace and a hotel where he had lived were found in a "briefing document" on Sepahvand's mobile phone.

The prosecution says Noori took pictures of the block of flats Pourmohsen lived in in Brentford, southwest London, in December 2024.

It is also alleged that Sepahvand and Manesh went there to take photos and videos.

Another man targeted for surveillance was Kambiz Hosseini, the court heard.

The men even knew the name of his dog and the colour of his car, Jones said: "You can imagine the fear and psychological impact caused to him by discovering that all of those details about him, including the name of his dog, were known to the intelligence services."

Jones said Sepahvand's motivation was to try to resolve a criminal conviction he had in Iran for theft.

"He was not just in it for money. He quite explicitly wants something very particular in return for his work - he wanted his criminal conviction in Iran to be fixed," Jones told the jury.

The prosecution said Sepahvand's relationships with his contacts on Iran were not always good.

In one voice note he let out his frustration, saying: "This job is about committing an offenceâ¦ I'm supposed to put up my own money, put my own life at risk, put my car into it, put my time into it, leave my wife, leave my home, go chasing after their business, and in the end get completely screwed because of them."

He later said: "This is an illegal job. It's something that constitutes a criminal offence and it carries a heavy prison sentence.

"At the absolute minimum, they should transfer Â£10,000 for now."

The prosecution said that in total Sepahvand was to be paid Â£150,000 to find a target and to "finish them off".

The three men, who each had an interpreter in the dock, deny all the charges.

All three were granted temporary leave to remain in the UK after claiming asylum. They arrived in the UK between 2016 and 2022.

Sepahvand arrived in 2016 concealed in a lorry. The other two arrived in small boats.

The trial continues.

News.title: Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system
News.content:
The Conservatives have pledged to invest Â£10bn in a system to defend Britain against long-range missiles and drones, if they win the next general election.

The party said the "Britannia Shield" would offer the UK an integrated network of radar, command and control systems, as well as interceptor missiles.

The Tories initially said the system would be "in essence a British 'Iron Dome'", likening it to Israel's missile shield, however party leader Kemi Badenoch drew back from the comparison in broadcast interviews.

She said the plan would be funded from within their commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, paid for by welfare reform and reprioritisation of other spending.

Badenoch said that the Â£10bn cost would be split over 10 years, with Â£1bn allocated each year for the project.

Earlier this year, Gen Sir Richard Barrons told MPs on the Commons defence select committee "the cost of an iron dome at entry level is probably Â£80bn over 10 years".

Speaking to the BBC, Badenoch said: "We are not building the iron dome... we are designing something specific for the kind of threat that we face here."

She added: "It is not going to be the daily onslaught that Israel has, so we don't need that level of capability."

News.title: Christa Pike awake and speaking days after botched Tennessee execution
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Christa Pike, an inmate who survived Tennessee’s botched attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday evening.

“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement.

“Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” the statement continued.

Her attorneys said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her.” The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.

open image in gallery Christa Pike is alive and speaking nearly a week after a botched execution in Tennessee ( Reuters )

Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as Tennessee officials attempted to put her to death nearly a week ago last Wednesday.

On Sunday, her lawyer, assistant federal defender Stephen Ferrell, told CNN, “She's still in the hospital on a ventilator, critically ill. We don't really know the prognosis yet and may not know for several days.”

Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in a jealous rage in 1995. She became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row.

open image in gallery Christa Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of her 19-year-old Knoxville Job Corps classmate Colleen Slemmer ( Knoxville News-Sentinel )

open image in gallery Christa Pike was on a ventilator in the hospital after the botched execution ( AP )

Asked by CNN if she’d regained consciousness after the execution attempt, Ferrell replied: “Not that I’m aware of,” adding that doctors were still trying to clear the high barbiturate dosage out of her system.

Pike's execution was delayed for more than eight hours Wednesday as the U.S. Supreme Court considered, and ultimately overturned, a federal appeals court ruling to halt her lethal injection so judges could thoroughly review whether the jury that sentenced her to death should have considered sexual abuse she said she suffered as a child.
