Ronaldo left the national team squad in Copenhagen on the eve of a Nations League fixture against Denmark after he was an unused substitute for a 2-1 win away to Norway on September 27.

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner claims in his statement that Jesus had told him he would play 30 minutes against Norway on the day of the game only to go back on his word.

"Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn't called on," Ronaldo said. "The manager had broken his word to me."

Ronaldo and Jesus, who used to work together at Al Nassr, subsequently held a meeting, which was also attended by the sporting director of the Saudi Pro League club, Simao Coutinho.

According to Ronaldo's statement, Jesus agreed to clarify the situation and say that his captain never demanded minutes and that it was a mistake to let him warm up without bringing him on.

Ronaldo says an eight-point document was drawn up to summarise what had been discussed in a subsequent meeting between Jesus, Al Nassr sporting director Coutinho and Tiago Craveiro, the player's strategic adviser.

The eight points Ronaldo says Jesus agreed to say in his press conference 1. I myself, and no one else, proposed to Cristiano a plan for him this sporting season with the National Team. It was a long and very good conversation.

2. I know how much he lives and loves the national team and the weight he has in the world, and even more the weight and the positive influence he has had on the national team for 24 consecutive years.

3. The plan I proposed to Cristiano was accepted.

4. He never questioned my options. He was exemplary, loyal and professional.

5. The match in Norway was not part of the plan I drew up for him. However, I felt that he had managed to recover physically from the first match and I warned him that I might have to use him. Cristiano agreed.

6. I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game. If it were today I would not do it.

7. To close the subject: I want Cristiano in the National Team. In fact I do not want him a little, I want him a lot. Fortunately he also believes in me. He believed at Al Nassr and he does here as well.

8. About not greeting the fans. We have already spoken about that. Someone who has played more than 230 matches for the national team does not receive lessons from me on love for Portugal. It was a moment of frustration that erases nothing. He is the player who gives the most autographs, takes the most selfies, and shows the most affection to the fans. Let us not invent problems where they do not exist. When we are not happy we react.

However, Ronaldo felt the Portugal head coach's press conference bore no reflection to the conversation they had shared, which he claims ended in Jesus asking him for a hug.

"It was the second time he had broken his word to me," Ronaldo said. "I decided to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises."

Jesus denied that any such agreement had been made with the player in a later press conference on Sunday when he left the door open for Ronaldo to return to the Portugal fold.

Ronaldo apologised to his team-mates and the Portuguese people over his departure from the squad and said he will accept whatever punishment is handed down to him by the Portuguese Football Federation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cristiano Ronaldo returned to Al Nassr training after he left the Portugal squad. Pictures courtesy of @AlNassrFC.

The forward, who is his country's record appearance holder and goalscorer, also said he hopes his international career will not be limited to simply playing in a farewell game for Portugal.

Ronaldo added: "I have heard a great deal of talk about farewell matches, that I must have a dignified farewell and that the Federation wants to give me that opportunity. I learned in life, often hungry and with nothing to eat, that no one gives anything to anyone.

"I can promise all my fans, naturally and especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches; there will be time for that. But when I think of the national team, what I really think of is competing.

"That is what I thought on the day I was given the news of my father's death. I was at a camp with our national team and I decided to stay there until the end of the match the following day. I did for the country what I would never do for any club."

Sky Sports News has approached the Portuguese Football Federation for comment.

Sports.title: O'Neill confirms decision to stay on as Celtic boss
Sports.content:
Martin O'Neill has confirmed his decision to stay on as Celtic manager after reflecting on his future over the international break.

The Celtic manager admitted before the international break that he would consider his future after three consecutive defeats and talk to the board.

The 74-year-old has now declared himself up for the challenge after two defeats by Rangers sandwiched a Europa League setback against Ferencvaros.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Scottish Premiership match between Celtic and Rangers

When asked how ready and determined he was to lead the team forward, O'Neill told the club's Celtic Player: "I am. I'm extremely prepared for it.

"We had a difficult week. It can happen, you can lose to your arch-rivals, you can lose a European game.

"It's certainly not the end of the world, as it seemed to be described. But (I'm) ready to go.

"I did think I would take a little bit of time and it didn't take me that much time to think about it.

"I want to lead the club, I want to try and win the league, which is what we set out to do, and just as determined now as ever before.

"It was a time of reflection for a moment or two and, yes, some things that you think about.

"But overall, I'm back, I'm raring to go and the team's ready."

O'Neill, whose side face Motherwell at Fir Park on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, added: "What you try and do is analyse the things that you've done or perhaps the things that you haven't done.

"Throughout my managerial time, I've been exactly that. I think I look to myself, first of all. Maybe a wee bit different as a player, because I think I used to blame every other player for my own bad performance. But as a manager, you've got to look at yourself.

"And if you feel as if something has dropped away, of course you have to analyse it.

"Now, there wasn't a great deal in some of the games. If we get the equaliser just after half-time in the Rangers game, totally different ball game, totally different. But it wasn't to be. So you have to reflect on a few things like that.

"But overall, did the reflection, did all of that and a bit of self-analysing and just prepared for the battle."

O'Neill also revealed that Jota had played 45 minutes of a training-ground friendly against Falkirk on Friday, as the Portuguese winger steps up his comeback attempts following 18 months out with a knee injury.

The Celtic manager has also been encouraged by Alistair Johnston and Callum Osmand getting back on the training pitch following hamstring injuries.

O'Neill added he would assess the fitness of Hyun-Jun Yang on Friday after the South Korea winger experienced hamstring trouble on international duty.

Analysis: Celtic were always calm over O'Neill future

Sky Sports News' Anthony Joseph:

Martin O'Neill was never going to be sacked by Celtic after three humiliating defeats in one week before the international break - but there was a real potential of him walking away from the job.

After losing 1-0 at home to Rangers on September 20, O'Neill said he would take some time to think about whether he would continue as manager of the club.

Those comments sparked widespread reports and supporter speculation that the 74-year-old was on the verge of resigning.

Sky Sports News understands Celtic have always remained calm about the situation, despite the recent results. There was no appetite to pull the trigger themselves, especially when the teams are sitting at the top of the league.

That was proven when Celtic CEO Michael Nicholson backed O'Neill in a statement announcing the club's latest financial results. He said: "We will now come together and support Martin and the players, as we focus our efforts on achieving success domestically and in the Europa League."

The ball has been completely in O'Neill's court and - as he has said today - he very quickly indicated his intention and desire to stay.

Celtic face a tricky next five games back - Motherwell away (live on Sky Sports), Benfica away, Hearts at home (live on Sky Sports), Celta Vigo at home and Hibernian away (live on Sky Sports).

It's going to be an interesting month ahead for O'Neill and Celtic.

Sports.title: 'FIA to blame for F1's Bahrain GP software farce'
Sports.content:
David Croft has criticised the FIA for the chaotic formation lap scenes at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, describing a software glitch that saw several drivers slowing to a crawl or stopping completely as a "farce".

F1 and the FIA have new technical regulations this year which saw the introduction of a new power unit which is almost 50 per cent electric.

Sepang saw the first wet conditions of the season, and the FIA later confirmed that a combination of low engine speeds, low grip, wet-weather energy-management settings and the configuration of the circuit had caused an unintended loss of power.

Speaking on the F1 Show podcast, Sky Sports F1 commentator Croft questioned why such a scenario had not been simulated before the season began.

"We had a shakedown in Barcelona and six days of testing in Bahrain before the season started. Why on earth were situations like this not tried out before we went racing?" he said.

"Nikolas Tombazis [FIA single-seater director] says there are bugs all the time with software. Behind the scenes, people are working on those bugs, and what they try and do is do updates during the night time when people aren't actually using their computers.

"Not during the course of a Grand Prix, when someone has now suddenly realised we've got a situation on our hands.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit.

"Before the start of the race, it looked like it was the day where we were going to break the duck and have some wet weather running.

"We've had dry weather all the time, so we've had plenty of time to simulate this, to stop it happening in front of hundreds of millions of people during the course of a race.

"This falls on the FIA. I'm sorry, but you are the governing body. You are supposed to have the upper hand when it comes to these rules and regulations, the directives, the power units and everything.

"You weren't on top of things when it came to that race, and it was a farce."

When the drivers left the pit lane following a rain-delayed start, several almost ground to a halt, including race leader Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, with numerous other drivers in the midfield also experiencing issues.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chaotic formation lap halts race start at Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

The unusual scenes left spectators and viewers unsure what was happening, with the aborted start followed by a lengthy wait while the problem was resolved.

The FIA said its emergency software fix took around 20 minutes to issue and install, although the overall disruption was considerably longer.

"We had no idea why those cars were going so slowly," Croft said. "We had no idea why we were waiting around for 40 minutes to get a race on.

"There's a lot going on, and we need to understand and appreciate that the FIA are trying to keep across a million and one different things.

"But sometimes taking a step back, identifying issues that could come during a season, during a scenario, and taking preventative measures is the best way forward, rather than just trying to react on the spur of the moment.

"I want to see a bit more strategic thinking when it comes to these sorts of issues.

"Let's go through other simulations, FIA, and other things that could go wrong with these power units. Let's get the bugs fixed and get the simulations in place now."

Tombazis acknowledged after the race that the software had not been tested sufficiently in the specific conditions encountered at Sepang.

The FIA added that the issue had not been detected during testing or the laps to the grid and has promised a full review with the teams and power-unit manufacturers.

The controversy ultimately overshadowed what became an eventful and competitive Grand Prix as Verstappen emerged victorious, with Kimi Antonelli second and Hamilton completing the podium after a dramatic recovery.

"I don't want that for the sport that I love. I actually want people to be talking about great racing.

"That's what we should be talking about, but these issues need addressing."

Sports.title: Was it right to default Medvedev for hitting spectator with ball?
Sports.content:
Daniil Medvedev was defaulted for hitting a spectator with the ball during his semi-final with Novak Djokovic at the China Open, but was it the correct decision or should he have been able to continue playing?

Medvedev was trailing Djokovic 7-5 5-3 and had lost a point when he hit the ball coming off the wall.

The spectator, who was ​sitting in the first row behind Medvedev, clutched his left eye and appeared to ‌be in pain as he walked out of the gallery, assisted by stadium staff.

Medvedev did not protest the umpire's decision to disqualify him.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Jonathan Overend said: "From the first camera angle we saw the ball leaving Medvedev's racket and weren't sure where it had gone, but I later saw a different angle filmed from the stands and it clearly went straight from the racket into the face of this spectator and so from the minute that was obvious, it was an instant default.

"It was absolutely the correct decision. The rulebook is very clear about that and it was unfortunate for Medvedev. We take him at face value when he says he didn't mean to do it, but it did leave his racket with force and it did strike the spectator.

"It appeared to me that umpire Mohamed Lahyani appeared initially to be uncertain about whether or not to default him but it was only when the supervisor got involved and further views were taken into account that it was clear that it did strike the spectator on the full and disqualification was the correct decision and clearly everyone on court felt that regrettably was the right course of action."

Overend described Medvedev as a "curious character" with the former US Open champion mimicking Djokovic being tired or injured on court which he felt "didn't feel appropriate" in such a match and such an opponent.

"For the disqualification to happen a few games later, it was out of character in the sense that I haven't seen him do that before but with Medvedev over the years you expect the unexpected and there is a certain volatility to him so maybe we shouldn't have been too surprised," he said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Djokovic vs Medvedev at the China Open

'He wouldn't intentionally hit a spectator'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking after progressing to the China Open final, Djokovic has his say on how his match against Medvedev ended, after the Russian was defaulted for hitting a spectator with a ball

Johanna Konta also feels Medvedev was "unfortunate" to have been defaulted after watching numerous replays of the incident.

The former British No 1 said: "I can almost with certainty say he wouldn't intentionally hit a spectator with a ball. However, we have seen him do other things out of frustration from kicking the microphone, smashing rackets, and mouthing off.

"He's got quite a vocabulary on him, so it's not out of character for him to get frustrated but he obviously misjudged the angle of his racket, he misjudged the height of the backboard, he misjudged his whole surroundings.

"Frustration I wouldn't necessarily say is conducive to clarity of mind, so more than anything if you're feeling angry and frustrated, you won't necessarily be in control of your ability as if you weren't, so he wouldn't have intentionally done that."

Overend claims you have take Medvedev at "face value" with people believing he did not do it intentionally. When reviewing the footage, he said: "I don't think you're saying for certain that he's not doing that deliberately because he hits it at pace.

"He slices it but it is travelling at pace. He's intentionally coming right under the ball to stun it, but then he plays a really bad shot."

Konta said: "Medvedev was caught in between when you slice and you try and hit it back to you against just hitting it flat against the backboard, but I think he realises that the ball kid is there and I think if you're frustrated and you're thinking 'I can't hit the backboard because if it hits the ball kid I'm going to get defaulted' I wonder if he got caught in no-man's land and that's why it looks in between two shots because where he has hit it is right above the ball kid's head.

"I cannot see Medvedev doing it intentionally. I cannot imagine what that felt like in the pit of his stomach."

Do the ATP need to unify the criteria once and for all?

"Where tennis has to be careful here is making sure there isn't a grey area with regards to this rule," explained Overend.

"I think back to the Winston-Salem final of 2024 which was when Alex Michelsen launched a ball like Medvedev into the spectators, very, very close to the court, but then the umpire went over to the spectators to see whether anybody had been hit directly and because it didn't appear to hit anybody directly or injure them, Michelsen, who was absolutely convinced that he was going to get defaulted from that match was effectively let off and he was allowed to continue.

"That to me is a grey area because that is almost saying the severity of the impact dictates whether the player is disqualified or not.

"Tennis has got to be quite careful that if there is a rule in place here, which there is, it's enforced with consistency. In my opinion, launching a ball at pace, into spectators, is an instant disqualification and has to be for the safety of everyone. Players have been defaulted for less, let's put it this way!"

Sports.title: UEFA monitoring Man City case as it considers potential action
Sports.content:
UEFA is monitoring developments and will wait until the end of the Premier League's disciplinary process before deciding whether to take any potential action against Manchester City.

City have been found guilty by an independent commission of breaking the Premier League's financial rules between 2009 and 2018, including five charges of failing to comply with UEFA's Financial Fair Play rules.

UEFA financial rules at the time meant clubs were effectively limited to spending what they earned within set break-even requirements.

The independent commission found that City's owners put in £830m of their own money and disguised it as sponsorship income for nine seasons.

City are appealing against the decision and maintain they have a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence which will clear their name.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kaveh Solhekol explains how the other Premier League clubs are reacting to Manchester City's rule breaches ahead of the appeal process

In 2014, City entered into a settlement agreement with UEFA which included a £49m (£32m of which was suspended) fine after they were charged with breaking Financial Fair Play rules.

In 2020, City were found guilty of breaking UEFA's Financial Fair Play rules, fined €30m (£25.4m) and banned from playing in European competitions for two years.

City appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sports and the ban was overturned, with CAS ruling that UEFA had not established that City's owners had disguised equity funding as sponsorship contributions, while other breaches were time-barred.

CAS reduced City's fine from €30m (£25.4m) to €10m (£8.5m) for failing to co-operate with the UEFA investigation and stated that most of the alleged breaches "were either not established or time barred".

UEFA has a statute of limitations of five years for financial rule breaches, whereas the Premier League does not have a statute of limitations.

UEFA's case was triggered by hacked City emails which were published by German magazine Der Spiegel in 2018.

City said the internal documents were "out-of-context materials purportedly hacked or stolen" as part of an "organised and clear attempt to damage the club's reputation".

The Premier League investigation had access to documents and evidence which were not available to UEFA when it were building its case against City.

City and UEFA have been contacted for comment.

Analysis: How long will Man City's appeal take?

Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol:

"The appeal went in on Thursday at 7pm and so, according to the Premier League's rules, the appeal has to be done and dusted in 12 weeks from then, which takes us into the week before Christmas.

"The appeal can only last five days and those five days can only be in one block.

"The appeal panel, which has to be a different three-person panel from the original panel, would have 30 days to make up their minds and deliver their judgement. That would take you into the third week of January.

"Now that is the speeded-up timeline which has been introduced into the Premier League's rules this season.

"Now, Man City could argue that this speeded-up timeline should not apply in this case because this case has been going on for years and this new rule has only been introduced this season. That is something to look out for."

Details of Man City's appeal strategy explained

Latest from Sky Sports News' Lyall Thomas:

Manchester City are likely to argue as part of their appeal that the extra funding for their sponsorship deals came from the Abu Dhabi government rather than the club's owners, Sky Sports News understands.

City's lawyers argued during the 2024 hearing that the funding had come from the Abu Dhabi government, but this was rejected by the independent commission, which "concluded it was an explanation that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme".

However, it is understood City are expected to continue contesting this argument.

Manchester City is majority owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan's Newton Investment and Development LLC. Sheikh Mansour is also a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi and he is the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

The separation of UAE state investment and those that are private from the Abu Dhabi royal family has long been a subject of debate and criticism.

What did the independent commission find?

Manchester City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

The club filed accounts that concealed the true state of its finances.

Manchester City were significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits and broke "well over 100" Premier League regulations.

Manchester City failed to co-operate and act in good faith towards the league during the investigation, with three out of four alleged breaches upheld and one charge not proven.

The commission also said it was "regrettable" that a decision had taken so long to reach, with the hearing having taken place between September and December 2024.

City: Process was not impartial

Following the publication of the guilty verdict on September 29, a Manchester City statement read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Manchester City's statement erroneously refers to a Premier League commission. It is an independent commission.

Why Man City's appeal could drag into 2027

Latest from Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol and Amar Mehta:

Manchester City's appeal could drag on into next year if they argue that the process should not be run according to Premier League rules which were introduced for this season.

City have filed their appeal and the new rules about appeals state that this part of the disciplinary process has to be concluded within 12 weeks and the appeal hearing can last no longer than five days.

City's lawyers could argue that they were charged in 2023 and a hearing was held in 2024 - when the rules about a speeded-up appeals process were not in the Premier League Handbook.

A legal expert told Sky Sports News Manchester City would have a strong case for arguing that the new rules should not apply in this case.

The new rules were introduced to ensure that clubs, where possible, were punished in the same season as relevant rule breaches.

Sports.title: Harry Kane doubles up on landmark night as England cruise past Czechia
Sports.content:
It was a night that belonged to Harry Kane. Yet another one. It began with him being shown a replay of his first England goal during a pre-match interview with ITV – the header against Lithuania in 2015, just 79 seconds after he came on as a substitute for his debut. It ended with him reflecting on two more in what was a supremely comfortable Nations League victory over Czechia. Some things never change.

It remains a numbers game for Kane. They are getting bigger and ever more impressive. On the ­occasion of his 125th cap, the one that took him level with Peter Shilton at the top of the all-time England list, he moved to an astonishing 91 goals. Nobody will be surprised if he reaches the century. The only question appears to be when.

England know how to beat the game’s smaller fry. Under Thomas Tuchel, they have played 16 matches against teams ranked outside the world’s top 20. They have won 15 and drawn one – against Ghana at the World Cup. They have conceded only once – against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, also at the World Cup. Czechia, who are ranked No 50, were never in the contest.

Kane is similarly inevitable. The captain even claimed the assist for the breakthrough goal with a cross into the corridor of uncertainty that spooked Vladimir Coufal so severely he shot into his own net. Kane’s passing was very good. When he was withdrawn in the 82nd minute, he left to a great ovation.

The victory meant that England virtually guaranteed their progress into the Nations League quarter-finals and, perhaps more importantly, saw them close out this elongated window with plenty of optimism. One of the main goals was to put as much distance as possible between themselves and the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina. It was mission accomplished.

Kane will break the caps record when England host Croatia in November and that will be the night when he is truly feted. As an aside, he would want to do it at Wembley rather than in Madrid against Spain where England’s next-but-one game will be staged. Was that why he was so keen to play in all four of the matches during this window? It might have been a part of it.

Then again, Kane always wants to play. He was one of only three England players to start each of the matches in this series. The others were Manchester City’s Marc Guéhi and Elliot Anderson. Was the City manager, Enzo Maresca, happy about that? Probably not. Does he have bigger problems at the moment? Yes.

Kane’s act of drawing level with Shilton was the box-office detail. His name was on everybody’s lips; his face on the big screen before kick-off. He was pictured alongside Shilton when his name was read out with the teams. The Wembley crowd roared.

Kane was at the heart of the opening goal, providing the teasing cross from the right and it was some finish from the player just inside the six-yard box. One that Kane would have been happy to call his own. The problem from a Czechia point of view was that it came from their right-back. Coufal could feel Eberechi Eze at his back as he faced towards his own goal, albeit the England winger was not that close. Coufal stretched and everybody had the time to have the same thought: you do not have to do this. Coufal did it. He could not check his momentum and steered firmly past his goalkeeper.

View image in fullscreen Czechia’s Vladimir Coufal scores an own goal to put England ahead. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

Trent Alexander-Arnold, who Tuchel recalled at right-back, was involved in the buildup and he caught the eye, especially when surging up and inside. He repeatedly got into advanced areas and there was one moment in the first half when he stormed into the No 9 position on to an Anderson pass. He just could not bring it under his spell. Alexander-Arnold had extended Lukas Hornicek with a whipped free-kick at the outset.

Jude Bellingham was excellent. Of course he was. There were fizzed passes from him that took the breath, getting England into dangerous positions, including one for Morgan Rogers in the 25th minute that the Chelsea attacker wasted. There were those strutting runs and it was Bellingham, as much as anybody, who advertised the fact that England were going to break through.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Anderson should have made it 2-0 after a Bellingham lay-off; Kane sparked the move and Alexander-Arnold’s cross drove it. The second goal arrived before half-time and it had to be Kane. It would have been all about the buildup were it not for the identity of the scorer. Anderson’s lofted ball up the inside right was a beauty and Rogers’ first-time cross on the half-volley was even better, cut unerringly towards you-know-who in the middle. Kane was unmarked. Hornicek was helpless.

Kane wanted more. As usual. He got it. As usual. There was the moment shortly after the restart when he unloaded from the edge of the area and watched the shot kiss the top of the crossbar. Hornicek was beaten. Then he was for real.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane’s header puts England 3-0 up at Wembley. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

It was Lewis Hall – impressive at left-back – who swung over the corner, which came after Hornicek kept out an audacious Bellingham flick. Only Jiri Slama knows why he gave Kane so much room in front of goal. It was always going to end badly for the Czechia defender. Kane rose and the header had too much power for Hornicek.

There was the minor irritation for Tuchel when Myles Lewis-Skelly got himself booked in the 53rd minute for pulling back Pavel Sulc. The midfielder will be suspended for England’s next game and it was certainly not a great idea for him to get in the face of Michal Sadilek shortly afterwards. Sadilek had fouled Rogers and was booked. It was a needless risk from Lewis-Skelly.

England toyed with Czechia in the second half with Eze running through some of his party tricks. It was Kane who provided the substance.

Sports.title: Sturm warning for Pocognoli as abject Scotland turned over by Slovenia
Sports.content:
This now constitutes a rocky start for Sébastien Pocognoli as Scotland’s manager.

The claiming of four points from three Nations League games was adequate until Slovenia inflicted this defeat. It was the abject nature of Scotland’s display this time that was so stark. Pocognoli’s team were comprehensively outplayed by a side who themselves are no better than functional.

November feels significant for Pocognoli. Put simply, Slovenia met a Scotland who were far, far too easy to play against. Pocognoli has to prove this is the dawn of a new era as opposed to the beginning of an error. This is no patient football domain.

A pre-match presentation to Andy Robertson, who reached the 100-cap mark during Scotland’s win in North Macedonia on Saturday, carried wider meaning. Gordon Strachan and Alex McLeish, Robertson’s first two Scotland managers, were joined on the Hampden pitch by Steve Clarke. This marked a swift and welcome return to the national stadium for Clarke, who departed the Scotland job in unsatisfactory circumstances following failings at the World Cup. Clarke, bashful by nature, took as significant a bow as he was ever likely before supporters but Robertson’s warmth towards the Ayrshireman was clear.

Scotland find themselves in a post-Clarke state of flux. He was the manager who made this nation relevant on the wider stage once again. There was, however, a widespread criticism that Clarke’s team lacked ambition. Pocognoli has been charged not only with maintaining at least decent results while delivering an alternative brand of football. It remains to be seen whether the dual quest is fanciful or not.

The first quarter of the game mirrored the opening half when these teams met in Ljubljana. Scotland looked uncertain and ragged. Slovenia were perfectly comfortable, not only in a defensive sense but when springing into attack. Adam Cerin should have afforded the visitors a 13th-minute lead but failed to connect with appropriate force, allowing Jack Hendry to boot clear when just three yards from his own goal. This venue, which should be an asset to Scotland, was eerily quiet.

Ryan Christie raised the mood. That the goal was horribly ugly mattered not a jot to anyone of a Scottish persuasion. A short free-kick was played wide to Ben Gannon-Doak, whose deflected cross was headed on to a post by Hendry. Modern football’s madness means Oli McBurnie will be credited with an assist for the header he was undoubtedly trying to score with. The ball instead landed at the feet of Christie, who flicked it home from close range. Christie will be a bigger asset to Pocognoli than he initially appeared to realise. Here, the Bournemouth player supplied breathing space.

Robertson demonstrated his ongoing value before the break. Zan Vipotnik seemed certain to equalise before the Tottenham left-back’s rescue act, courtesy of a sliding block. Ominously for Scotland, Danijel Sturm had totally bamboozled their three-man defence when supplying Vipotnik.

View image in fullscreen Scotland’s Sébastian Pocognoli looks away in horror on the touchline. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

It was impossible to argue Slovenia were not worthy of their equaliser, which landed 11 minutes after half-time. It came from a Scotland throw-in, where possession was cheaply conceded. Sturm played through the centre and towards Aljosa Matko, who brushed Luis Binks aside as if the Brøndby defender was not even there. The Scotland goalkeeper, Angus Gunn, as is something of a theme, was weak in trying to deal with Matko’s shot. Sturm should have sent Slovenia in front two minutes later but saved the blushes of a hilariously open Scotland defence by shooting over. This had to be alarming for Pocognoli.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

McBurnie’s withdrawal meant 20 caps have come and gone for the Hull striker without scoring. With 70 minutes played, this felt like the least of Scotland’s worries. Slovenia were comprehensively outplaying their hosts. Pocognoli switched to a back four for the first time in this elongated international window shortly before Matko was denied his second goal of the night by an offside flag. The decision was not at all debatable.

Neither was the goal which took Slovenia ahead. This time Matko turned supplier, having rampaged down the right flank and crossed for the onrushing Sturm. Gunn was left with no chance as Sturm slammed the ball past him. For the first time in his brief tenure, Pocognoli was subjected to Tartan Army boos.

Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake were denied claims for Scotland penalties. McPake was lively having stepped from the bench. Too many of his teammates either underperformed or are not cut out for this level. It is up to Pocognoli, and sharply, to source answers.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo accuses Portugal coach Jorge Jesus of broken promises
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has accused the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, of twice breaking his word, saying a failed agreement to publicly explain ⁠his omission against Norway drove him out of the camp but insisting he remained available after any punishment.

In a lengthy statement, the 41-year-old gave his ⁠account of the dispute ⁠that prompted his ​departure from Copenhagen before Portugal’s Nations League match against Denmark last week.

Ronaldo said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would ⁠miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 ⁠minutes.

“Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn’t called ​on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager had broken his ‌word to me.”

Portugal’s captain and ‌all-time leading scorer said a subsequent meeting with Jesus, attended by his club side Al-Nassr’s sporting ‌director Simão Coutinho, produced an agreement for the coach to clarify events at his next press conference.

According to Ronaldo, an eight-point document was prepared saying he had never demanded playing time, had respected Jesus’s decisions and that the coach asking him to warm up without bringing him on had been a mistake. Ronaldo said the agreed notes did not require Jesus to apologise to him ‌but said the coach’s public remarks bore no resemblance to their private discussion.

“It was the second time he had broken his word to me,” Ronaldo said. “I decided ​to leave the training camp without waiting for any further broken promises.”

The statement provided Ronaldo’s account but on Sunday, after Portugal’s win over Norway, Jesus denied he had made any agreement with the player but left the door open for his return.

The Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) did not immediately respond to a request for ⁠comment about Ronaldo’s statement.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Ronaldo apologised for failing to greet supporters after the Norway ​match and for leaving his ​teammates, accepting that his captaincy made ​his conduct more serious. “The consequences of my actions must be assessed and punished ​by the Portuguese Football ‌Federation,” he said.

Despite ​the rupture, Ronaldo said ​he was not limiting his international ambitions to a farewell appearance. “If I’m physically fit, playing for my club – scoring goals, I hope – after serving whatever suspension is imposed on me, I’ll be available, as I’ve always been until now, to compete and win for our national team,” he added.

Sports.title: Fifa reportedly allowed DR Congo into World Cup despite ineligible player in qualifying
Sports.content:
Fifa allowed the Democratic Republic of the Congo to compete at this summer’s World Cup despite reports suggesting an internal investigation found that the country had fielded an ineligible player in qualifying.

The player in question, the goalkeeper Lionel Mpasi, starred for his nation at the tournament, including against England in the last 32. Mpasi, who was born in France and played for Les Bleus at youth level, had never completed the process of switching nationalities, Fifa reportedly found. No punishment was levied against the Congolese federation, Fecofa.

The news will again raise questions over the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, with a series of governance scandals having brought heightened scrutiny on his position. Fifa’s investigative teams are independent and the president has no input into their proceedings. Fifa is understood to have denied that Infantino played a part in the decision-making process over Mpasi, but his name is likely to remain in focus owing to a former university associate, Véron Mosengo-Omba, being elected unopposed as president of Fecofa this May.

The Nigerian Football Federation submitted a complaint over the DRC apparently fielding ineligible players during a World Cup playoff tie between the nations, which the DRC won on penalties, in November.

According to reporting by the New York Times and Le Monde, Fifa investigators were aware of Mpasi’s situation before the DRC defeated Jamaica in a final intercontinental playoff round in March. Faced with a series of possible responses, including banning the DRC from the playoffs, Fifa chose to reject the Nigeria complaint on the grounds it had not been submitted within the necessary timeframe.

Nigeria appealed against the decision and government representatives have suggested they could seek financial compensation for their loss, with a member of the national sports commission , which regulates Nigerian sport, telling ESPN: “Nothing has been decided yet, but we will seriously consider seeking compensation from Fifa for all of the economic losses this has cost Nigeria.”

Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation, which includes Jamaica among its members, said it “takes player eligibility matters very seriously and expects the applicable regulations and procedures to be applied consistently and fairly in all competitions”. In a statement it asked that any “concerns regarding player eligibility” be “thoroughly reviewed and addressed through Fifa’s appropriate governance and disciplinary bodies”.

Fifa, Concacaf, Caf, the Nigeria Football Federation and Fecofa, were all approached for comment.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

On Tuesday the Norwegian football federation confirmed it had submitted a three-pronged complaint to Fifa over its governance, including the decision to overturn a red card awarded to the USA’s Folarin Balogun after a telephone intervention by Donald Trump. The other instances cited by the NFF are the Fifa peace prize and the abandoned plan to sell a share in the World Cup to investors, known as the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme.

“Each of these cases must be assessed based on the facts of each individual case,” said the president of the NFF, Lise Klaveness. “At the same time, the cases point to a more fundamental question: has Fifa’s position, authority or influence been used in a way that was not appropriate, and if so, did the mechanisms that were supposed to prevent this function work as they should?”

Sports.title: Too nice: do Arsenal lack the grit and tenacity to end WSL title drought?
Sports.content:
Arsenal, 10 points adrift of the Women’s Super League leaders, are poised to undertake a “big review” of their season during this international break to try to determine where things have gone so horribly wrong – again – in the early stages. After their 4-2 loss at Manchester City on Sunday, it felt as if the agenda needs to include an unusual but potentially critical question: is this team nasty enough to win a WSL title?

The technical ability throughout the world-class squad Arsenal have assembled could hardly be higher but the levels of grit, resilience and tenacity need examining in a group that appears unable to match Chelsea and Manchester City when it comes to the mental aspects of a title race. Arsenal last won the WSL in 2019.

When speaking to sources close to the Arsenal players, it is common to hear of the squad being like a “family”, very supportive of each other and full of “great people”. Those admirable traits, and a general sense the club is full of nice characters, often come across when watching games or during player interviews. Arsenal have built a team of good eggs; polite, courteous and professional individuals who people would be glad to call friends. In the vast majority of scenarios in life this is, quite obviously, a good thing. But are they too nice to beat City?

It is quite hard to imagine many of the Arsenal squad raising their voices in anger. It is equally hard to recall the last time anybody at the club engaged in so-called “housery”; perhaps not since Katie McCabe’s hair pull against Chelsea in last season’s Champions League quarter-final. The irony is that McCabe is one of the senior, influential players who left this summer – in her case to join Chelsea – and McCabe, regardless of what fans might think of her, is someone Arsenal could rely on to roll up her sleeves and get stuck in, to raise her game in a hostile atmosphere and be combative.

Last term, no Arsenal players – not even McCabe – registered in Stats Perform’s list of the top 20 WSL players for percentage of duels won. Only one Arsenal player has been shown a red card in a WSL game since 2021-22. Admirable discipline, yes, but are they lacking that fire in the belly?

This season, the team appear to be without a dogged, refuse-to-lose type of character in the mould of Lucy Bronze, whose never-say-die attitude has frequently come to England’s aid in crucial moments at major tournaments; or the gritty battling spirit of Erin Cuthbert, who has helped Chelsea lift seven league titles; or – to take an Arsenal example – a leader such as Gabriel Magalhães, a rock for others to lean on during tough games.

It is possible to be successful without a Roy Keane in your squad and Arsenal do have Leah Williamson, who has led England to two European titles, so it would be wrong to imply there is no leadership in this group. Leaders can step up in different ways but recently Renée Slegers, when praising her senior players’ reactions to their disappointing draw in Paris, mentioned there had been “lots of hugs” and praised how supportive everybody had been for each other. That sounds like the sort of unified workplace culture millions would envy, but to win titles sometimes you need to fall out, yell, be angry and demand higher standards.

View image in fullscreen Only one Arsenal player has been shown a red card in a WSL game since 2021-22. Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/WSL Football/Getty Images

On Friday I asked Slegers whether Arsenal had enough of a nasty edge to win the league, and she replied defiantly: “I think so, and nastiness or that grittiness, that can express itself in different ways, and I think we have certain ways in which we express that and [in] which we can do that. But of course, with our performances where we haven’t been at our best, you maybe don’t see those moments as much which we can bring, but we’re convinced that we can bring that to games as well, in our way, the Arsenal way, because it’s definitely there.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That was not evident on Sunday in the little – but important – moments, such as shortly after Arsenal had twice taken a lead they would surrender. City seemed unfazed and carried the resolve of a team who had no doubt they would win.

Part of the way that belief has been instilled into the defending champions was evidenced in a clip, released by Sky Sports, of Andrée Jeglertz’s pre-match team talk, which he concluded with the words: “The most important thing: we are Manchester City, we are playing at home and we are winning this game.” The matter-of-fact, defiant instruction was not easy to imagine hearing in this Arsenal dressing room with any real conviction right now, not from the players and not from Slegers, who has many excellent qualities as coach, and is, by all accounts, an intelligent, detail-oriented coach of whom the players are very fond.

In decades to come, all the nice characteristics this Arsenal squad demonstrate will no doubt stand them in good stead in the real world, with their friendships, but the cliche “nice guys finish last” is starting to feel increasingly appropriate for this amiable side.

Sports.title: Football Daily | South Korea’s golden boys and a brouhaha over military service
Sports.content:
FINAL DRAFT

In his 1965 song Draft Dodger Rag, Phil Ochs detailed the occasionally ludicrous lengths some young American men went to avoid conscription to the military. While he listed ruptured spleens, poor eyesight and flat feet as more mundane ailments, mentions of bone spurs (Donald J Trump), conscientious objecting (Muhammad Ali) and 30-day hygiene protests (Ted Nugent) were all conspicuous by their absence from the protest singer’s lyrics. Ochs almost certainly had no idea that the best way to avoid the draft in South Korea is to be really good at sport.

Monday’s Football Daily revealed that mere seconds after captaining his country to gold at the Asian Games, Lee Gi-hyuk was overcome with an ill-advised urge to publicly brag how victory meant he could not be drafted for military service. The South Korea skipper was joined in his tone-deaf celebrations by teammates Yang Min-hyuk (of Tottenham) and Park Seung-soo (of Newcastle). Their exemption came on the back of a government promise offering any podium-toppers from South Korea a free pass from their 18 to 21 months of obligatory service to be conducted before they turn 35. The subsequent public outcry was deafening, no doubt prompted by the vast majority of able-bodied South Koreans who don’t get so lucky, as well as South Koreans who view conscription as a duty to be honoured, rather than a hardship to avoid at any cost.

“I got caught up in the happiness, adrenaline and excitement of the moment,” simpered Lee in his subsequent apology. “I am deeply sorry to the fans who are currently fulfilling their military duty, as well as to all those who sincerely supported us.” While the defender promised to reflect on his behaviour, it has now emerged he may also be forced to ponder the notion that he has potentially kiboshed future opportunities for other athletes to take advantage of an exemption that has been in place for more than 50 years. It seems South Korea’s Ministry of National Defence was already reviewing plans to completely abolish special sports exemptions and his post-match braying is likely to accelerate the process, making him as popular as a rattlesnake buried in a game of lucky dip.

“Ultimately, we have plans to cut back or scrap the supplementary service, including one designed for artists and athletes, and reflect it in the basic outline for defence reforms,” droned a military suit. “From the perspective of the defence ministry, we are deeply sorry for the remarks made by some people in the sports industry.” Despite their victory, South Korea’s gold medallists will still have to complete three weeks of basic training and 544 hours of community service for their country. Given their high profiles and ill-advised boasting, Football Daily suspects these recruits can look forward to no end of barked orders, miles of marching on the drill square and an unnaturally high allocation of cleaning duties in the latrine.

Sports.title: Union Berlin’s Marie-Louise Eta: ‘I wanted to impress through my work, not because I am a woman’
Sports.content:
In April Marie-Louise Eta became the first woman to lead a men’s top-flight team in one of Europe’s big five leagues, stepping in as interim head coach of Union Berlin following the dismissal of Steffen Baumgart. Her job was to keep Union in the Bundesliga and she did just that with two wins, a draw and two losses in her five games. They finished 11th.

It was not the first time the trailblazer had made history. Three years earlier she had become the first woman to serve as an assistant coach in the men’s Bundesliga and in 2024 she led the Union men’s team in one game. The Bayern Munich manager, Vincent Kompany, described her appointment as something that could open doors for younger women who want to become coaches.

This season Eta is in charge of the Union women’s side and, trying to take stock of a momentous 12 months, the 35-year-old tells Moving the Goalposts: “For me, it was never about being the first. It quickly became clear that it wasn’t about making history, but about supporting a team and achieving success together once again.”

There was a lot of media attention on her gender and she says her first matches were not “just about football at that time, but also very much about the issue of women in the game”. It was, she admits, very intense. Union lost their first two games, against Wolfsburg and RB Leipzig, but then came a draw against Cologne and a 3-1 victory at Mainz. At full-time, Eta punched the air and joined her players in applauding Union’s fans. She ended her spell with a 4-0 victory over Augsburg.

“I wanted to impress through my work, my performance and my approach as a manager, not because I’m a woman or because I’m supposed to represent or embody something special,” she says. “I wanted to be judged by the same standards as my male colleagues.”

When she was appointed there was sexist and derogatory abuse on social media, which the club publicly condemned and described as “embarrassing and insane”. There was also a lot of positivity, however, and Eta says women and girls messaged her to say that her journey had encouraged them.

View image in fullscreen Eta received a huge amount of attention during her five-game stint, both good and bad. Photograph: Alex Grimm/Getty Images

“My hope is that my journey will encourage young girls to believe in their own potential and to pursue their goals,” she says. “If I can play even a small part in opening further doors, I’ll be very pleased. Ultimately, however, it shouldn’t be gender that decides, but performance and the quality of the work.”

What did she learn? “It is important to stay true to yourself and remain clear-headed. As a coach, it’s not just about tactics and football, but above all about bringing people along with you, giving them confidence and solutions, and helping them develop.”

The plan was always that she would take charge of the women’s team for this season and she wants “to build a team that plays football with courage, energy and intensity” and to “dictate games and be dominant”. She adds: “It isn’t just about results and league positions. It’s just as important to me that the players continue to develop, that we improve as a team, and that we play a style of football we can identify with.”

Union had a difficult start to the season with Bayern Munich first up. They lost 4-1 and failed to pick up a point in their first four games but have since beaten RB Leipzig , Stuttgart and, in the cup, Magdeburg.

The tactical changes have reflected that search for an identity. Eta began with a 4-4-2 but then switched to a 4-3-3. The formation changed but the ambition did not. Eta has never thought about legacy: “For me, it’s always been about football and working with people to achieve success together as a team.”

Eta may have no interest in defining herself as a symbol. But she cannot control what other people see when they look at her. For the young girls who wrote to her, she is proof that the boundaries of football have moved.

Sports.title: Liverpool star Milos Kerkez listed as an 'enemy of Ukraine': Hungary's foreign minister is forced to step in after defender and his father are accused of 'supporting Russia's aggression'
Sports.content:
Milos Kerkez is at the heart of a political storm after being included in a list of 'enemies of Ukraine' alongside his father.

It comes following an incident involving the Hungary defender and Ukraine during their first Nations League encounter in this current international break.

Ukraine won 1-0 in Budapest on September 25 in a match that did have some feisty encounters.

One moment saw Kerkez's Hungary, and Liverpool, team-mate Dominik Szoboszlai involved in a scuffle with Ukraine's Victor Tsygankov.

As those two made their feelings known, Kerkez ran over and promptly grabbed Tsygankov by the collar.

In defence of his son, Kerkez's father Sebastijan - who is of Serbian descent - is reported to have uploaded a picture of the incident to his Instagram story with the song Russian Paradise by rapper AK-47 accompanying it. Some have interpreted that to be a reference to ongoing conflict in Ukraine.

Hungary defender Milos Kerkez (centre left) is in a list of 'enemies of Ukraine' after this incident with Victor Tsygankov (right) during a UEFA Nations League encounter last month

Kerkez rabbed Tsygankov by the collar after the latter confronted Dominik Szoboszlai

As a result, both Kerkezes are believed to be included on Myrotvorets, a database of 'enemies of Ukraine' which includes pictures and details on the individuals included.

It must be noted though that the list, which also includes Hungarian MP Balazs Hidveghi, is not run by or affiliated with the Ukrainian government.

The incident though has turned the sporting matter into a political one, with the Hungarian deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs Anita Orban stepping in and condemning 'possible threats' aimed at the left back.

She wrote on social media: 'I strongly condemn the stigmatisation, any form of blacklisting, and any potential threats directed at Hungarian citizens Milos Kerkez and Balazs Hidveghi.

'Throughout the weekend, alongside the government meeting, I was in constant consultation with Ukrainian government representatives, the Hungarian Football Federation (MLSZ), the embassy, ​​and my colleagues to ensure that all parties involved took action within their respective spheres to resolve the situation.

'Sport should be about performance, community, and respect. I thank the two national associations for their cooperation.'

Kerkez missed the reverse fixture on Monday night, which Hungary won 2-1, due to suspension, but downplayed any ill-feeling to his opponents after September's scuffle.

'Personally, I have never supported and I do not support any aggression in my life,' he told Hungarian outlet Telex. 'I am not a person who considers anything that harms others acceptable.

'At the same time, there is always tension in a football match, and in the match against Ukraine, all I did was defend our captain, my friend, and I would have done this even if any other country had been our opponent.'
