World.title: Hungary officially enters race to host 2036 Olympics – Budapest named as main venue
World.content:
Hungary is officially among the countries in the running to host the 2036 Summer Olympics and Paralympics, with Budapest named as the central location for the proposed Games.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) confirmed that Hungary is one of seven interested parties currently in continuous dialogue over the 2036 Olympics. The other candidates are Germany, India, Qatar, South Korea, South Africa and Türkiye.

The interested parties have until 31 October 2026 to formally indicate their interest. They will then present their projects to the IOC’s Future Host Commission in November.

Budapest at the centre of Hungary’s bid

Olympic bids are formally submitted by cities rather than national governments. Hungary has identified Budapest as the main host location for its project.

The other interested parties have also named their proposed host cities: Germany has put forward Munich, India Ahmedabad, Qatar Doha, Türkiye Istanbul, South Korea Seoul and South Africa Cape Town. Qatar’s proposal could also involve neighbouring countries in hosting events.

The IOC says potential hosts will be assessed on several factors, including their venue masterplan, athlete experience, funding strategy, political and public support, ability to deliver the Games and plans for a long-term legacy.

The projects will also be assessed on how well they fit local development plans and the goals of the Olympic movement.

The Olympics Park in Budapest, Hungary. Photo: Wikimedia Commons

If you missed it: Will Budapest miss out? India throws its hat into the ring for the 2036 Olympic Games

When will the host be chosen?

The selection process will take several years. The current interested parties will present their projects to the Future Host Commission in November 2026. By March 2027, the IOC is expected to complete feasibility assessments and open a more detailed Strategic Dialogue with the candidates.

The IOC Executive Board will then narrow down the field. In December 2028, the selected Preferred Hosts will enter a final Targeted Dialogue with the IOC and provide detailed plans and financial and legal guarantees.

The 2036 Olympic host is expected to be elected by IOC members in mid-2029.

The IOC says no additional candidates will be considered for the 2036 Games after 31 October 2026.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

A long-standing Budapest ambition

A Budapest Olympics has been a long-standing ambition in Hungarian politics, particularly under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

Budapest previously submitted a bid for the 2024 Olympics, but the application was withdrawn in 2017 after the Momentum movement collected around 266,000 signatures for a referendum on the proposal.

Since then, Hungary has continued to develop major sports infrastructure, including the Puskás Arena, MVM Dome, National Athletics Centre and Duna Arena. Budapest has also hosted major international sporting events, including the World Aquatics Championships and World Athletics Championships, as well as European Championship football matches.

These developments have frequently been cited as evidence that Hungary now has much of the infrastructure needed to host an Olympic Games.

The Puskás Arena in Budapest. Photo: BKK

What does Budapest’s current Olympic plan look like?

Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony has previously said he does not oppose the idea of hosting the Olympics in principle, but has attached conditions to any potential bid.

In September, Karácsony said that the capital’s Olympic concept does not require state spending during the current parliamentary term and does not include the construction of new stadiums. He described the proposal primarily as an urban development strategy focused on improving infrastructure in Budapest and across Hungary.

Under the concept, he said, an eventual Olympic Games would be organised together with as many major cities and other municipalities outside Budapest as possible.

However, Karácsony has also stressed that major projects such as the Olympics are difficult to discuss while Budapest is locked in financial disputes with the central government.

The Tisza government has not yet stated its position

Péter Magyar, now Hungary’s prime minister, previously expressed reservations about an Olympic bid. In 2024, he said Hungary did not need an Olympics under the circumstances at the time, while arguing that the event could become a national project if it had broad public support.

Magyar also previously said that the Tisza Party would only seriously consider an Olympic bid if the government provided additional funding for healthcare, education and social services, restored funding to Budapest and organised a national referendum on the issue.

World.title: PM Magyar announces wealth and small-business tax details
World.content:
Hungary will introduce a new wealth tax on assets worth more than HUF 1 billion from 2027, while the government plans to significantly broaden access to the KATA small-business tax scheme and remove a special tax allowance for professional athletes, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Tuesday.

In a video posted on social media, Magyar outlined changes to three areas of taxation: the new wealth tax, KATA and EKHO, a simplified tax scheme used by certain professionals including journalists, artists, performers and athletes.

Wealth tax to target assets worth over HUF 1 billion

The new wealth tax will come into force on 1 January 2027 and will have two rates. People with wealth exceeding HUF 1 billion will pay 1% on the portion above the HUF 1 billion threshold, while assets exceeding HUF 100 billion will be subject to a 1.5% rate, according to Magyar’s announcement.

The tax will cover a person’s overall wealth, including property, investments and company holdings. Assets held abroad or placed in wealth-management structures will also be covered.

Loans will be deductible from the taxable base. Taxes already paid on property and vehicles will also be deductible from the wealth tax itself, with the government saying this is intended to help avoid double taxation.

The government plans to introduce detailed rules for calculating the value of assets, primarily based on their actual market value. This will apply to both real estate and company holdings. The tax will be paid once a year through self-assessment. The first declaration will be based on taxpayers’ assets at the end of 2026 and will be due by 31 August 2027.

Only people whose wealth per person reaches HUF 1 billion will have to file a declaration. The Hungarian Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) is expected to provide a calculator to help taxpayers determine their taxable wealth. Magyar also criticised attempts to lobby against the new tax, saying people with less than HUF 1 billion in wealth would have nothing to do under the new system.

KATA to become available to more small businesses

The government is also planning a major overhaul of KATA, Hungary’s simplified tax scheme for small businesses. The changes would once again allow part-time entrepreneurs, pensioners and university students running businesses alongside their studies to use KATA.

KATA taxpayers would also once again be able to invoice companies and other organisations, rather than being restricted to invoicing private individuals. The government expects more than 100,000 additional small businesses could become eligible for the scheme as a result. (1 euro = 366 forints)

However, the monthly fixed tax will increase. For full-time KATA taxpayers, the monthly amount will rise to HUF 100,000. Those using KATA alongside another job will pay HUF 50,000 per month.

There will be a transitional arrangement for those who invoice exclusively private individuals. They will pay HUF 75,000 per month in 2027, with the HUF 100,000 rate applying from 2028.

The government says the higher tax is partly intended to improve social security protection for KATA taxpayers. The amount used to calculate their sick pay, maternity benefits and future pension will also be increased.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

15% tax on certain business income

The revised KATA system will also introduce a 15% tax on income earned from invoicing companies and other organisations. However, the fixed KATA tax already paid will count towards this liability. As a result, a full-time KATA taxpayer will not face an effective additional tax burden on company income until their annual company revenue exceeds HUF 8 million, according to Magyar’s explanation.

The annual KATA revenue limit will also increase from HUF 18 million to HUF 22 million.

The government argues that the changes will make KATA available to a much wider group of small businesses while maintaining it as a relatively simple and predictable form of taxation.

The HUF 100,000 monthly rate represents a substantial nominal increase from the HUF 50,000 rate introduced when KATA was launched in 2013. However, the tax rate has not changed since then, while Hungary has experienced roughly 80% inflation over the period. In today’s money, the original HUF 50,000 would be worth around HUF 88,000–89,000.

Professional athletes to lose special EKHO allowance

The government will also change the rules for EKHO, or simplified contribution taxation. Under the current system, the general annual income limit for EKHO is HUF 60 million, but professional athletes have been allowed to use the preferential system on income of up to HUF 500 million.

That special limit will be abolished from 2027, Magyar said. Professional athletes will instead be subject to the same HUF 60 million annual limit as other professions eligible for EKHO.

Magyar said there was no justification for professional footballers earning HUF 10–20 million, and sometimes HUF 50 million, per month to have substantially different tax rules from journalists, actors or other professionals using EKHO.

The government said it supports Hungarian sport and wants to see successful Hungarian clubs and athletes, but intends to remove what it considers unjustified exceptions from the tax system.

World.title: Former FM Szijjártó travelled to Russia every few months, spending more time there than in Germany
World.content:
Former Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó travelled to Russia 16 times during his final four-year term in office – roughly once every three to four months – while visiting the country more often than Germany, according to detailed Foreign Ministry data obtained by 24.hu.

The figures show that Szijjártó travelled extensively during his 2022–2026 term, visiting 96 sovereign states, or almost half of all UN member countries. He made a total of 342 foreign trips involving 468 destinations. The former minister has since joined Chinese carmaker BYD.

Russia was a more frequent destination than Germany

Szijjártó’s 16 trips to Russia stand out in the data, particularly given the country’s war against Ukraine and Germany’s position as Hungary’s most important economic partner. The Russian trips were spread across his four years in office, meaning Szijjártó travelled to Russia on average every three to four months.

The figure does not include meetings with Russian officials held outside Russia. Szijjártó visited Luxembourg, where EU meetings are frequently held, the same number of times. His 16 trips to Russia, however, exceeded the number of times he travelled to Germany during the period.

Have you read this? Former Hungarian foreign minister Szijjártó questioned over BYD role in closed-door security hearing

Brussels was his most frequent destination

Belgium was Szijjártó’s most frequently visited country, with 38 trips, mainly to Brussels for EU and NATO-related meetings. The United States was second with 31 visits. Several of these trips included meetings at Donald Trump’s Florida residence.

Neighbouring Serbia ranked third, with Szijjártó travelling there 25 times during his term. Overall, his foreign travel covered 96 countries – equivalent to 49.7% of the world’s 193 UN member states.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

590 days spent abroad

The data also provides insight into just how much time Szijjártó spent travelling. Out of the nearly 1,450 days covered by his previous government’s term, he spent 590 days on foreign trips.

Despite the extensive travel schedule, Szijjártó often spent little time abroad, favouring short visits and returning home quickly. According to the data, he actually spent more nights sleeping on aircraft than in foreign accommodation.

The Foreign Ministry spent a total of HUF 512 million on accommodation for foreign trips during the period, of which HUF 53.9 million was attributed to Szijjártó.

The most expensive trip cost HUF 262 million

The data also reveals substantial differences in the cost of individual trips. Szijjártó’s most expensive foreign trip cost HUF 262 million, with the Foreign Ministry’s previous travel data showing that chartered aircraft accounted for a particularly significant share of spending on his foreign visits.

The latest figures come after 24.hu previously reported on the ministry’s spending on private aircraft for Szijjártó’s foreign travel, including almost HUF 300 million spent on private planes that ultimately did not take off.

World.title: EUR 8 million AI data centre planned in Transylvanian town with large Hungarian community
World.content:
A new artificial intelligence (AI) data centre worth more than EUR 8 million is being developed in Reghin, Transylvania, with the first NVIDIA servers expected to become operational before the end of the year.

The project, led by Romanian IT company Expert IT, will initially install 56 high-performance NVIDIA B300 graphics processing units (GPUs) across seven servers, G4Media reported. The company is also considering a much larger expansion involving another 512 GPUs. The investment is part of a wider EUR 10 million development planned by Expert IT on a 1.7-hectare site in Reghin, Mureș County.

56 NVIDIA GPUs to power AI models

The first phase of the project will cost more than EUR 8 million and involves not only the servers and GPUs but also the electricity supply and cooling infrastructure needed to operate them.

Expert IT chief executive Mihai Farcaș Dan said the 56-GPU order is the largest purchase of its kind in Romania this year. The company has already completed discussions about a potential expansion involving a further 512 graphics cards.

“The servers are due to become operational this year and are intended for developing large models,” Farcaș Dan told Radio Târgu Mureș.

The company has been developing its investment plans in Reghin for around 12 years, with AI becoming an increasingly important focus over the past three to four years. Details of how the first phase of the investment is being financed have not yet been disclosed.

AI could help doctors diagnose patients faster

One of the project’s main areas of focus will be healthcare. Expert IT is considering working with Romanian clinics and universities to develop AI systems capable of supporting communication between doctors and patients, assisting medical professionals and analysing medical imaging.

The company hopes such systems could eventually help speed up diagnoses in areas such as oncology and cardiology, where rapid identification of serious conditions can be particularly important.

The planned AI models could, for example, analyse large datasets and medical images to identify patterns and support doctors in reaching a diagnosis more quickly. The project could therefore involve healthcare and academic institutions from several parts of Romania.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Transylvania is becoming an AI data centre hotspot

The Reghin project is far from the only major AI-related data centre development underway in Transylvania. In Luna, Cluj County, US-based DriverAI and Romanian partner Leviatan Group are planning an 80-megawatt facility known as the Quantum AI Data Center.

The first phase has been estimated at around US$1 billion, with the centre intended primarily to provide computing capacity for running and training AI models. That project is still in the preparation stage, however, and the selected site is currently involved in a legal dispute following a challenge by a business using an adjacent plot.

Mureș County is also preparing another major data centre in Vidrasău. The Mureș County Council and Mureș Industrial Park are planning a facility costing almost RON 240 million (around EUR 45 million).

The approximately 1,700-square-metre centre would provide data storage, processing and server hosting, as well as computing capacity for artificial intelligence applications. Funding for the project has reportedly already been secured.

Meanwhile, the George Emil Palade University of Medicine, Pharmacy, Science and Technology of Târgu Mureș is developing its own high-performance computing infrastructure.

Its nearly RON 60 million (EUR 11.2 million) DEEP_AI project will support research based on artificial intelligence, machine learning and large-scale data analysis, including work on communications security and the detection of cyberattacks.

Romania wants to become a regional AI hub

The developments in Transylvania are part of a much wider push to expand Romania’s AI infrastructure. According to Telex, Romania is also planning the Black Sea AI Gigafactory, a huge project designed to establish the country as a regional centre for artificial intelligence. The planned facilities in Cernavodă and Doicești would eventually host more than 100,000 AI processors.

One of the biggest challenges facing such projects is securing enough electricity to power the enormous computing capacity required by modern AI systems.

World.title: Commercial ship sinks after drone attack off Bulgaria, Hungary’s PM reacts
World.content:
A commercial ship sank and another was damaged in a drone attack in the Black Sea off Bulgaria early Tuesday, with Hungary’s Prime Minister Péter Magyar expressing solidarity with Bulgaria following the incident.

The attack took place in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, around 80 nautical miles (approximately 130 kilometres) east of Cape St Athanasius and the town of Byala, according to Dnevnik.bg. The identities of the attackers have not yet been officially established, although there are reports that the drones may have been Russian.

One ship sank, crew missing

The attack reportedly took place at around 3 AM and involved two cargo vessels: the Togo-flagged ALFA WATAN and the Palau-flagged ABLE.

According to Maritime.bg, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the ALFA WATAN sank following the attack. A nearby Bulgarian vessel headed towards the site after the explosion, but so far rescuers have found only an overturned boat, three overturned life rafts and life jackets. The crew of the sunken vessel remains missing and the search operation is continuing. Authorities have not yet released information about the ship’s cargo.

The second vessel, which was carrying wheat, was also hit and caught fire. Its 18-person crew consisted of 11 Turkish and seven Indian nationals. All of them managed to abandon the vessel and were rescued. Two sailors were injured and taken by speedboat to the port of Varna. One suffered burns, while the other sustained a head injury.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Bulgaria launches emergency response

Bulgarian authorities immediately launched a response following the overnight attack. Radev convened a meeting involving representatives of the defence, interior, transport and environment ministries, the president’s office and the country’s security services.

The prime minister described the attack as completely unacceptable and a serious violation of international law and maritime regulations. The exact origin of the drones is under investigation.

Authorities are also monitoring another vessel, the EMIL, which has been drifting without a crew since August due to a malfunctioning steering system. A military aircraft carried out reconnaissance over the vessel two days before the latest incident.

Bulgarian authorities are tracking its movement to ensure it does not enter the country’s territorial waters or pose a threat to the coastline. They are also monitoring the possibility of pollution or an oil spill.

If you missed it: Hungary to stop blocking next stage of Ukraine’s EU accession talks, Financial Times reports

Another Black Sea ship was attacked a day earlier

The incident came just one day after another suspected drone attack on a grain carrier in the Black Sea, this time in Romania’s exclusive economic zone in international waters, Index reported. Romanian authorities sent several rescue vessels and helicopters to the scene. One person was killed and another is still missing following that incident.

Péter Magyar expresses Hungary’s solidarity

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar also reacted to the attack on Tuesday. In a Facebook post, Magyar said Hungary stands in full solidarity with Bulgaria following the incident.

“At dawn, two commercial ships were hit by a drone attack in Bulgaria’s territorial waters in the Black Sea. One ship sank, and the attack, whose origin is currently unknown, has injured people. Hungary assures Bulgaria of its full solidarity.”

The Hungarian prime minister did not speculate about who was responsible for the attack.

World.title: Kosovo Political Leaders Trade Blame as Another Election Looms
World.content:
Protesters in front of Kosovo parliament building in Pristina, October 6, 2026. Photo: Adeline Ahmeti/BIRN

Kosovo politicians traded blame over the country potentially heading towards its fourth parliamentary election in less than two years, as political parties again failed to agree on electing a president.

When deadline for MPs to elect a new head of state expires after midnight on Tuesday, it will trigger snap polls.

But the issue has become tangled up with demands for legal changes to curb the powers of the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which sparked anger by convicting four Kosovo Liberation Army leaders of war crimes last month.

Two opposition parties, the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, and Alliance for the Future of Kosovo, AAK, called for draft amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers to be passed on a second reading before they would come to an agreement with the government on electing a president.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti, the leader of the ruling party, Vetevendosje, told a press conference that electing a President was the priority.

“The President needs to be elected today, while the law [on the Hague-based court] can follow later, respecting the 72-hour deadline [of parliament’s procedural rules]. I pledge that the law will pass its second reading on Thursday morning,” Kurti said.

“If the PDK publicly pledges to secure at least half of its MPs’ votes for [presidential candidate] Professor Bekim Sejdiu – given that we have the rest from the [opposition Democratic League of Kosovo] LDK … then we will proceed with the second-reading vote,” he promised.

Kurti accused the PDK and its chairman, Bedri Hamza, of not making any substantial steps towards an agreement.

But speaking after Kurti, Hamza claimed that “the PDK’s stance has been and remains consistent: approval of the law on the Specialist Chambers in both readings”.

He repeated that the draft amendments to the law and the election of the President “are not linked matters” but merely coincided over the same period.

Hamza recalled that Sejdiu was not even an agreed presidential candidate within his own party, the Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK.

Sejdiu was the joint candidate that Kurti and LDK leader Lumir Abdixhiku agreed to on August 31 – but six LDK MPs then announced they would not support him, leaving a potential vote without the necessary quorum. This led to Sejdiu withdrawing his candidacy for the presidency.

Meanwhile, the LDK also said it did not support changes to the law on the Specialist Chambers.

On Monday, MPs voted to amend the law on the court to limit the jail sentences it can hand down to 15 years. The court last month sentenced former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and three other former KLA chiefs, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi, to 25, 25 18 and 13 years in prison respectively for war crimes.

But despite Monday’s vote backing the amendment, it still needs a review by a parliamentary committee before it can return for a second reading.

After Monday’s parliamentary session ended, protesters took to the streets to demanded that MPs vote on a second reading the same day. They blocked MPs from leaving the chamber, burned garbage bins and threw fireworks and explosives at the government building, but without damaging it.

Protests have been continuing since the Specialist Chambers’ first-instance verdict on September 16.

Clirim Haziri, organiser of the “Not In My Name” protest against the verdicts in Pristina, said on Tuesday that if MPs do not adopt the law and send the country towards elections, “this protest will not end today; we will follow your every step – there will be no [electoral] campaign for you.”

World.title: Bulgarian PM and Opposition Quarrel Over Black Sea Drone Attack
World.content:
Bulgaria’s opposition has criticised the government over its response to a drone attack on two foreign commercial cargo vessels on Tuesday in Bulgaria’s zone in the Black Sea.

The strike occurred at around 3 a.m. about 70 nautical miles east of the town of Byala and sank a Palau-flagged ship. A Togo-flagged ship was damaged by fire. The total number of sailors injured in the strike is unclear.

Prime Minister Rumen Radev called the attack “a crude violation of international law” but is yet to name the aggressor.

“It’s clear the drones were either Russian or Ukrainian,” he told media, adding that “worse cases have happened before”, without clarifying what events he was referring to.

Radev later stated: “As I have long said before, if this [Ukraine] war is not ended on time, it will continue to expand its territorial reach, become more brutal, increase the risks and turn into a global conflict.”

Acting President Iliana Iotova, formerly vice to Radev during his 2016-2026 presidential mandate, signed a decree to assemble Bulgaria’s security council on Wednesday. But Radev indirectly downplayed the need for such a decision, saying: “It would make people speculate with all kinds of nonsense.”

Opposition members criticised Radev for not naming Russia as the aggressor, alleging it was symptomatic of his sympathy for the Kremlin, following his reluctance for years to aid Ukraine – an agenda allegedly shared by Iotova, a runner in upcoming presidential elections on October 25.

“Although the budget for the military has doubled, there’s no adequate protection for Bulgarian citizens. There’s no real President, no real leader,” Assen Vassilev, co-leader of the opposition party We Continue the Change, told media.

“It is clearly a strike from Russia but Radev is not brave enough to say it,” said Ivaylo Mirchev, of Democratic Bulgaria, who asked why Radev had seemed more concerned when a non-threatening decoy drone was found near the border with Romania.

Sixteen crew members of the struck vessels, comprising Turkish and Indian nationals, have meanwhile been evacuated.

One who identified as a Turkish citizen told media on the Bulgarian shore: “I think the Russians threw at us a naval mine, there was a fire, not like one from a drone, since it came from underneath. I think it’s a Russian [attack] because we were carrying Ukrainian cargo.”

No government official has commented on the nature of the cargo carried by the vessels, or on whether there is a likely connection to Ukraine.

Two crew members sustained serious injuries – one with severe burns and another with head trauma – and were transported to the military hospital in Varna for treatment. Rescue missions are ongoing.

On September 18, Bulgaria announced it would start further supplying infrastructure facilities with drone-countermeasure systems, the move announced days after a fire ​broke out at a weapons depot, raising concerns about the security of munitions manufacturers.

World.title: Serbian Student Targeted by Spyware Attack Sues Authorities
World.content:
Lawyers representing student activist Jelena Kontic filed a criminal complaint on Tuesday with the Prosecutor’s Office for High-Tech Crime over the installation of Pegasus spyware on her phone, allegedly by Serbian security forces.

“The complaint was filed against individuals within the Security Information Agency [the state intelligence service] and the police whose identities have yet to be established, as well as responsible individuals at NSO Group, the Israeli company that manufactures Pegasus,” a Serbian digital rights NGO, SHARE Foundation, said in a press release.

Kontic is one of 14 members of the student movement, opposition politicians and activists who were targeted with advanced spyware. SHARE Foundation and The Citizen Lab, a research unit of the University of Toronto, revealed the alleged attacks on September 2.

SHARE Foundation added that Kontic’s case is the first confirmed successful Pegasus spyware infection in Serbia.

Given the precedence, Kontic told BIRN that “she expects the forensic examination of her phone and the processing of the case to present a challenge for the prosecution”.

Kontic only learned that she had been targeted when she received a notification from Apple. Forensic analysis confirmed that her device had been compromised remotely through a so-called “zero-click” attack.

“The attack exploited a vulnerability in the iMessage app on her iPhone, without her knowledge or any interaction on her part,” SHARE Foundation added.

The complaint covers five criminal offences: unauthorised collection of personal data, unauthorised interception and recording, creation and introduction of computer viruses, unauthorised access to a protected computer, and abuse of office.

Kontic’s lawyers, as quoted by SHARE Foundation, argued that the prosecutor’s office was required to act as soon as the case became public, and that the offences are punishable by imprisonment.

BIRN asked the High-Tech Crime Prosecution in September whether it had opened an investigation into the alleged attacks, but it did not respond.

But one day after the student movement published the information about the 14 people targeted with spyware, on September 3, the Security Information Agency dismissed the claims as “trivial sensationalism”.

Serbia’s Commissioner for Information of Public Importance and Personal Data Protection told BIRN on September 17 that it had not opened a case, as it lacked vital information.

“The Commissioner has not initiated a new proceeding, as at this time he does not have specific information and evidence concerning the circumstances of individual cases that would make it possible to establish grounds for action within his jurisdiction,” it said.

Kontic is part of the students’ movement that has become the main opponent of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party.

The movement was created after the fatal collapse of part of Novi Sad railway station in November 2024 triggered mass protests. The movement later formed the Student List, which is running in the parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25.

World.title: Kosovo Protesters Against Hague Court Gather Again After Clashes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Protesters led by the Kosovo Liberation Army War Veterans’ Organisation started to reassemble outside parliament in Pristina on Tuesday after violent clashes the previous evening.

Angered by the convictions of four wartime KLA leaders including ex-President Hashim Thaci, they want MPs to pass legislation limiting the powers of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers war crimes court.

MPs on Monday voted to amend the law on the Hague-based court, which is part of Kosovo’s justice system, to say it may not impose jail sentences exceeding 15 years. But the amendment still needs a parliamentary committee review before it can return for a second reading.

After the parliamentary session ended, protesters demanded MPs vote on a second reading the same day. They blocked MPs from leaving the chamber and forcibly pushed ruling Vetevendosje party MP Fahrush Rexhepi back inside the parliament’s perimeter.

They then burned garbage bins and threw fireworks and explosives at the government building, but without damaging it. Clirim Haziri, organiser of the “Not in My Name” protest, declared that no MP would leave “without stepping over our bodies”.

Police said three persons were arrested and six police officers were injured. Naser Syla, from the University Clinical Centre of Kosovo, on Monday evening said 12 people had received medical assistance, including one police officer.

Peaceful protests have been continuing since the Specialist Chambers issued a first-instance verdict convicting the four former KLA leaders of war crimes on September 16.

The so-called special court sentenced former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and three other former leaders of the KLA, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi, to 25, 25 18 and 13 years in prison respectively for war crimes.

They were found guilty of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder from April 1998 to June 20, 1999, in Kosovo and several locations in Albania.

Other amendments passed on Monday include for the jail sentences to be served in Kosovo. Based on the current law, “the Specialist Chambers may order the transfer of a convicted person to a third country for service of his or her sentence of imprisonment”.

They also allow for Kosovo’s President to grant pardons, for the work of the court to be subjected to monitoring by international organisations, and for a constitutional review of the law to be conducted by the Constitutional Court of Kosovo.

The court is a hybrid tribunal. Although it is part of Kosovo’s judiciary, it is staffed with internationals and located in The Hague. It was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies because of concern of potential witness intimidation if the processes were to be held domestically in Kosovo.

The court has a mandate to try crimes committed from January 1, 1998, to December 31, 2000, based on a Council of Europe report by Swiss Senator Dick Marty, which made allegations of war crimes and organ trafficking by KLA fighters.

An EU Special Investigative Task Force, led by former US prosecutor Clint Williamson, concluded that there was enough evidence to indict suspects for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but not enough to bring charges for organ trafficking.

The amendments to the law would also change the mandate of the court to only cover crimes allegedly committed after the Kosovo war ended, from July 1, 1999, until December 31, 2000.

The draft also says the court will not have jurisdiction over acts not committed in relation to the allegations of organ-trafficking in the Marty report – for which it has already been established that there is not enough evidence for trials.

Following the first-reading vote in parliament on Monday, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, founded by Thaci, demanded that the second reading be held that same day.

This proposal was rejected by the Speaker, Albulena Haxhiu, who said it was not on the agenda and who insisted that the party leaders – PM Albin Kurti and leader of Vetevendosje and Bedri Hamza of the PDK, meet first.

Hamza and Kurti held a meeting on Monday, but it did not result in an agreement.

Kurti said the top priority was electing a state President. During the parliament session, Kurti said: “A law regarding the Hague court is necessary, but so is a President of Kosovo. Proceeding with one without the other could be highly detrimental. We cannot claim to be defending Kosovo’s interests in The Hague while allowing an institutional vacuum to develop within Kosovo.”

Parliament’s deputy speaker from the PDK, Vlora Citaku, disagreed. She said after the parliament session that voting on the new law was “a national obligation, whereas the election of the president is a matter of agreement”.

World.title: From Streets to Polling Stations: Serbia’s Student Movement Takes Electoral Test
World.content:
When Serbia’s students began blockading their universities after the fatal collapse of the canopy at the railway station in Novi Sad in November 2024, entering parliament was not part of the plan.

Their demands were directed at Serbia’s institutions: publication of documentation relating to the station reconstruction, prosecution of those accused of attacking students commemorating the victims, the dropping of charges against arrested students, and increased funding for higher education.

“At that point, we did not even know what the electoral process involved. We simply wanted justice,” said Milica Najdanovic, a student at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering.

Five months of university blockades and mass protests changed the calculation. Concluding that their original demands would not be met, the students added another: early parliamentary elections.

World.title: One Click, Money Gone: Albania Battles Spike in Cyber Fraud
World.content:
It all started with a text message in May. Gentjana Driza was waiting for a delivery from e-commerce marketplace Temu when she received a message apparently from Albania Post, telling her to pay a small customs fee.

The message contained a link. Driza clicked on it and was taken to a series of forms. According to her complaint to the police, she believed the request genuinely came from Albania Post, so she followed the instructions and entered her personal and banking details.

She soon realised she had been scammed. Notifications began appearing on her banking app showing substantial transfers from her account. The transactions continued even after she contacted her bank and blocked her card.

Over the next three days, around 100,000 lek (1,085 euros) was taken from Driza’s account. The exact amount remained unclear, as transactions continued to be processed.

World.title: Nationalist Parties Celebrate Wins in Bosnia Election, But Many Voters Stay Home
World.content:
“It was not a surprise because we as citizens cannot free ourselves from the ethno-national frameworks,” political analyst Tanja Topic told BIRN after Bosnia’s dominant nationalist parties claimed victory on October 4 in the general election.

The [Bosniak] Party of Democratic Action, SDA, the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ BiH, and the [Serb] Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, each remained the strongest force in their respective ethnic camps, while many voters stayed at home – and a new challenger shook up the Bosniak field.

Topic said most voters clearly looked past the corruption, crime, nepotism and clientelism on which power rests, as each wave of national homogenisation follows another, leaving the country stuck in a vicious circle.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament Moves Towards Changing Law to Curb Hague Special Court
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



The first reading of the special court law amendment at the Kosovo parliament, October 5, 2026. Photo: Antigone Isufi/BIRN.

Kosovo MPs on Monday voted to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers so the Hague-based court, part of Kosovo’s justice system, may not impose a sentence of imprisonment exceeding 15 years. The amendment has not been adopted yet, as it must undergo a parliamentary committee review and return for a second reading.

Outside parliament, protesters who had staged an all-night vigil in front of the legislature chanted: “Vote [for] the law.”

The vote comes amid anger in Kosovo after the court sentenced former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci and three other former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi, to 25, 25 18 and 13 years in prison respectively for war crimes on September 16.

The four were found guilty of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder from April 1998 to June 20, 1999, in Kosovo and several locations in Albania.

Critics have, among others, claimed that the court did not apply the “lex mitior” principle, which allows defendants to be sentenced under the most favourable law of the time that the crime was committed. According to the applicable law of former Yugoslavia, the maximum prison sentence is 15 years.

The amendments include for the sentences to be served in Kosovo. Based on the current law, “the Specialist Chambers may order the transfer of a convicted person to a third country for service of his or her sentence of imprisonment”.

The amendments also grant Kosovo’s President power to grant pardons, the work of the court to be subjected to monitoring by international organisations, and for a constitutional review of the law to be conducted by the Constitutional Court of Kosovo.

It is not certain whether a second reading will take place on Monday.

Bedri Hamza, chair of the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, which Thaci founded, and which proposed the amendments, said before the vote that the law does not belong to his party, even if it “is a PDK initiative”.

The verdict, which is to be appealed, caused outrage in Kosovo and people have been protesting daily ever since.

It also led to the initiative to change the law on the court. The court is a hybrid tribunal – although it is part of Kosovo’s judiciary, it is staffed with internationals and located in The Hague.

It was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies because of concern of potential witness intimidation if the processes were to be held domestically in Kosovo.

The court has a mandate to try crimes committed from January 1, 1998, to December 31, 2000, based on a Council of Europe report by Swiss Senator Dick Marty, which made allegations of war crimes and organ trafficking by KLA fighters.

An EU Special Investigative Task Force, led by former US prosecutor Clint Williamson, concluded that there was enough evidence to indict suspects for war crimes and crimes against humanity, but not enough to bring charges for organ trafficking.

The amendments of the law aim to change the mandate of the court to only cover crimes allegedly committed after the Kosovo war, from July 1, 1999 until December 31, 2000. The draft amendment says that the court will not have jurisdiction over acts that were not committed in relation to the allegations of organ-trafficking in the Dick Marty report – for which it has already been established that there is not enough evidence for trials.

On Monday, before the law was put to a vote, Prime Minister Albin Kurti reminded MPs that the country faces another crisis, over the election of a President.

“A law regarding the Hague court is necessary, but so is a President of Kosovo. Proceeding with one without the other could be highly detrimental. We cannot claim to be defending Kosovo’s interests in The Hague while allowing an institutional vacuum to develop within Kosovo,” he said.

Tuesday is the constitutional deadline for Kosovo to elect a President and finalise the formation of institutions deriving from the June 7 elections. If a President is not elected, the country faces its fourth parliamentary elections in less than two years.

Even if the law amendments pass the second reading, they will be enforced only after the appeals panel at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers issues a verdict for Thaci and the three others.

World.title: Kharkiv mayor: No safe place left in the city as winter approaches
World.content:
The northern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv is now targeted by Russian drones as well as missiles, but the city lives on mayor Ihor Terehhov told ERR.

Being just 30 kilometers from the Russian border, Kharkiv has suffered a lot over the past four and a half years but is unbowed and is trying to rebuild what has been destroyed,

The mayor noted the coming winter will be very hard without any "energy truce", but the city survived the last winter and the previous ones too.

Mayor Terehhov was talkng to ERR at a time when Russia has been hitting Kharkiv in lethal strikes involving bombs, missiles and drones.

It is mid-autumn already and winter is approaching. How is Kharkiv preparing, and how did it survive the last winter?

If there is no so-called energy truce — Ukraine ending strikes on Russian oil refineries in exchange for Russia ending attacks on energy and other critical infrastructure in Ukraine, which is currently widely under discussion — then the coming winter will be very hard. We understand that perfectly.

I warned everyone last autumn that the winter would be tough, and so it has turned out to be. The enemy has been destroying energy infrastructure, targeting thermal power plants and water supply, leaving residents without basic utilities.

We all understand this all too well, yet we survived last winter, even though it, too, was hard. Due to the strikes on the power plants, we had not a single megawatt of electricity generation of our own. The heating system was damaged. There had been 50 attacks on electricity and heating networks. So it was a hard winter, but we held out. As for next winter, we are preparing for that too. We have been preparing since 2022.

Two years ago, in our previous interview, you spoke about the need to create energy "islands". What are these islands, and have they been created?

We wouldn't have survived last winter without those energy islands. I can't tell you everything, but if I were Estonia, I would be setting up energy islands too. It is effective. In essence an energy island is an autonomous energy source fed by small boiler houses. People get electricity, heat and water from it.

How many people currently live in Kharkiv? Initially people left, and then, as you said, they began to return. Two years ago you estimated the population at 900,000. Kharkiv has also become a destination for internally displaced people from the front line and occupied areas. What is the trend today?

During the war there have been times when the city's population fell to 350,000 and even to 320,000. But the trend has been positive, and currently around 1.4 million people live in Kharkiv, of whom 225,000 are internally displaced persons. This is a serious challenge for the city — these people have to be resettled and cared for.

Our hospitals cater to these people; their children attend our schools. They have lost everything, and it is our duty to care for them, but they also need help from the state. They have been left homeless, so the state should issue them housing certificates, but so far no state program has been implemented. So there are many challenges we face every day. But the fact that there are 1.4 million people living in Kharkiv today is actually good news.

How is responsibility for internally displaced people divided between the city, the oblast and the central government? Is the city obliged to provide them with housing?

In my view, providing housing for those who have lost everything — that is, internally displaced people — is the state's obligation. I mean a construction program for internally displaced people, so they have the opportunity to get living space where they want. The situation is not like this in Kharkiv alone. Yes, most of our people are displaced from Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. So such a program is needed.

As for Kharkiv residents, we currently have 160,000 people who have been left without shelter. No other major Ukrainian city has suffered destruction like Kharkiv has. As of today, we have 10,000 damaged, severely damaged or completely destroyed residential buildings, but during the war we have managed to repair and restore nearly 4,000 buildings. Of course, the city's budget deficit is very large, and according to government forecasts it will be even larger next year.

Where is the money coming from?

Financial assistance from international partners is required. It is no secret that we depend on funds allocated by our international partners. This is public information; both the president and the government have said so. We have to use state and city budget funds very carefully.

Ihor Terehhov- Source: Tarmo Aarma

On September 28, Russian attack drones destroyed practically the entire stairwell of a multi-story block. Do you have reserve apartments to relocate residents somewhere?

We offered people accommodation in a dorm. Two families initially agreed, but then said they would go to live with relatives. Most of the residents of that building are internally displaced people who were renting apartments there. And now they are looking for other apartments.

For our part, we closed the building shell (a temporary measure where holes in walls and broken windows are covered with plywood — ed.), restored the electricity supply and restarted the heating and water systems. All of this is financed out of the city budget. The victims have been documented and are receiving payments. But the stairwell is still destroyed, from the third floor to the fifth, and with this I think the state should already allocate money for restoration. At first we were restoring everything ourselves at our own expense, but the city budget is already exhausted.

So what is the city's current budget deficit? How much money do you need?

That is a complicated question. You could say there is a deficit, but also say there isn't, depending on how you calculate it. Without reconstruction costs, we are on the edge, but still not in deficit. If we want to carry out the programs we consider necessary, then a deficit comes up. For us, the most important thing is to ensure reconstruction support and that payments are not delayed, as sometimes happens.

I saw three buildings in [residential district of Kharkiv] Saltivka that had been heavily damaged at the start of the war, then repaired, and now they are in order and people are starting to return (apartment repairs are not the city's responsibility but the residents' — ed.). But the Saltivka area is not the safest place in Kharkiv, to put it mildly. Is it worth spending money on rebuilding something that could be destroyed again the very next day?

I am convinced that rebuilding is essential. If we don't do it, people will stay in other countries and not return. People do not come back to places where there is nowhere to live, work or educate their children. We consider it important that Ukrainians, Kharkiv residents, come back from abroad, which means we have to rebuild in any case. Moreover, the current situation is such that a strike can hit practically any Ukrainian city. There is no city in the country so safe that you could say it definitely won't be attacked.

Have you been taking part in international conferences on Ukraine's reconstruction? In June a conference like that took place in Gdansk, Poland; next January one is going to be held in Tallinn.

I was at the Gdansk one. We held a special event and we managed to attract money from international partners, specifically for preparing for the heating season. That meeting was a productive one for Kharkiv.

I was in the Pyatykhatky neighborhood, and anti-drone nets are being installed over the road there. At the same time, some nearby streets are not covered with nets; I saw at least one car destroyed by a drone strike. On what criteria do you decide what to cover with nets and what not to?

The nets are not installed by the city but by the regional military administration, and they are installed where the military says so. Only the military decides where the anti-drone nets get placed. For our part, we are also installing protection against fibre-optic FPV drones. We do this in conjunction with the military, but at the city's expense. This protection is our know-how, developed in cooperation with the military and engineers.

Which places in Kharkiv are currently the most dangerous, and which are the safest?

In Kharkiv, as in the rest of the country, there is no safe place. I can't tell you that Pyatykhatky is dangerous but the city center — say Shevchenkivskyi or Kyivskyi districts — is more or less safe, because at any moment it could be hit by anything, from a missile to an FPV drone. As long as the war continues, nowhere in Ukraine can be a hundred percent safe.

Do you have any advice for your Estonian colleagues — mayors, municipal leaders — on preparing for crises?

Estonia is a sovereign state and we respect that. If you need our advice, there is no problem there. We will talk and show everything as openly as possible, though that information is not intended for the wider public consumption.

World.title: Pay raises drive surge in applications for senior teacher status in Estonia
World.content:
Interest among teachers in obtaining senior‑ and master‑teacher qualifications has grown, as these come with higher salaries. But a larger number of higher‑paid teachers is putting additional pressure on school budgets.

This academic year, a national teacher career model took effect in Estonia, linking qualification levels to salary. Since higher levels bring a pay increase, interest has tripled in just a couple of years.

On Monday — Teachers' Day — the autumn application round ended. As of that day, 170 portfolios had been submitted for senior‑ or master‑teacher qualification.

"Already now we have as many senior‑teacher applications as we had in the entire previous year. We have several rounds, so the number will definitely rise," said Margit Timakov, board member of the Estonian Teachers' Union.

However, not all applications meet the criteria for a higher qualification level.

"It's clear from the portfolio whether a person takes the application seriously or not. When the number of applications grows, the number of rejections grows as well — we still have those who come just to try their luck," Timakov noted.

At Mahtra Basic School, five of the school's 60 teachers are considering applying for senior‑teacher status, and two senior teachers already work there. Mahtra school also pays both senior and master teachers more than one‑third above the national minimum salary. This makes managing the budget more difficult.

"I often wonder how to make ends meet, but in the end it works out. The most important thing is that the person standing in front of the class knows what they're doing and wants to be there. And they want to be there when they receive fair pay," said Mahtra Basic School director Edgar Roditšenko.

At Nõmme Basic School, three teachers are considering a higher career level. For now, there is enough salary funding.

"If you want good teachers, you must also find the finances. As far as I know, we currently have the resources, but what happens when interest grows significantly — that's hard to predict. School leaders are beginning to question how sustainable this system is," said Nõmme Basic School director Õnnela Leedo‑Küngas.

It is also unclear how many higher‑level teachers the education system actually needs.

"We haven't yet analyzed nationally how many master‑teacher‑profile teachers the system requires. Right now, it's trial and error," Timakov said.

World.title: Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center director Hendrik Agur suspected of fraud
World.content:
Hendrik Agur, director of the Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center (IVKHK), has been formally named a suspect in fraud committed as a public official. According to the suspicion, Agur submitted false information to receive compensation for using his personal car.

The Prosecutor's Office confirmed that Agur is suspected of fraud as a public official.

"According to the suspicion, Agur submitted expense‑compensation requests to the Ministry of Education and Research for nearly a year starting in August 2025, claiming reimbursement for personal car use on trips that did not actually take place. The initial suspicion is that he requested compensation amounting to €4,500. He has since repaid the damage caused to the ministry," said lead prosecutor Daniel Toom.

As the criminal investigation is ongoing and evidence collection continues, both the time period covered by the suspicion and the estimated damage amount may still be clarified.

Agur told ERR that he misunderstood the nature of the compensation and has now repaid it.

"The suspicion is justified, and in summary, I submitted false information," Agur said.

"From the beginning, I misunderstood the nature of the car‑use compensation and treated it as part of my salary. But that understanding was incorrect, and I have now repaid the compensation in full," he said, adding that he is cooperating fully with the police.

On Tuesday, Agur sent a letter to colleagues, noting that media coverage about him will likely appear soon, concerning the personal car‑use compensation he received as a school director.

"During job interviews with the school's governing body before I started, I misunderstood the concept of personal car‑use compensation and treated it as a component of monthly salary. From August 2025 to June 2026, I submitted monthly compensation requests in the state employee portal totaling €5,500 (€500 per month)," he wrote.

Agur said he was summoned for questioning by police in early August regarding suspected false information in his compensation requests.

"I realized I had fundamentally misunderstood the nature of the personal car‑use compensation and on 12 August repaid the full amount to the Ministry of Education and Research," he added.

Agur assured colleagues that despite the situation, he remains fully committed to developing the school.

The Ministry of Education and Research is aware of the criminal investigation involving Agur and is cooperating with law‑enforcement authorities.

"Hendrik Agur has acknowledged errors in the travel logs submitted to the ministry, expressed regret over the incident, and repaid the compensation he received," said ministry spokesperson Kersti Ringmets.

She added that the ministry's priority is ensuring stability at the Ida‑Virumaa Vocational Education Center and continuity in the transition to Estonian‑language education. If new circumstances emerge during the investigation, the ministry will take them into account in future decisions.

The ministry will also review its internal control and oversight systems in connection with the case.

Agur took office as director of the IVKHK on 1 August 2025. Before that, he served as director of Kohtla‑Järve High School.

World.title: Risky maneuvers preceded deadly 2025 helicopter crash in Finland
World.content:
The investigation into the helicopter crash in Finland that killed five people found that the aircraft had been flying in a formation‑like manner while disregarding standard group‑flying practices, and had performed several dangerous maneuvers before the collision.

On 17 May 2025, two helicopters were en route from Tallinn to Piikajärvi airfield in Finland. Both took off from the Linnahall heliport in Tallinn at 11:17.

The two Robinson R44 helicopters carried five people: businessman Priit Jaagant, his wife, and Mihkel Kapp in one aircraft; Oleg Sõnajalg and Tiit Kuusk in the other.

The helicopters flew together and collided near Eura airfield at 12:34 at an altitude of about 200 meters. All five people on board were killed.

Finland's Safety Investigation Authority (OTKES) and Estonia's Safety Investigation Bureau (OJK) presented their findings on Tuesday.

Investigators determined that the helicopters flew in a manner resembling formation flight but did not follow the principles required for such operations. In group flying, pilots must agree in advance on key procedures, positioning, and designate a lead aircraft. In this case, the helicopters' positions changed repeatedly — one leading at times, then the other.

OTKES lead investigator Janne Kotiranta said the dangerous maneuvers were such that the accident could have occurred already over the Gulf of Finland.

Investigators noted that without agreed positioning and procedures, predicting the other aircraft's movements becomes extremely difficult, increasing the risk of collision.

After one hour and 16 minutes of flight, the helicopters approached Eura airfield.

Over the airfield, the Jaagant helicopter on the left suddenly turned sharply right toward the north. The second helicopter continued on its original course.

The aircraft collided at 12:34 over the northeastern corner of Eura airfield at roughly 200 meters above ground.

Emergency services received several calls, including an automatic emergency call from a mobile phone onboard one of the helicopters.

The first call came at 12:35 from an airfield employee, triggering rescue operations. The caller reported seeing two small helicopters collide about one kilometer north of the airfield. He said the helicopters broke apart in the air and had people onboard.

The crash sites were located in dense spruce forest, about 150 meters from the nearest forest road and roughly 100 meters apart.

Paramedics and a medical helicopter doctor confirmed all occupants dead at the scene.

Limited visibility and distraction

Trajectory analysis showed that neither pilot recognized the other's intentions or noticed the other aircraft before the collision.

A reconstruction by OTKES indicated that the pilot of the helicopter that veered dangerously right may have had his view obstructed by the passenger seated beside him.

Investigators also found that the pilots' attention may have been focused on aircraft controls, conversations with passengers, or external distractions such as events, people, or other traffic at Eura airfield — rather than on monitoring each other. Attention may also have been directed toward approach procedures for the destination.

Investigators could not determine from onboard systems whether autopilot was used. They said it is possible it was engaged at some point. Autopilot use can reduce situational awareness, including monitoring surroundings during turns, because the pilot is no longer actively executing the maneuver.

No technical faults were found that could have contributed to the collision.

A collision‑avoidance system would not have helped in this case, investigators said. Because the helicopters flew close together for most of the journey, such a system would have issued continuous alerts.

The ELT emergency locator transmitter did not activate during the crash. The device is designed to send a radio signal to help rescuers locate the aircraft. Failure to activate can slow rescue efforts and delay aid.

In this case, the ELT's non‑activation did not affect locating the wreckage, as eyewitnesses immediately began searching, investigators noted.

World.title: Estonian justice ministry after tougher penalties for migrant smuggling
World.content:
Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta has submitted a proposal to the Riigikogu and the government seeking significantly tougher penalties for illegally transporting foreign nationals across the state border.

Pakosta (Eesti 200) sent the Government Office and the Riigikogu Legal Affairs Committee a proposal to amend a bill changing the Penal Code that is currently awaiting its second reading. The ministry wants to significantly toughen penalties for illegally transporting foreign nationals across the state border, or migrant smuggling.

Under the bill, the maximum prison sentence for organizing a standard illegal border crossing would be increased to five years, while offenses committed under aggravating circumstances would be punishable by one to seven years in prison.

Aggravating circumstances would include committing the offense in a life-threatening manner, repeatedly or involving two or more people. The maximum penalty under the relevant section would also be increased from one year to three years in prison.

The Ministry of Justice cited hybrid attacks originating in neighboring countries and a sharp rise in the number of migrants and smugglers in Estonia as reasons for the changes.

"Countries near Estonia have recently come under hybrid attack, with hostile neighboring countries facilitating attempts by large numbers of migrants from third countries to cross state borders. In connection with this, there has also been a noticeable increase in the number of illegal border crossers arriving in Estonia. Illegal border crossers are often assisted by criminals whom migrants pay to smuggle them into the European Union and arrange their illegal border crossings," Pakosta said in the proposal.

While 11 such crimes were registered in Estonia last year, 26 were registered in the first eight months of this year. According to the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), 27 people who were in Estonia illegally were caught while traveling onward within the Schengen Area in 2025, compared with 181 in the first eight months of this year.

Pakosta said that both organizing illegal border crossings and facilitating illegal stays in Estonia are serious crimes that currently carry relatively lenient penalties. Existing law does not even allow authorities to take into account whether an offense is a repeat violation or involves bringing several migrants into the country at once for greater financial gain.

She added that the recent rise in the number of such criminal incidents, as well as the apparent lack of difficulty criminal networks face in recruiting accomplices, shows that the risk of punishment is not sufficiently deterrent.

Estonian police detained suspects in organizing illegal migration. Source: PPA

"In other words, the penalties introduced into the existing law in 2015 no longer reflect the current situation, are not sufficiently deterrent and must therefore be increased. In addition, to deter repeat offenders, the maximum possible penalty for such offenses must also be increased so that repeatedly transporting foreign nationals illegally across the border or transporting several foreign nationals illegally across the border becomes a first-degree criminal offense," Pakosta wrote in the proposal.

Both the Ministry of the Interior and the Prosecutor's Office have said tougher penalties are necessary, she noted.

Pakosta also wants to add a provision to the bill under which damaging an object of importance to national defense would be punishable by one to eight years in prison.

Under the proposal, objects of importance to national defense would include buildings, structures, vehicles, equipment or other property used for activities essential to carrying out crisis-related duties by the Estonian Defense Forces, the Estonian Defense League (Kaitseliit), a security agency, a rescue agency, the Police and Border Guard Board or a defense industry company.

As an example, Pakosta cited the fire in Tallinn in August this year at a building used by defense industry company Milrem Robotics.

Milrem Robotics. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

World.title: UK prog band Marillion to perform in Tallinn
World.content:
In April, the neo‑prog band Marillion will give two full‑length concerts in Tallinn on two consecutive evenings, each with a different setlist.

Marillion will take the stage in Tallinn on Friday, 16 April, and Saturday, 17 April — together forming a single, cohesive Marillion Weekend.

Marillion Weekend is a format created by the band itself, built around specially curated setlists for each night and offering fans a chance to experience Marillion's work more broadly than during a typical concert.

Since 2002, Marillion Weekend repertoires have ranged from well‑known concert favorites to rarely performed tracks and long epics, and in some years have included full albums played in their entirety.

Marillion will perform a different concert programme on each of the two nights. Only two-day tickets will be available for the event, providing admission to both concert evenings.

Each evening will also feature a local guest act: Indrek Patte band on 16 April and Pantokraator on 17 April.

Formed in Aylesbury in 1979, Marillion became one of the best‑known representatives of emotionally charged, dramatic progressive rock in the 1980s. The band, whose name was inspired by JRR Tolkien's "Silmarillion", released its debut studio album in 1983. In total, they have released 20 albums, the most recent in 2022.

World.title: Gallery: Young Estonian artists' fall exhibition opens in Tallinn
World.content:
The "Buy Young Art" fall exhibition has opened at Tallinn's Art & Tonic gallery where visitors can see works by 88 young Estonian artists free of charge. The exhibition will conclude with an art auction on October 23.

Nearly 400 works by 203 artists were submitted for this year's fall exhibition, with the jury selecting works by 88 artists. According to Reigo Kuivjõgi, organizer of "Buy Young Art" and gallerist at Art & Tonic, this year's selection is characterized by the high quality and diversity of the works.

"I am pleased that this time the selection includes more completely new artists than usual who will make their debut at the fall auction. This also makes the exhibition particularly interesting, as young artists with very different styles and approaches have come together under one roof," Kuivjõgi said.

Now in its 11th year, the "Buy Young Art" exhibition and auction gives young artists an opportunity to introduce their work to a wider audience while also bringing young Estonian art closer to enthusiasts and buyers.

"This year's selection is truly diverse and offers an opportunity to explore different artistic media, as in addition to painting, it also features graphic art, drawing, collage, photography and sculpture. The prices of the works also vary widely and start at just €1. When it comes to young art, there is always something for everyone, whether an experienced collector or someone buying art for the first time," Kuivjõgi explained.

Entrepreneur and art enthusiast Kristjan-Thor Vähi, head of Invego and a member of the selection jury, said the high quality of the works made choosing among the candidates quite a difficult task.

"There are many different approaches and truly fresh ideas in the work of young Estonian artists and I really like the fact that they dare to experiment. The exhibition offers a good opportunity to become better acquainted with their work and see what our young artists are doing right now," he said.

According to Vähi, initiatives such as "Buy Young Art" are important for young artists because they help their work reach a broader audience beyond the art world.

"When an artist is at the beginning of their career and is still relatively unknown, an opportunity like this to show their work is very important. It is important for young Estonian art to be visible and accessible and the more young art reaches the public, the more confident people will become about buying it and thereby supporting local artists," he said.

The "Buy Young Art" fall exhibition is open at the Art & Tonic gallery through October 22. All works displayed at the exhibition will be offered at a public auction on October 23.

World.title: Evelin Kasenõmm: Asia puts drones to work — Estonia should follow suit
World.content:
Europe may lead on drone rules, but Asia leads on putting them into practice — and Estonia's first move should be establishing two or three permanent drone corridors, writes Evelin Kasenõmm.

A new economic layer is emerging in Asia, often called the low‑altitude economy, meaning business activities and public services operating in low airspace, along with the infrastructure needed for them.

There is no point for Estonia to compete with Asian countries in drone manufacturing volume. Our opportunity may instead lie in developing digital services needed for safe and automated drone use. Estonia's long‑term experience in spatial data and 3D city models provides a strong technological foundation for this.

China is building an industry out of low‑altitude airspace

China has made the low‑altitude economy a national economic policy area, covering drones, air taxis, logistics, agriculture, urban monitoring, rescue operations, and the necessary infrastructure. According to China's civil aviation authority, by the end of 2025 the country had nearly 3.3 million registered drones — 51 percent more than the year before. Low‑altitude traffic service stations were already operating in 23 provinces1. In major Chinese cities, drones are used for delivering food and medical supplies, firefighting, urban monitoring, and maintaining public order.

Rapid growth has also brought stricter control: in 2026, mandatory drone registration and electronic identification requirements took effect, and conditions for airworthiness and operating permits for larger drones were clarified.

Japan uses drones to solve labor shortages

In Japan, drone adoption is accelerated by an aging population, labor shortages, mountainous terrain, and the difficulty of serving sparsely populated areas.

A framework created in 2022 allows compliant drones to fly beyond the pilot's line of sight even over populated areas. This enables inspection of power lines, railways, or coastlines without the pilot needing to follow the entire route.

Japan's next step is a national drone corridor system. A drone corridor is a digitally managed flight path with predefined routes, permitted altitudes, obstacles, network quality, possible landing sites, and safety requirements.

Technical specifications, guidelines, and a nationwide development map for the corridors were completed in 2025. Corridor management software was published as open source, and an official registration system is planned for 20262.

Drone logistics focus mainly on mountainous regions, small islands, and depopulating areas, where mail, medicines, and small parcels are delivered. Drones are also used in disaster zones. In agriculture, they are integrated with autonomous machinery, satellite data, and shared data platforms to reduce labor needs and improve precision.

Japan's experience shows that drone services are most likely to become permanent where they solve a clear and growing societal problem.

South Korea turns trials into standardized services

South Korea is expanding its drone industry through municipalities and standardized service models. Since 2019, drone delivery, rescue, monitoring, and other public services have been tested. In 2025, 26 municipalities participated.

In the national drone delivery program, services were launched in 2024 on 32 islands, 17 parks, and one port, with flight bases, delivery points, routes, ordering apps, and real‑time flight monitoring. In 2025, the service expanded to 166 areas. Korea is also testing medical logistics, safety monitoring, and transporting island‑produced goods to the mainland3.

Standardization is at the core of Korea's model. The state creates a unified safety and service model that different regions and companies can use. Drone delivery is becoming a practical service that people can order.

The country is also investing in the K‑UAM program. UAM (urban air mobility) refers to air taxis and other new aircraft used in and between cities. Although air taxi timelines have proven overly optimistic, the infrastructure created by the program enables smaller cargo and service drones.

Europe leads regulation, Asia leads implementation

Are Asian industrial countries far ahead of Europe in civilian drone use? Such a generalization would be misleading. The European Union has created one of the world's most comprehensive drone regulatory frameworks. The rules are based on flight risk rather than whether the drone is used for hobby or business.

Europe's strength also includes U‑space, whose legal framework has been in force since 2023. Essentially, it is a digital drone traffic management environment that allows filing flight plans, checking restrictions, issuing flight permissions, tracking drones, and avoiding conflicts with other aircraft.

SESAR — Single European Sky ATM Research — is Europe's joint air traffic modernization program. It has tested cooperation between drone service providers, integration of drones with conventional air traffic, medical logistics, and simultaneous beyond‑visual‑line‑of‑sight flights. Trials show that the technology can work in urban and cross‑border environments4.

Europe's bottleneck is slow and fragmented implementation, as decisions are made by member states. As a result, Europe has many successful pilot projects but fewer everyday services. Europe leads drone regulation; Asia leads drone deployment.

Estonia's opportunities

Estonia's strengths in the drone field include high‑quality spatial data, digital public services, a small and relatively manageable airspace, strong communications and cybersecurity competence, and the ability to integrate state and private‑sector information systems5.

We also have practical use cases. Islands are suitable for transporting medicines and small parcels. Power lines, railways, coastlines, and wind farms require regular inspection. Security agencies need rapidly collected spatial information. Estonia's variable and cold weather allows testing systems in conditions valuable for many foreign markets.

Currently, Estonia often treats drone flights as individual operations where the operator checks restrictions, requests permission, plans the route, and conducts the flight. In a service‑based world, much of this information exchange must happen automatically.

A flight‑planning system should be able to request up‑to‑date data on airspace restrictions, buildings and obstacles, terrain height, weather, and mobile network coverage. The system could evaluate the route, submit a permit request, and transmit drone identification data during the flight. Creating such a digital layer may be Estonia's opportunity.

I see Estonia's first step as creating two or three permanent drone corridors. One would serve logistics between islands and the mainland, another would support energy infrastructure inspection, and a third would handle coastal, forest, or rescue monitoring. A corridor must include reliable connectivity, spatial and weather data, agreed safety requirements, digital permitting, and shared infrastructure for multiple companies. Pilot projects for drone corridors are already underway in Estonia.

In parallel, public‑sector demand must be created. Multi‑year service contracts for detecting power line faults, assessing forest damage, or transporting lab samples and medicines would give the private sector reason to invest in automated solutions and create validated services in Estonia that could later be exported.

In the drone economy of the next decade, a significant part of the value will come from systems that allow drones to fly safely, with minimal human intervention, and legally. Estonia has succeeded before by turning a complex state process into a simple digital service. Opening our low‑altitude airspace to new services could be the next such field — but we must act much faster than we are now.
