He said relief and rescue operations were being carried out effectively in the affected areas through coordinated efforts by the Central and state governments.

World.title: Twenty-five years of leadership, an India transformed
World.content:
In my 48 years in public life, I have seen political parties rise and fall. I have seen leaders emerge with great promise and fade away. I have seen governments change, economies transform and technology alter our lives beyond recognition. One lesson has become increasingly clear to me: ultimately, leadership matters.

In today’s world, technology, knowledge, capital and ideas are freely available. But the true differentiator for nations is leadership — one with vision, integrity, credibility and the ability to execute.

World.title: The China-U.S. rapprochement
World.content:
The world, understandably, has been watching carefully the unfolding summitry between the United States and Chinese Presidents over the last several months. It had been a long time between drinks: just under a decade in the case of President Donald Trump’s last visit to Beijing in late 2017; and just over a decade since President Xi Jinping stood on the White House lawns in 2015 with President Barack Obama.

Editorial | Superpower summit: On the Trump visit to China

Whereas now it is four summits in little more than six months: Beijing, Washington, Shenzhen and then Miami. Now it is everything, everywhere, all at once, with some speculating that we are seeing the birth of a new G-2.

More a new phase

It is natural for the world to wonder what, if anything, has fundamentally changed in the strategic architecture of the U.S.-China relationship. It is always hard to parse the difference between the language and theatre of politics and diplomacy, and what is actually happening on the ground.

Despite the pomp and circumstance in both the Beijing and Washington summits, the reality is that nothing much has changed in the fundamentals of the relationship. Whatever public language might be used, the U.S. and China remain fully engaged in an all-pervasive strategic competition on which of them will emerge as the dominant Indo-Pacific and then global power for the 21st century — militarily, in the economy, technology, foreign policy as well as the underlying ideological contest between democratic capitalism and China’s alternative authoritarian model.

Whatever the diplomatic surround sound might be, core decision-makers in both Washington and Beijing continue to have a deeply realist view of this ongoing strategic contest — or what the Chinese Communist Party (CCP)has long called the “struggle for the future of the international order”. Strategic competition is not going away. The real question is whether that competition can be managed within the framework of some mutually acceptable rules of the road. Or whether it is left unmanaged with a rolling risk of crisis, conflict or even war.

What the U.S. and China appear to be doing is moving towards an imperfect form of bilateral management mechanism. This process began in May last year with the regularisation of the political channel between U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng. This followed the imposition of trade-destroying tariffs of 125% in April 2025 by Mr. Trump, which were then promptly matched by 125% from Mr. Xi. To preserve their respective national economic interests, both sides then walked back from the brink of a full trade war. Since then, Mr. Bessent, Mr. He and their teams have now met eight times — on average every two months. And after a tumultuous decade across every dimension of the relationship, the Bessent-He channel has indeed had a stabilising effect.

Beijing’s push for stability

China in particular has sought stability as it moves into 2027. Later next year, the CCP convenes the 21st Party Congress when Mr. Xi will be appointed to a record fourth term as General Secretary and where he hopes to appoint a fresh phalanx of personal loyalists to the party’s most senior positions. While Mr. Xi’s authority remains unchallenged, he will want as benign a domestic economic environment as possible.

China’s dilemma is that the domestic drivers of economic growth are performing poorly. Private domestic consumption is in the doldrums. Private residential construction is into its sixth year of recession. Private fixed capital investment is also flat-lining. That leaves public investment (i.e., China’s gargantuan techno-industrial strategy) and net exports as the two primary pistons driving the Chinese growth engine.

The last thing Beijing wants is for the U.S. to resume a full-scale trade war which Mr. Trump is perfectly capable of doing. Just look at what he did in 2018 and in 2025. China therefore has been doubling down on its “stability narrative” with the U.S. Its new concept of “constructive strategic stability” is about maximising “cooperation”, managing “competition within defined bounds”, while also managing “strategic differences”, which is code language for Taiwan. In China’s conceptual universe, if these three pillars are properly attended to, then the cardinal objective is achieved: stability.

It is an elegant schemata. It is China’s effort at “managed strategic competition” with the U.S. Moreover, the U.S. has formally accepted this framework in official readouts from the Beijing Washington Summits. But the U.S. has added the explicit caveat that any such bilateral framework be both “fair and reciprocal”.

For Washington realists, that is enough to drive a bus through any “constructive strategic stability” narrative on any day of the week. Furthermore, Beijing would be wildly optimistic if it concluded that Donald Trump is likely to be constrained in his future freedom of manoeuvre because of some grand, overarching foreign policy narrative. The President just does not operate that way.

A fragile truce

What concerns China most is if what is called the “Busan Tariff Truce” agreed to last October falls apart. That original 12-month truce has only been extended two months. If the U.S. concludes that China has not been helpful on U.S. agricultural exports, or in the normalisation of the critical minerals and rare earths trade with the U.S., there is a real risk that the Busan Truce collapses. And if the European Union were to move in the same direction on tariffs given the crisis in European manufacturing, the consequences for an export-dependent Chinese economy would be large.

For all these reasons, both tactical and strategic, the U.S.-China relationship remains deeply fragile. Even if the Busan Truce extends beyond December, the effective general U.S. tariff rate against China will remain much, much higher than, for example, India’s. Beyond trade, there also remains a formidable array of export controls on critical technologies, including world-class chips where China remains several years behind the U.S. And that leaves to one side a bilateral foreign investment regime which remains deeply restrictive at both ends of the relationship.

Therefore, breathless reporting about an emerging “G2” between the U.S. and China in some sort of global strategic condominium is fanciful. Whatever tactical accommodations may occur in the trade relationship, the fundamental nature of the strategic competition between Washington and Beijing continues. Remember it was Donald Trump, on the very eve of Mr. Xi’s state visit to Washington DC, who stated, “Whoever wins in AI, wins.” That is Xi Jinping’s view too. That does not exactly sound like an emerging G-2 to me.

Kevin Rudd is Global President and CEO of Asia Society, New York, and the 26th Prime Minister of Australia

World.title: Fertiliser hoarding, black marketing to be curbed in rabi crop season in Rajasthan
World.content:
The Fertiliser Distribution Regulatory Task Force in Rajasthan on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) gave direction for ensuring timely distribution of full quantity of fertilisers allocated by the Centre during the upcoming rabi crop season. Farmers in the State will get uninterrupted supply of fertilisers in accordance with their demand.

An effective action will also be taken to curb irregularities such as hoarding, black marketing, forced tagging and illegal storage of fertilisers. As many as 744 fertiliser inspectors have been deployed across the State to oversee the task.

Chief Secretary V. Srinivas, who presided over a meeting of the task force here, said the interests of farmers would be safeguarded by ensuring “smooth and transparent” distribution of diammonium phosphate (DAP) and urea. “There will be no shortage of fertilisers during the critical rabi sowing period,” Mr. Srinivas said.

Principal Agriculture Secretary Manju Rajpal said the committees appointed under the ‘Dharti Mata Bachao’ campaign were holding regular meetings to monitor the availability of fertilisers. At present, the State holds the stocks of 3.73 lakh metric tonnes of urea, 1.04 lakh metric tonnes of DAP, 95,000 metric tonnes of nitrogen, phosphorous and potassium, and 2.09 lakh metric tonnes of single superphosphate.

The Centre allocates fertilisers to the States on a month-wise and company-wise basis. The Agriculture Department has devised district-wise plans based on the allocations received by the State government and the actual demand from the districts.

World.title: Traffic snarls at Delhi’s brand-new flyover persist week after opening
World.content:
A week after the Barapullah Phase-III flyover was thrown open with a promise of cutting the journey from Mayur Vihar to AIIMS in Delhi to just 15 minutes, commuters are spending more than an hour inching through traffic on the newly opened corridor. On Tuesday, traffic queues stretching over 2 km brought the 3.5-km stretch to a crawl, with commuters reporting waiting times of 70–100 minutes.

Videos shared by commuters showed vehicles packed bumper-to-bumper on the elevated road, with even ambulances caught in the snarl.

“I have been stuck on the flyover for the past 25 minutes in a traffic jam,” a commuter travelling from Noida towards New Delhi told The Hindu around 10.30 a.m. When contacted an hour later, the commuter said they were still stuck in the traffic and that it had taken more than 70 minutes to get off the flyover.

Another commuter described the stretch as “completely blocked”, saying traffic had remained stationary for nearly an hour and questioning the absence of traffic personnel on that particular stretch.

Meanwhile, the Public Works Department (PWD) on Tuesday placed jersey barriers at the merger point, a police officer said.

“The jersey barriers, which are concrete or plastic road dividers used to channel vehicles, are aimed at preventing vehicles from joining the existing corridor at an abrupt angle, allowing traffic to merge more smoothly and reducing the sudden slowing that has been contributing to the bottleneck,” the officer said.

The traffic police also deployed personnel at the merger point to manually regulate the flow, allowing traffic from each side to pass one stream at a time to ease the bottleneck, he added.

Redesign sought

In a letter dated October 1, the Delhi traffic police asked the PWD to modify the merger near Sundial Park. The letter was based on a joint inspection conducted by senior traffic police officers and PWD officials on September 30 to examine traffic movement and the geometry of the new flyover and its adjoining stretches.

The traffic police found that the new flyover joins the existing corridor through a relatively sharp, almost rectangular alignment rather than a gradual curve. This forces traffic to merge abruptly and creates a bottleneck at the junction.

The issue was already evident within days of the flyover opening. Barapullah Phase-III was opened to public traffic on September 29 and by the following evenings, queues had stretched up to 3.5 km.

“Travelling to Bhikaji Cama Place from Ghaziabad was a nightmare. Traffic was stuck on the new Barapullah flyover for more than 30 minutes in the morning,” a commuter said. Suggesting that congestion could be reduced by discouraging unnecessary traffic, the commuter said the stretch could even be made a toll road.

Traffic pattern

The traffic police have also written to Google seeking an update of the traffic pattern on the new road. South Delhi Deputy Commissioner of Police (Traffic) Sandeep Gupta said the company had sought seven to 10 days to incorporate sufficient traffic data.

World.title: Gajendra Singh Patel accuses Hemant Soren government of encouraging infiltration in Jharkhand
World.content:
Newly-appointed Jharkhand BJP in-charge Gajendra Singh Patel on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) lashed out at the Jharkhand government over its failures, corruption, and law-and-order situation. He also cornered the government on student issues.

He attacked the State government over the issue of infiltration, voter lists, women’s safety, and employment. He asserted that the Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM)-Congress-Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) alliance has been in power in Jharkhand since 2019, yet the public has received nothing but disappointment.

At his first press conference at the party’s State office in Ranchi after assuming the post, Mr Patel, also the BJP National General Secretary, raised serious questions about the Jharkhand government’s performance and policies. Jharkhand BJP President Aditya Sahu, Leader of the Opposition Babulal Marandi and former Chief Minister Raghubar Das were also present.

Sharing his experiences from a two-day visit, Mr. Patel stated that the information gathered and his interactions with people across districts revealed a dire situation in the State.

“All promises made by JMM, Congress and RJD in its manifestos proved to be false. The government has failed to provide basic amenities such as healthcare, education, roads, electricity, drinking water, and irrigation facilities. Every section of society, including the poor, tribals, Dalits, backward classes, women, farmers, and the youth, is distressed,”Mr. Patel said.

A tribal leader from Madhya Pradesh representing the Khargone Parliamentary seat for the second time, Mr. Patel was appointed Jharkhand in-charge in September 2026.

He asserted that the BJP has undertaken historic initiatives for the tribal community, but ruling parties in the Jharkhand government have misled innocent tribals; however, the community now understands the reality.

Soren encouraging infiltration: Patel

Mr. Patel, who is also the National General Secretary, alleged that the Hemant Soren government is mired in corruption.

“Mineral resources like sand, coal, and stone are being plundered along with the misappropriation of the District Mineral Foundation Trust (DMFT) fund. Water, forests, and land are being openly looted. The BJP has vehemently opposed this rampant loot at every level, from the streets to the legislative assembly. The current government has failed to undertake any work in the public interest,”Mr. Patel said.

Referring to the recent students’ protests over alleged irregularities in the recruitment exams of Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and Jharkhand State Selection Commission (JSSC), Mr. Patel said that the State government is playing with the future of the youth.

“Paper leaks and irregularities in examinations have destroyed the futures of lakhs of young people. When the youth took to the streets to protest democratically, they were subjected to atrocities. The youths and students of Jharkhand are angry by the government’s style of functioning,”Mr. Patel said.

He also questioned the Hemant Soren government over the issue of alleged infiltration in Jharkhand. Mr. Patel asserted that instead of curbing it, the state government is actively encouraging it. He further alleged that instead of taking action, the government machinery is engaged in providing direct or indirect assistance to infiltrators.

SIR is a transparent process

He pointed out that Prime Minister Narendra Modi took effective steps to strengthen the democratic process by enrolling genuine voters and removing ineligible ones from the electoral rolls; however, this government is opposing even a transparent process like Special Intensive Revision (SIR).

“By spreading misinformation and misleading the tribal community, this government is inciting unrest, which is highly inappropriate. The government will not succeed in its agenda,”Mr. Patel said.

He also raised questions regarding the state’s law and order situation and criticised the government over the issue of women’s safety. He remarked that an atmosphere of fear prevails in the state, and criminals are operating without any fear of the law, adding |that murders, robberies, kidnappings, and shootings are taking place openly.

World.title: Kerala High Court sets aside detention order of Thiruvananthapuram councillor R. Sugathan
World.content:
The Kerala High Court on Tuesday set aside the detention order issued by the Thiruvananthapuram Collector against councillor R. Sugathan under the Kerala Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act (KAAPA Act), 2007.

A Division Bench of Justices Anil K. Narendran and S. Murali Krishna set aside the detention order and directed the Superintendent of Central Prison and Correctional Home, Viyyur, to release Mr. Sugathan if he was not required in any other case.

The court held that his detention order lacked application of mind and that he had been served with several illegible pages in the documents pertaining to his arrest. The unexplained delay in considering his representation seeking cancellation of the order or his temporary release violated his constitutional rights against arbitrary arrest and detention.

The Collector had considered seven criminal cases registered at the Vattiyurkavu police station for ordering Mr. Sugathan’s preventive detention, classifying him as a ‘known rowdy.’ The court noted that final reports had been filed in six of the seven cases, and investigation was under way in the seventh one. The court had allowed anticipatory bail in one of the cases and had directed Mr. Sugathan to appear before the investigating officer within one week. Mr. Sugathan had sought an extension of time to surrender thereafter, which had been granted.

Mr. Sugathan informed the court that he had filed representations to the Additional Chief Secretary (Home) and the Chief Secretary against the detention order. He stated that there was delay on the government’s part since they allegedly waited till the receipt of the opinion of the advisory board, established under the KAAPA Act.

He contended that the authorities concerned failed to consider the sufficiency of bail conditions imposed in one of the cases, which prevented him from committing similar crimes. He claimed that the preventive detention proceedings were initiated due to “political malafides” as he was a councillor of the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation.

Director General of Prosecution T. Asaf Ali argued that Mr. Sugathan had been on the rowdy list since 2014. Altogether, there were 22 criminal cases registered against him. He argued that the councillor refused to receive the arrest intimation and service of documents, and he attacked the police personnel who went to arrest him, along with his co-accused. He also contended that even if some of the documents or pages were illegible, it would not vitiate the detention order.

World.title: SIR in Delhi: disposals of Form 7 nearly six times those of Form 6
World.content:
For every Form 6 application for inclusion in Delhi’s electoral roll disposed of during the ongoing claims and objections phase of the special intensive revision (SIR), nearly six Form 7 applications seeking objections to the inclusion of names or their deletion from the draft roll have been cleared, data accessed by The Hindu showed.

According to the weekly constituency-wise forms disposal report, only 569 Form 6 applications were disposed of between August 31 and October 4. In comparison, 3,209 Form 7 applications were cleared during the same five-week period covered by the data. More than two-thirds of these Form 7 applications, or 2,352, were disposed of in the last two weeks alone, while no Form 6 application was disposed of last week.

Since the claims and objections phase began on August 31, 1.94 lakh applications seeking enrolment and 5,431 forms seeking deletion of names have been received so far, according to data from Delhi Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) Ashok Kumar’s office.

The data also showed that 2.12 lakh Form 6 and 51,747 Form 7 applications had already been received before the claims and objections period began, between June 16 and August 30.

The claims and objections period ends on October 30, while disposal of the applications and notices has to be completed by November 30. The final roll is set to be published on December 4.

During the claims and objections period, an Indian citizen aged 18 or above can submit Form 6 to seek inclusion of their name in the final SIR roll, either as a first-time voter or if their name was left out of the draft roll published on August 31. An elector can simultaneously file Form 7 to object to or seek deletion of another elector’s name from the roll.

Once an objection is received, a poll official serves a notice on the concerned elector, giving them 15 days to respond before any action is taken. A Booth Level Officer (BLO) is also required under the rules to verify the address and make three attempts to deliver the notice. For Form 6 applications, a BLO is assigned to conduct physical verification and submit a report, based on which a decision is taken. “There is a seven-day window for assigning a BLO; however, there is no set deadline for disposing of Form 6 applications,” an official said.

Queries were sent to Mr. Kumar’s office over the lower rate of Form 6 disposal compared with Form 7, but no replies were received till the time of going to press.

Special camps

Meanwhile, Mr. Kumar’s office is organising a special camp at all polling station locations on October 11 to maximise enrolment of electors left out of the draft roll. Another round of special camps for enrolment of young electors will be held at all colleges, universities and other educational institutions in Delhi on October 7 and 8, his office stated in an official release.

World.title: Delhi court seeks report on ‘custodial torture’ charges by protesters
World.content:
A Delhi court has granted bail to 17 students and journalists who were taken into police custody on Monday and sought a report from Delhi Police on allegations of “custodial torture” levelled by two protesters.

Judicial Magistrate Animesh Kumar of the Patiala House Courts issued four separate bail orders on Monday night. The arrested persons were protesting outside the Parliament Street police station earlier in the day, demanding registration of an FIR against a police officer accused of molesting a woman journalist during a protest in the national capital against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Unlawful assembly

Delhi Police had registered a case against the 17 accused, alleging that they were part of an unlawful assembly, obstructed a public area, roughed up police personnel and caused damage to public property.

Acknowledging the gravity of the allegations, the court pointed out that while any person has the right to protest peacefully, assaulting police officers on duty is a matter of serious concern<NO> which cannot be permitted under the garb of peaceful protest.

In its order, the court said, “It should be noted that allegations against the accused are serious in nature. One police official has allegedly sustained injuries as per the medico-legal case (MLC) produced by the IO.”

It, however, took into account the age of the accused. The judge said the allegations against the accused were “serious” in nature but they were not “habitual offenders”. The counsel for the accused had argued that some of the arrested persons had sustained injuries.

CCTV footage

“However, their medico-legal cases were not conducted immediately after the incident,” the court noted. It added, “Since the accused Dharmender and Samarth have levelled allegations regarding custodial torture, let a report be called from DCP New Delhi regarding the same. The relevant CCTV footage of the Parliament Street police station be preserved.”

The judge cited that their careers were still ahead of them and, hence, bail was justified on the facts of the case.

The police had sought 14 days of judicial custody for the arrested persons. It also argued that they might commit further offences or tamper with the investigation.

World.title: Pakistan successfully tests launch of extended-range Fatah-IV cruise missile: ISPR
World.content:
Pakistan conducted a successful test launch of the indigenously developed extended version of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile, the military’s media wing said in a statement on Tuesday.

In a statement, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said, “Equipped with advanced avionics and state-of-the-art navigational aids, the weapon system is capable of engaging targets at extended ranges with high precision and lethality.”

“The test also validated additional technical parameters of various sub-systems incorporated for improved accuracy and enhanced survivability,” it added.

According to the statement, the launch was witnessed by senior officers from the Pakistan Army along with scientists and engineers of the developing agency.

It added that President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir and all service chiefs commended the successful test and “appreciated the technical prowess, dedication and commitment of all those who contributed towards achieving this milestone”.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi congratulated the nation on the successful test, said a statement issued by his ministry.

“The successful test of the extended version of Fatah-IV cruise missile is an important advancement in the defence sector,” Naqvi was quoted as saying. He also congratulated the scientists and engineers who worked on it and appreciated their efforts.

In May, the Army Rocket Force Command conducted the successful test fire of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile.

A month earlier, the Army Rocket Force Command had also conducted the successful training launch of the Fateh-II missile system. The same month, the Pakistan Navy successfully fired a locally developed anti-ship ballistic missile to engage targets at an extended range.

World.title: Petrol price up by Rs1.19 per litre, high-speed diesel's down by Rs1.91 in latest revision
World.content:
The government on Tuesday increased the price of petrol by Rs1.19 per litre and reduced that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs1.91 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs394.83 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs395.85 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 7 (Wednesday).

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months.

On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.

Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: PTI long march: CM Afridi-led convoy camps in Mattani for the night, heads to Khyber next
World.content:
PESHAWAR: The PTI convoy led by Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Tuesday reached Mattani, located on the outskirts of Peshawar — its latest stopover in the party’s long march that is being carried out to demand the release of jailed party founder and ex-prime minister Imran Khan.

PTI Information Deputy Secretary in KP Ikram Khatana told Dawn that the protesters, who set out from Kohat earlier in the day, would spend the night in Mattani.

“They will leave for Khyber at 2pm tomorrow,” he said.

The march began on Sunday (Oct 4) from Lakki Marwat, and the Afridi-led convoy reached Kohat on Monday night.

The protesters aim to reach Khairabad — which borders Punjab — by Oct 8, where the KP chief minister will announce the next plan of action. And while the plan for the trek beyond Khairabad is yet to be announced, the PTI — which is in the government in KP and in the opposition in the Centre — had previously announced Islamabad as its final destination.

However, the Centre has warned the party against any protest or gatherings in Islamabad. But, PTI decided to embark on the march after weekend talks with the federal government to bridge their differences failed for multiple reasons , particularly over the counterterrorism policy.

Before setting out for Mattani, CM Afridi addressed the PTI supporters at University Chowk in Kohat and criticised the federal government over its counterterrorism policy.

“Your failed policy did not end terrorism. Let me propose a policy under which peace can be established in 100 days,” he said, according to a statement released by his office.

He said he was “not afraid of anyone and neither are the youth of KP”.

“I have shared the draft of my demands on social media”, he continued, referring to a set of proposal he said he had sent to the opposition team negotiating with the government last week. CM Afridi said if any of his demands was unconstitutional or illegal, he would cancel the long march.

The provincial chief executive rued that the PTI had employed all legal and constitutional means for the fulfillment of its demands, including meetings with Imran. But when one was not served justice, the Constitution allowed for peaceful protest, he added.

He said the PTI would protest peacefully.

He maintained that the people wanted a resolution of their issues through the provincial government’s policy, adding that there had been military operations in KP for the past 22 years but terrorism was still prevalent.

“Your failed policy did not end terrorism. Let me propose a policy under which peace can be established in 100 days,” he remarked.

He added that once they would decide to move to Islamabad, nobody would be able to stop them. Referring to the PTI postponing the launch of its march from Sept 27 to Oct 4, he said “they now have problem that this is Test match”.

CM Afridi also said that there were reports that Imran’s health was again deteriorating in jail. He said if “Imran’s health is played with or he suffers any harm”, the jail administration, prime minister and other relevant authorities would be responsible.

March will not be allowed to move beyond Attock: Kundi

Earlier in the day, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi vowed that PTI’s long march would not be allowed to proceed beyond Attock in Punjab — which borders KP — saying the party “did not have the capacity” to do so.

Kundi made the remarks while speaking to Geo News programme ‘Geo Pakistan’.

“They cannot go any further than Attock,” Kundi said, challenging PTI to “try to take a step”.

He contended that the party did not have “enough capacity” to march further.

“They claim to have two million people with them […] show us the people; they don’t have the capacity.”

Kundi said the province was suffering from terrorism and “yet, they [PTI] want to march to Islamabad instead”.

Speaking about his recent meeting with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi in Peshawar, the governor recalled that the two often held meetings to discuss the security situation, and during last week’s meeting, the two also discussed “dialogue with the PTI as well as the way forward in relation to PTI’s long march”.

Kundi cautioned: “If there is a mishap during the long march — especially if someone from southern KP who wants to reach Islamabad to carry out a plot [is involved] — what screening mechanisms does PTI have in place to prevent that from happening?”

He also assailed the PTI-led KP government for “staying silent” on terrorist incidents.

“When the federal government asks for their support against militancy, they say that the army should leave the province and that we should hold a dialogue with Afghanistan,” Kundi said, accusing the incarcerated PTI founder of “having militants settled in KP in the past”.

“He was called Taliban Khan,” Kundi added, referring to Imran.

Kundi further claimed that KP Chief Minister Afridi was taking “directions from PTI leader Murad Saeed”, whom the governor described as a “runaway”.

He vowed that Saeed “will be brought before the people and made to pay for his actions”.

Speaking about the possibility of governor’s rule in KP, Kundi said: “If the president and prime minister hand the task to the province […] and deem governor’s rule necessary, the province will ensure its implementation.”

He held that governor’s rule was the last resort. “Surgery is the last option; first, you are put on medication. No one wishes to do it,” he said, referring to governor’s rule.

“We want to continue, but if you are pushed to the limit and there is no option left, then it is considered.”

On Monday night, after reaching Kohat’s Lachi tehsil, CM Afridi said while addressing PTI supporters that this time, the party’s struggle was a long one that required endurance and sustained mobilisation, according to a statement issued by his office.

“We must not exhaust ourselves. Our struggle is a long one,” he said, adding that, however, from Oct 8 onwards, a “T20 match” would begin.

Kundi also posted on social media that he had chaired an “important security meeting” with KP Chief Secretary Shahab Ali Shah, KP’s Inspector General of Police (IGP) Zulfiqar Hameed, and other senior officials.

“The province cannot afford complacency when terrorism, crime and law-and-order challenges continue to threaten our people,” Kundi said, calling on the provincial government to “make the safety of its people its foremost responsibility”.

“Political activity cannot come at the expense of security, and every institution must focus on protecting lives and maintaining peace,” he added.

Separately, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also urged the PTI to end its long march and invited the opposition to sit with the government to resolve contentious issues through political dialogue.

The march so far

After launching the already-postponed march from Lakki Marwat on Sunday afternoon, the KP CM’s caravan reached Karak at night, where Afridi addressed supporters at Jail Chowk.

Ahead of the march, movement on several roads in KP’s Dera Ismail Khan, Upper and Lower South Waziristan, Tank and Hangu was restricted under Section 144 for varying periods .

On Sunday, former KP CM Ali Amin Gandapur, who was leading PTI workers from DI Khan to Lakki Marwat, took a U-turn from Yarik because of road blockades and the prevailing law and order situation.

Noting that Section 144 had been imposed in the area for three days, Gandapur stressed that the party leadership had clearly directed workers not to damage public property or engage in any activity that could worsen the situation.

Nevertheless, he contended that the return should not be viewed as a withdrawal from the protest movement, but as a temporary decision.

In Karachi , a planned protest campaign in different areas was disrupted after police deployed personnel at several locations, blocked roads and detained several party workers and leaders.

The PTI claimed that police detained more than 75 of its leaders and workers, including women, from different parts of Karachi. It further alleged that arrests made in other parts of Sindh, including Sukkur, put the total number of detained PTI workers across the province at more than 100.

World.title: PTI says Imran's cousin Qasim Zaman taken into custody after Rawalpindi DC orders detention under MPO
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: PTI founder Imran Khan’s cousin, Qasim Zaman, was taken into custody by the authorities when he went to the Adiala jail to meet the ex-prime minister on Tuesday, the party said after the Rawalpindi deputy commissioner (DC) ordered his detention under the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance (MPO) for 30 days.

PTI’s Awais Younas Chaudhry told Dawn that Zaman used to visit the Adiala jail to meeting Imran as the Islamabad High Court (IHC) had allowed the jailed ex-premier twice a week meetings — on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

“On Tuesday he [Zaman] reached the Gorakhpur Naka near the prison at around 2:40pm and informed the jail authorities that he was there to meet Imran,” Chaudhry said, adding that, however, police detained him and shifted him to an unknown location.

Later, Rawalpindi DC Nadeem Nasir’s order for Zaman’s detention under the MPO surfaced.

The MPO allows the authorities to order detention and restrict judicial review of such orders.

In his detention order, DC Nasir cited the ordinance, as well as letters by the police officials.

The Sept 6 order, a copy of which is available with Dawn, said police informed the DC that Zaman was a political activist “who is instigating/ planning to organise unlawful assembly/ commit violence, deliver unlawful speeches to cause damage to human life and public/ private properties”.

“He is also inciting the public to commit violence/ damage public /private properties and trying to stop the public functionaries from performing their duties in current situation, and him being at large is likely to disturb the public peace, safety and tranquility,” the order said, citing information shared by police.

The ordered further stated that under these circumstances, the Rawalpindi City police officer recommended his detention “in order to prevent him from acting in a manner prejudicial to public safety and to ensure maintenance of public order u/s 3(1) MPO, 1960 for a period of 30 days”.

The Rawalpindi District Intelligence Committee also endorsed the police’s stance during its meeting on Tuesday and “unanimously recommended that the above-named person be detained to prevent him from any unlawful activities”, the order said.

In light of these developments, the Rawalpindi DC ordered Zaman’s detention under the MPO for 30 days.

“His custody shall be placed under the supervision of the superintendent of Central Jail, Rawalpindi,” the order stated, adding that Zaman had the right to file an appeal to the Punjab Home Department against the directive.

Previously, the authorities had also detained all three of Imran’s sisters — Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi — under the MPO ahead of the PTI’s protest march, which was earlier scheduled to set out for Islamabad on Sept 27. However, the march was postponed to Oct 4 and as per the current itinerary, the protesters aim to reach a Khairabad in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Oct 8, when KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi would share the future plan of action.

Meanwhile, there have been reports of the arrests and detentions of several PTI members and workers, including provincial ministers and lawmakers.

Usually, Imran’s sisters — Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi — would be the ones to reach Adiala every week in the hopes to meet him. But Qasim was visiting the prison following their detentions.

Imran has been in prison since 2023. The IHC has allowed Imran twice-a-week meetings — on Tuesdays and Thursdays — with his family, lawyers and other associates. Despite the order, the PTI founder has been restricted from meeting visitors.

On Aug 18, the Supreme Court (SC) also directed the authorities to allow Imran meetings with his family as it ordered his medical checkup at Islamabad’s Shifa International Hospital, a private facility.

After the SC’s interim order, one of Imran’s sisters, Noreen, was allowed two consecutive meetings with him. But there has been no other meetings since her last one on August 25.

Advocate Awais said that other lawyers, including PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, PTI General Secretary Salman Akram Raja, Khalid Yousuf and Riaz Shah, had also reached the Adiala jail today, but were not allowed to meet Imran.

“It is nothing but contempt of the IHC order,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) condemned Zaman’s detention, describing it as an act of “blatant fascism” and a violation of fundamental constitutional and human rights.

In a statement, TTAP spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmad Yousafzai demanded the immediate and unconditional release of Zaman, saying that his arrest was an example of state coercion, political victimisation and violation of basic human rights.

The spokesperson highlighted that Imran’s sisters had been detained earlier and now his “non-political cousin” had also been taken into custody outside the prison.

“Targeting citizens merely because of their relationship with Imran Khan is an open violation of the Constitution and law,” the statement said.

The opposition alliance urged the authorities to immediately stop what it termed the harassment and arrests of citizens through the use of state power.

Yousafzai said the alliance would continue to oppose any actions that undermined citizens’ constitutional and human rights.

World.title: Dar warns of 'serious implications' for regional peace, security if Pakistan deprived of water share under IWT
World.content:
Attempts to deprive Pakistan of its rightful share of water would have “serious implications” for regional peace and security, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Tuesday, in an address regarding the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT).

The deputy premier was addressing the International Water Symposium convened by the Embassy of Pakistan in Austria in collaboration with the Diplomatic Academy of Vienna, according to the Foreign Office.

Water and the IWT remain a contentious issue between India and Pakistan, following New Delhi’s unilateral abeyance of the accord in April last year after an attack on tourists in India-occupied Kashmir. The development preceded a brief military conflict between the two sides in May 2025.

In his keynote address delivered via video message, Dar stressed that there should be “no misunderstanding” about Pakistan’s resolve to safeguard its rights and interests under the IWT and international law.

“Any attempt to deprive Pakistan of the waters rightfully allocated to it would have serious implications for regional peace and security,” he said.

Stressing that water was fundamental to human survival, prosperity and environmental sustainability, Dar pointed out that its availability was increasingly determining the stability of relations among states. He added that for countries sharing transboundary river systems, a “permanent interdependence” was created by their geography.

“The fundamental question, therefore, is whether shared waters will be governed through cooperation and agreed legal frameworks, or become instruments of political pressure and confrontation,” he said.

For Pakistan in particular, the deputy premier added, water security was inseparable from food security, as the waters of the Indus River System sustained the lives and livelihoods of over 250 million people in the country.

He highlighted that this water sustained agriculture, food security, energy production, economic development, and life-supporting ecological systems.

“Any attempt to undermine Pakistan’s rights over these waters carries consequences that extend far beyond a bilateral disagreement,” DPM Dar stressed.

The IWT, which Pakistan signed in 1960 after a decade of negotiation, replaced what the deputy premier termed “upstream discretion” with binding legal obligations, establishing a framework of “certainty and predictability” for both countries. This, he said, reflected a fundamental recognition that “waters upon which millions depend must remain insulated from the fluctuations in political relations”.

However, he said, this principle was now being challenged as India had unilaterally placed the treaty “in abeyance” in April 2025, although it contained no provision permitting either party to do so.

He highlighted that on Aug 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) had issued a unanimous award on the status of the IWT, ordering India to uphold the treaty and restricting its work on a hydropower project. The PCA had unequivocally confirmed that the treaty “remains fully in force” and that India remained bound by its obligations under it, as there were no grounds justifying its suspension or termination.

“This is an important reaffirmation of Pakistan’s position, as well as a fundamental principle of international law,” Dar stated. “Pacta sunt servanda: agreements must be kept.”

The deputy premier stressed that the court’s decision reinforced that the rights and obligations established under the IWT could not be displaced unilaterally. However, he pointed out that India continued its “intransigent behaviour and illegal actions”.

“Pakistan has consistently sought to address its differences with India through dialogue, diplomacy and the dispute resolution mechanisms provided under the treaty,” he said, adding that the country was also participating in the Neutral Expert proceedings under the treaty administered by the PCA’s Vienna Office.

He emphasised Pakistan’s constructive participation in both the Neutral Expert proceedings and the PCA’s award processes, which he said demonstrated the country’s confidence in the IWT’s institutional mechanisms.

The deputy premier highlighted that the credibility of international law depended “not only on the conclusion of treaties, but also upon their faithful implementation and respect for decisions rendered under their agreed procedures” — a principle Pakistan had consistently upheld, he added.

Dar stressed the “profound” humanitarian, economic and security implications of the use of water as an “instrument of pressure”. He added that India’s illegal actions had implications extending beyond the region, as they would establish a “dangerous precedent” for other transboundary river basins that relied on international agreements.

“Amidst challenges to the international law-based world order, the international community should be strengthening treaty-based cooperation, not permitting its erosion,” he said.

“The principles of equitable and reasonable utilisation, the prevention of significant transboundary harm, and cooperation remain essential to international water governance. Their application must, however, respect the specific rights and obligations established under the treaties governing individual river systems.”

The deputy premier also highlighted Pakistan’s continued commitment to dialogue, diplomacy and the peaceful settlement of disputes and termed cooperation over shared waters “indispensable” to regional peace, development and sustainability.

He said that the way forward depended on three fundamental principles: the implementation of the IWT in letter and spirit; for all differences and disputes to be addressed through its established mechanisms and for these decisions to be respected; and the strengthening of technical engagement, transparency and data-sharing by both countries in accordance with the treaty.

“Our preference remains clear: cooperation over coercion, dialogue over confrontation, and the rule of law over unilateralism,” DPM Dar said. “The future of transboundary water governance must rest on cooperation, mutual respect, and the faithful implementation of international obligations. Pakistan stands ready to pursue this path.”

The IWT allocates the eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas and Sutlej — to India, while the western rivers — Indus, Jhelum and Chenab — are largely allocated to Pakistan. The 1960 water-sharing agreement has also established mechanisms for data-sharing and dispute resolution.

In April 2025, India announced a unilateral suspension of its obligations under the treaty, following an attack on tourists in India-occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam that killed 26 — an incident New Delhi blamed on Islamabad without evidence, while Islamabad denied the allegations.

Following India’s actions, Pakistan termed any attempt to suspend its water share an “act of war”, noting the IWT had no provision for unilateral suspension. It later argued that Delhi’s action was a violation of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

In its order, the PCA backed Pakistan’s stance, declaring that the IWT between the two countries remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.

However, in a statement issued by its foreign ministry, India — which is officially a member of the intergovernmental court — said it did not recognise the court and “categorically” rejected the verdict.

World.title: PM Shehbaz says law took its course in AJK after 'unfortunate events' in recent months
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday expressed dismay over the “unfortunate events” in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) in recent months, adding that, however, the law took its course.

He was addressing a ceremony in Islamabad in which four AJK Council members – nominated by the AJK Legislative Assembly – were administered the oath by PM Shehbaz, who is the chairman of the council.

Referring to the “unfortunate events” in recent months in AJK, he said: “We all regretted it, wished that they did not do that. We all tried to make them understand with utter seriousness”.

The premier did not name anyone specifically but was seemingly referring to protests by the now proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC).

The government and the JAAC have been at odds over various issues, most notably the committee’s demand to abolish the 12 refugee seats in the AJK Legislative Assembly, which resulted in violence-marred protests across the region.

On June 5, the JAAC was declared a proscribed organisation by the regional government and placed under the First Schedule of the region’s anti-terrorism act (ATA). A day later, AJK authorities launched a crackdown on the JAAC, arresting scores of its leaders and later placing 147 of its activists on the Fourth Schedule of the ATA.

In his address, PM Shehbaz recalled that an all-parties conference was held in Muzaffarabad where “everyone spoke freely, though they were absent”.

He said it was agreed during the meeting that after elections in the region, the new legislative assembly’s decision or the law passed by it, through consensus or majority, would be respected — an apparent reference to a decision on refugee seats.

“But, unfortunately, they did not accept this noble suggestion. Nevertheless, the law took its course. […] Pakistan had to fulfil its political and legal obligations given that forces were working against Pakistan and the Kashmir cause on a foreign agenda,” the prime minister said.

He also spoke about the four-day military conflict with India in May last year, saying that the Pakistani military, under the leadership of Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir, had played a “historical role” and taught the adversary “a lesson that it can never forget”.

“I, once again, pay tribute to Pakistan’s armed forces and CDF Munir and congratulate them.”

At the onset of his address, he congratulated the newly-elected members of the AJK Council.

“This council is a bridge between Pakistan and AJK. It is my honour to have this opportunity to make this bridge stronger.

“We will work harder for the progress of AJK and serve the people of AJK.”

He also called on the AJK president and prime minister to fulfil their constitutional duties and resolve the public’s issues.

“The federal government will mobilise resources to support your development efforts,” PM Shehbaz stated.

The four council members sworn in today were former AJK Legislative Assembly speaker Chaudhry Latif Akbar of the PPP from Muzaffarabad, former minister Mushtaq Ahmed Minhas of the PML-N from Bagh, former minister Chaudhry Muhammad Saeed of the PML-N from Mirpur, and Chaudhry Manzoor Ahmed of the PML-N from Muzaffarabad.

They were declared elected unopposed as no other candidate entered the contest.

World.title: UN chief hails Pakistan's 'pivotal role' in US-Iran conflict, calls for 'return to diplomacy'
World.content:
United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday lauded Pakistan’s “pivotal role” in mediating between the United States and Iran as he called on the parties to end the conflict and return to diplomacy.

Addressing a press conference in Islamabad alongside Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, he said: “Pakistan’s spirit of engagement is front and centre on issues of international peace and security.

“I salute Pakistan’s leadership for helping to create the conditions for dialogue between the US and Iran and mediating that conflict. Your efforts helped deliver the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, the subsequent ceasefire and the framework for future negotiations. Every Pakistani should be proud of that pivotal role,” he said.

“And from Islamabad, I want to send a loud and clear message to all parties: end the conflict, return to diplomacy and restore navigational rights in accordance with international law. There will never be peace in the region until the right of self-determination of the Palestinian people is recognised, as Pakistan has long championed,” he said.

At the outset of his speech, the UN chief said that it was “wonderful to be back in Pakistan”.

“I am in the closing months of my tenure as UN secretary general. Before that, I served ten years as UN high commissioner for refugees,” he said.

“Pakistan has shown that, even in difficult circumstances, perhaps especially in difficult circumstances, compassion and responsibility must go hand-in-hand,” he said.

He asserted that Pakistan mattered not only because of its size, but because it brought an “essential perspective” to global debates.

“For decades, Pakistan opened its doors to millions of Afghans fleeing conflict and instability. Communities around this country shared whatever they had with people seeking protection and safety,” Guterres said.

He added that the UN was committed to working together with the country to uphold protection principles and ensure that returns of Afghans “proceed in a voluntary, safe and dignified way”.

According to the UN chief, Pakistan had put a spotlight on the value of multilateralism, dialogue, mediation and diplomacy at a time of growing division and mistrust around the world.

“Those same values are vital within societies as well,” he stated.

“Here and around the world, we know that inclusive institutions, respect for human rights, and a vibrant civic space are necessary to help strengthen social cohesion, build trust and enable people to contribute fully to their country’s future.”

Guterres also appreciated Pakistan’s contributions to United Nations peacekeeping.

“Pakistani women and men have served with courage and distinction in some of the most difficult and dangerous environments,” he said.

“More than 180 brave Pakistani souls gave their lives in the service of peace. We honour their sacrifice.”

The chief highlighted Pakistan’s leadership with Denmark on UN Security Council (UNSC) resolution 2823, which strengthened accountability for crimes against UN peacekeepers.

One hundred and fifty-three countries co-sponsored the resolution, which according to Guterres, was the largest number of co-sponsors for a UNSC resolution in UN history.

The UN chief also shared his plans to visit United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP) later in the day to pay tribute to the mission and to peacekeepers worldwide.

Commenting on terrorism in the country, he said: “Pakistan has endured immense suffering. Thousands of people lost their lives. Families and communities across the country continue to bear scars. We stand with Pakistan in confronting this threat of terrorism.”

He added that addressing terrorism and legitimate security concerns was necessary and indispensable.

“Experience shows that the strongest and most effective security responses are those grounded in international law, human rights and the rule of law.”

Towards the end of his speech, Guterres spoke about the climate crisis.

“My last visit to Pakistan came during the catastrophic floods of 2022. I will never forget the utter devastation I saw,” he said, referring to the unprecedented floods four years ago that affected approximately 33 million people and claimed the lives of 1,700 people.

“But I also saw the resilience, determination and solidarity of the Pakistani people,” Guterres said. “Pakistan is on the frontlines of climate chaos despite contributing only a tiny fraction of global emissions.”

He appreciated Pakistan’s response to the crises, including establishment of the Loss and Damage Fund and the country’s growing clean energy transition.

However, he asserted that leadership from vulnerable developing countries cannot substitute for responsibility from developed countries.

“The G20 represents 80 per cent of global emissions. We need a drastic reduction in those emissions this decade,” he highlighted.

“The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities must apply, but all countries must do their part,” he said.

Meanwhile, Dar said he “greatly appreciated” Guterres’ visit, which he asserted was a reflection of the “long-standing and close cooperation” between Pakistan and the UN.

“It also shows our common resolve to strengthen multilateralism and our cooperation at a time of profound global challenges,” he said.

“We have consistently sought to uphold the purposes and principles of the UN charter, advance international peace and security, contribute to peacekeeping and strengthen multilateral solutions to global challenges.”

Dar referred to Guterres as a “great friend” of Pakistan, adding that the country would not forget his solidarity during the 2022 floods as well as his efforts to mobilise international support for recovery and reconstruction.

During its time as an elected member of the UNSC, Dar said Pakistan had tried to make “significant contributions” to international peace and security, with particular emphasis on dialogue, diplomacy, and the peaceful settlement of disputes.

“Our initiative on resolution 2788 on strengthening multilateralism and mechanisms for the peaceful settlement of disputes is a reflection of Pakistan’s approach in this regard,” the minister recalled.

“The unanimous adoption of that resolution reaffirmed the importance of negotiation, mediation, preventive diplomacy, and the good offices of the UN secretary general.”

He appreciated Guterres’ engagement with the follow-up to the resolution, including the participation and presentation of “solid recommendations” in the open debate held in July this year.

Dar said the country valued the secretary general’s “readiness” to extend his good offices in situations where dialogue and diplomacy could help reduce tensions and create space for peaceful solutions.

“This is particularly relevant at a time when the international community is confronted with multiple conflicts and crises,” he reiterated.

“Pakistan believes that the UN must remain at the centre of international efforts to address these challenges and that diplomacy must be given every opportunity to succeed.”

Pakistan, Dar said, had played a “proactive and constructive” role in promoting dialogue and de-escalation in the Gulf region. He appreciated Guterres’ support for Pakistan’s mediation efforts and his recognition of the importance of diplomatic engagement.

“Pakistan’s role in facilitating dialogue is consistent with our broader approach at the UN, which is to promote cooperation over confrontation, dialogue over conflict and peaceful settlement over the use of force,” he stated.

The minister said Pakistan supported the chief’s UN80 initiative, which seeks to make the UN more “effective, efficient and fit for purpose”.

“We believe that efforts to strengthen the organisation must reinforce its ability to deliver on its core mandates, while ensuring that the priorities and concerns of developing countries remain central.”

According to him, stronger, effective, inclusive, and representative multilateralism was needed at a time of growing geopolitical tensions, conflicts, humanitarian crises, climate vulnerabilities and economic pressures.

He further appreciated the UN chief’s “continued attention” to issues of particular importance to Pakistan, including regional peace and stability, counter-terrorism, climate vulnerability and development challenges.

“We also greatly appreciate the UN’s consistent position on the Jammu and Kashmir dispute and the reiteration of the UN framework and UNSC resolutions for resolving the dispute,” he said.

Dar said he briefed the UN chief on India’s unilateral move of holding the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance, which he referred to as a blatant violation of international law.

“We underscored the need to ensure that India stops weaponising water and fulfils its obligations under the IWT.”

He also highlighted Pakistan’s “deep concern” at the continued use of Afghan soil for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan. He urged the UN chief and the international community to help address these challenges.

Dar meets UN chief

Earlier in the day, Dar held a one-on-one meeting with the UN chief, with the two discussing regional and global issues relating to peace and security, the Foreign Office (FO) said. The FO said the discussions covered Palestine, Jammu and Kashmir, Afghanistan, counter-terrorism and the future of multilateralism.

Dar briefed the UN secretary general on Pakistan’s positions on Jammu and Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), reaffirming Islamabad’s call for a just and peaceful resolution of the Kashmir dispute in accordance with relevant UNSC resolutions.

According to the FO, Dar also highlighted Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to promote dialogue and de-escalation, including its facilitation of the Islamabad talks between the US and Iran. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to dialogue and diplomacy as the most effective means of resolving disputes.

The UN secretary general appreciated Pakistan’s longstanding contribution to the UN, as well as its diplomatic efforts to promote dialogue, mediation and de-escalation, the FO said.

President confers Nishan-i-Imtiaz on UN chief

President Asif Ali Zardari also conferred the Nishan-i-Imtiaz on Guterres in recognition of his “distinguished international service, leadership of the UN and contribution to global peace and development,” a handout by the President’s Secretariat said.

The award, first to any UN secretary general by Pakistan, was conferred in a special investiture ceremony held at Aiwan-i-Sadr, the statement said.

According to the handout the president also separately met with the UN chief and appreciated his principled leadership, his efforts for international peace, dialogue, diplomacy and peaceful settlement of disputes, as well as his constructive engagement with Pakistan and attention to the concerns of developing countries.

“The president said Pakistan remains steadfast in its support for the Palestinian people and their right to self-determination,” it added.

“He appreciated the [UN chief’s] consistent advocacy for Palestinian statehood and a two-state solution and said Pakistan would continue supporting efforts towards implementation of the relevant UNSC resolutions,” the handout detailed.

The president further reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to peace and stability in South Asia, stressing that durable peace required sustained dialogue between Pakistan and India and the resolution of all outstanding disputes, particularly Jammu and Kashmir, as agreed under the UN resolutions respecting the sentiments of the Kashmiri people.

He also conveyed Pakistan’s position that the IWT was a binding international agreement and could not be unilaterally suspended or placed in abeyance.

President Zardari, per the handout, stressed that water should not be used as a weapon and an instrument of political pressure and that Pakistan’s water rights, recognised by international courts, under the treaty must be respected.

On the subject of regional peace and diplomacy, Zardari said the country’s diplomatic efforts, including the Islamabad Talks, had been guided by the “imperative of de-escalation, dialogue and protection of human life”.

“He reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to facilitate diplomacy wherever it could be helpful, stressing that there is no alternative to dialogue for addressing regional disputes,” the handout said.

The president also spoke about counter-terrorism and Afghanistan. He said Pakistan remained a “committed partner” in the global fight against terrorism and has made enormous sacrifices in this cause.

“Pakistan continues to face terrorism from groups operating from Afghan territory and has shared evidence concerning external support to terrorist proxies targeting Pakistan,” the president said, stressing that Afghan territory must not be used against Pakistan or any other country.

UN chief’s visit

Guterres arrived in Islamabad in the early hours of Tuesday for a two-day official visit.

“Upon arrival, the secretary-general was received by Acting Foreign Secretary Ambassador Nabeel Munir,” the FO said in a post on X.

The UN chief also visited the National Disaster Management Authority’s (NDMA) headquarters on the first day of his visit.

The visit comes as Guterres’ 10-year tenure as UN chief is set to end on Dec 31. In its Monday statement, the FO said that during Guterres’ visit, Pakistan’s “efforts towards strengthening multilateralism and international peace and security, as well as its strides towards disaster preparedness and early warning, will be highlighted”.

PM Shehbaz met Guterres on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month. The two discussed major regional and international developments, including the situation in the Middle East.

In that meeting, Guterres commended Pakistan’s role and strong voice at the UN, as well as its contribution to international peace and security. The UN chief also appreciated Pakistan’s role and sacrifices in countering terrorism.

World.title: PM Shehbaz urges PTI to call off long march, resolve issues through dialogue
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday urged the PTI to end its long march to Islamabad and invited the opposition to sit with the government to resolve contentious issues through political dialogue.

The opposition has gone ahead with its march despite warnings from the Centre, which has vowed to prevent any gatherings in Islamabad. The protest aims to demand the release of jailed party founder and former prime minister Imran Khan.

Addressing the groundbreaking ceremony of the Kashmir Chowk underpass in Islamabad on Tuesday, the premier said it was “unfortunate” that the “dreadful shadows” of long marches were hovering again, despite the PML-N and the PPP making efforts to engage the PTI in talks.

The two parties, the prime minister said, held talks for two days in National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq’s chamber, and “it was hoped that politics of confrontation would end”.

“Unfortunately, that did not happen. They [PTI] only had one purpose: to ensure that the talks do not succeed,” the premier said, adding that the opposition party demanded changes to things already settled upon.

PM Shehbaz asserted that these protests and long marches affected the country’s economy and created hindrances in exports, imports and manufacturing.

“We collectively improved the economy in 2.5 years and reached macroeconomic stability. Now is the time for it to flourish,” the premier added.

“In September, our information technology exports, remittances and the country’s production improved,” he said.

“If someone harms it, is it not equivalent to being an enemy of the country?”

The premier stressed that putting the economy in shambles and the lives of people in danger will not be allowed.

“The law will take its course,” he said.

“I will still say: come to your senses. Will your actions harm the country or benefit it? … End your long march and protests. When you end them, we will surely sit down with you,” he said.

Earlier in the same ceremony, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said, without naming anyone, that people had to see for themselves which public representatives were working for their welfare and which ones were engaging in “negative politics”.

Responding to the premier’s remarks, PTI interim chairman Barrister Gohar Khan said that talks remained “limited to offers”.

“No positive step gets taken and it is a matter of great concern for us,” he said while speaking to reporters outside Adiala jail.

He pointed out that it had been almost a year since the party’s last meeting with Imran on Oct 16, 2025, calling this “inhumane”.

He also criticised that Imran was being denied meetings with his doctors, family, lawyers, and party, saying: “We did not want to sit for a photo session together with you.”

Gohar added that the party had always stood with the state and put Pakistan first, yet they were still not granted access to their leader.

Tallal says talks conditional on PTI calling off march

Separately, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry also spoke about the resumption of talks, saying that it remained conditional upon PTI calling off its marches and protests.

Addressing a press conference in Islamabad, he warned that constitutional and political measures were in place to respond to the PTI’s ongoing long march and held Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi responsible for the breakdown in negotiations.

“Political and constitutional measures are in place,” Chaudhry said.

Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry speaks to media on Oct 6, 2026. — DawnNewsTV

He added that the “wise” people part of the PTI’s delegation had tried to make the talks successful. Chaudhry further said that if the talks had succeeded, Pakistan would have had a united political front and the PTI would have gained “political space”. He added that a “hardening of the state” was now close, stressing that “enough softness has been shown”.

“The state is like a mother, but it also has to act like a father at times,” Chaudhry said.

“Constitutional options are under discussion, but the political option comes first,” he said. Commenting on the talks, Chaudhry told reporters that on the first day, Naqvi presented the government’s position regarding terrorism in KP, which included facts about the provincial government’s lack of involvement in the province’s affairs, budget and counterterrorism efforts.

Chaudhry said the next day, the PTI delegation returned to Islamabad to continue talks after discussing the terms of the agreement with KP’s senior leadership in Peshawar.

He said CM Afridi had previously reassured the Centre that the PTI delegation had the authority to reach an agreement on behalf of the provincial government.

“We were assured that on terrorism, they [PTI] agreed 100 per cent on the federal government’s points,” Chaudhry said, adding that it was only then that Naqvi travelled to Lahore to PM Shehbaz and informed him that the PTI and the PML-N had agreed on the terrorism issue.

“The prime minister said, ‘give as much political space as you can’,” Chaudhry told the media.

According to him, PM Shehbaz told Naqvi that “parties’ political capital comes and goes”. Chaudhry said the premier further told Naqvi that when Pakistan was on the brink of financial default, strict measures reduced PML-N’s political capital, but they ensured that the country would not default.

The second day of the talks started after the two sides had agreed on the issue of terrorism, Chaudhry said.

“The win for us in the draft agreement was that we would be successful in bringing the PTI to the same page for eliminating terrorism,” he said.

The draft was ready by 9pm on the second day of the talks, and Naqvi was getting ready to take it to President Asif Ali Zardari, according to the state minister.

“Everything was fine,” he said, adding that some back and forth happened on further edits, but they were all agreed upon.

“At the last minute, the opposition sat in a separate room for a while to consult with the KP chief minister. When they came out, they couldn’t look us in the eye and asked for permission to leave,” Chaudhry said. He added that the PTI delegation thanked the PML-N for patiently conducting the talks.

The nation had agreed on the two National Action Plans (NAP) against terrorism, Chaudhry said, adding that the second plan was agreed upon during the PTI’s government under former prime minister Imran. He said that NAP was linked to “Pakistan’s Constitution, its needs, security, stability and Islamic teachings”.

Citing Afridi’s statement that he wouldn’t allow a plan against the people of KP, Chaudhry questioned if Imran’s NAP was against the people of the province.

Chaudhry claimed that KP was unsafe for common people and politicians alike; however, he noted that at the same time, the PTI’s leaders and workers were safe from threats in the same region.

“The only one safe there is PTI,” he said, questioning, “Why do [terrorists] have a soft corner for you only?”

On the possibility of talks resuming, Chaudhry said that any further talks were conditional upon the PTI calling off its marches and protests.

“Don’t encourage terrorists. Instead, let’s kill them together,” Chaudhry further stated.

Opp-govt dialogue failure

Over the weekend, the government and opposition held two rounds of talks , which did not yield positive results, with counterterrorism policies and access to Imran emerging as two major sticking points.

On Sunday, the PTI said it wanted immediate access to party chief Imran for consultations, and even agreed to forgo other demands in return for a meeting with Imran. However, the government declined to make access to Imran part of the proposed agreement, the opposition party claimed.

Another deadlock was terrorism in KP. The federal government asked the KP government to support its counterterrorism measures and support emergency measures within 72 hours in the merged tribal districts, the PTI said.

Instead, the PTI proposed that authorised representatives of the federal and KP governments meet within 72 hours to develop a clear, comprehensive and mutually agreed strategy for peace and counterterrorism, the statement added. The PTI said the health and medical treatment of Imran Khan was also raised as a matter of fundamental importance.

Meanwhile, PTI leader Salman Akram Raja, who was a part of the opposition’s delegation, said the primary reason for the failure was disagreement on anti-terrorism actions in KP.

Raja said the opposition stood firm on its principled position that anti-terrorism actions should be based on an agreement between the federal government and the KP government, and would be framed in consultation with stakeholders.

After talks between the government and the opposition ended without headway, interior minister Naqvi on Sunday accused CM Afridi of “sabotaging” negotiations.

On Sunday, Naqvi also held a meeting with KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi to discuss the political and security situation amid speculations of ‘imminent’ governor’s rule in the province. A government source told Dawn that the government was seriously considering the imposition of the governor’s rule in KP.

But Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said on Monday that a return to negotiations was possible if there was an assurance of positive progress by the opposition regarding counterterrorism efforts in KP.

Speaking on Geo News’ programme ‘Capital Talk’, he said that the federal government aimed to end terrorism in Pakistan, protect its borders and keep people safe.

“The provincial government will have to play its role at any cost in this policy and operation,” he added.

He said that both sides were still in contact, and said that if “better sense prevails” amongst the opposition and they could provide “assurance of some positive progress” in this regard, then they could sit down for more talks.
