Ivanishvili also explained why, in his view, this did not happen in 2012. He said the government did not yet have sufficient resources at the time:

“Over these years, we have accumulated enough resources to begin fully strengthening our sovereignty…”

A statement made almost six months before the election gradually turned into a concrete political plan. In August 2024, Georgian Dream openly announced that it needed a constitutional majority in the election to declare the “collective National Movement” illegal. The European Commission included the plan in its report that year.

Then EU High Representative Josep Borrell, speaking in the European Parliament, described the promise to ban opposition parties as one of the worrying developments during Georgia’s election campaign.

Two years later, that campaign promise has turned into a concrete lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

Three lawsuits, three lists — how the number of parties facing a ban grew

The lawsuit changed three times over the course of one year.

The Constitutional Court registered the first lawsuit on 31 October 2025, under case No. 1912. Eighty-eight members of parliament signed it. They sought to ban three political forces:

Unity — National Movement

Coalition for Change

Strong Georgia — Lelo

Later, on 21 April 2026, 89 MPs filed a second lawsuit, No. 1958. They added a fourth party, Federalists, to the list.

The list of parties facing a ban grew again in September 2026.

On 24 September, the Constitutional Court registered lawsuit No. 1979, signed by 88 MPs. This time, the authorities are seeking to ban five parties, including former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia’s party, For Georgia.

The law gives the Constitutional Court a maximum of nine months to rule on such a case. Each new lawsuit has therefore sparked debate over whether that period starts again from the beginning.

The authors of the lawsuit hope the Constitutional Court will complete the process by January 2027, by which time all five parties would have been banned.

Opposition representatives, meanwhile, argue that Georgian Dream is actually prolonging the process by adding new parties.

On what grounds can a party be banned?

Georgia’s Constitution sets out specific grounds for banning a political party.

It prohibits parties whose goals include overthrowing or forcibly changing the constitutional order, undermining the country’s independence or violating its territorial integrity. The authorities can also ban parties that promote war or violence or incite national, ethnic, regional, religious or social hatred.

Only the Constitutional Court can ban a political party.

The Georgian Dream lawsuit relies on these constitutional grounds and argues that the listed parties’ activities target the state.

A significant part of the argument draws on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission, known as the Tsulukiani Commission.

One of the lawsuit’s key arguments concerns the opposition parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the 2024 election, parliament and the government.

The plaintiffs also link the opposition parties’ actions to “sabotage”, calls for Western sanctions against the Georgian authorities and attempts to “punish” the country.

The lawsuit, for example, treats the opposition’s refusal to recognise the election results and its view that Georgian Dream is an illegitimate government as “sabotage”.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also cited the legitimacy of the government when explaining why the authorities added Gakharia’s party to the list.

He said that although the party, unlike its “fellow opposition parties”, agreed to take part in parliamentary work, it still does not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government:

“It is true that they entered parliament, but to this day they do not recognise the constitutional order or the legitimacy of the government. Under these circumstances, the spirit of this political party’s activities is no different from that of the other relevant political parties,” he said.

Why these parties?

The lawsuit explicitly cites the parties’ political influence as a reason for seeking their ban. It also mentions other opposition parties, such as the Republican Party, which does not appear on the list, and says:

“At present, they do not have significant influence on politics or a realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold. Accordingly, at this stage, there is no apparent need to ban them.”

A brief overview of the five parties facing a ban: Политические силы, объединенные “Грузинской мечтой” в единый “черный список”, имеют разное происхождение, историю и идеологию. Некоторые из них действительно произошли из политической семьи «Единого национального движения». Некоторые пытались занять независимое пространство именно между ЕНД и «Грузинской мечтой». Политическое же ядро партии Гиорги Гахария и вовсе вышло из самой «Грузинской мечты». «Единство — Национальное движение» «Единое национальное движение» экс-президента Михеила Саакашвили — самая старая партия в этой пятерке и единственная, имеющая опыт пребывания у власти: в течение 9 лет она являлась правящей партией Грузии. На выборах 2024 года ЕНД официально получила 211 216 голосов — 10,17%. Уже долгие годы партия переживает кризис лидерства и на данный момент находится в режиме переходного управления. В августе 2026 года был создан временный управляющий совет, руководителем которого стал Иракли Павленишвили. Избрание постоянного председателя партии должно состояться позже. Главным лицом, принимающим решения в партии, по-прежнему остается Михеил Саакашвили, который уже пять лет находится в тюрьме. ЕНД позиционирует себя как резко проевропейская и евроатлантическая политическая сила. Её историческое ядро — это политическое наследие правительства Саакашвили. Именно правление ЕНД в 2004-2012 годах является главной мишенью большей части иска «Грузинской мечты» и обвинений комиссии Цулукиани. Coalition for Change Coalition for Change was created ahead of the 2024 elections and brought together several different political forces. The coalition included Nika Melia and Nika Gvaramia’s Akhali party, Zurab Japaridze’s Girchi — More Freedom and Elene Khoshtaria’s Droa. Akhali is a pro-European centre-right liberal party. Girchi — More Freedom has a more distinctly right-libertarian economic platform, while Droa has a liberal and activist profile. In the 2024 election, the coalition received the largest number of official votes among the opposition forces — 229,161, or 11.03%. Most of its leaders had previously been associated with the UNM. The coalition brings together parties that broke away from the UNM or emerged independently at different times. Strong Georgia — Lelo The core of Strong Georgia is the Lelo party, which Mamuka Khazaradze and Badri Japaridze founded in 2019. Both entered politics after careers in business. A broader coalition formed around Lelo in 2024. It included Ana Dolidze’s For People, Aleko Elisashvili’s Citizens and Levan Tsutskiridze’s Freedom Square. The coalition sought to present itself as an independent alternative to both Georgian Dream and the former ruling UNM. The party has a pro-European, centrist-liberal profile. Economic development, institutional reform and Western integration have remained central themes in Lelo’s programmes. In 2024, Strong Georgia officially received 182,922 votes, or 8.81%. Gakharia for Georgia Giorgi Gakharia’s party stands out from the other four parties in the group because of its origins. Gakharia was not a member of the government under Mikheil Saakashvili. Instead, he served as economy minister, interior minister and eventually prime minister under Georgian Dream. He resigned as prime minister in February 2021 and founded his own For Georgia party in May. The party initially sought to present itself as an alternative to both Georgian Dream and the UNM. It received 7.79% in the 2021 municipal elections and 161,521 votes, or 7.78%, in the 2024 parliamentary election. Gakharia’s case shows how broadly Georgian Dream applies the concept of the “collective National Movement”: today, the category also includes a political force led by one of Georgian Dream’s former leaders. Federalists Federalists are the newest party among the five. Giga Bokeria, Tamar Chergoleishvili and their allies founded the party in August 2024 after leaving European Georgia. Giga Bokeria chairs the party, while Tamar Chergoleishvili heads its Tbilisi organisation. The party identifies individual freedom, human rights, European development, free competition, decentralisation and strong democratic institutions as its core principles. Politically, it is a pro-European and liberal force with a more right-wing economic platform. Federalists did not take part in the 2024 parliamentary election. Bokeria and Chergoleishvili’s group has a long-standing political conflict with Mikheil Saakashvili and today’s UNM.

At the same time, the lawsuit notes that the question of whether these parties are unconstitutional could arise in the future if they gain significant influence over the political process.

Initially, the “Federalists” also fell into the category of parties with “no realistic prospect of crossing the electoral threshold”. However, in March 2026, they joined the “Opposition Alliance”, a nine-party coalition. In April, Georgian Dream also called for the Federalists to be banned.

Thus, according to the lawsuit, a party’s political influence is one of the factors that the plaintiffs themselves take into account when seeking to ban it.

Представители оппозиционного альянса, март 2026 года

How all opponents of the government became the “collective National Movement”

The “collective National Movement” is neither a party nor a legally recognised political organisation. It is a political term coined by Georgian Dream that it has used for years to group various opposition forces into a single political camp, thereby portraying its opponents as a common “enemy”.

Over the years, the boundaries of this category have gradually expanded. It has come to include not only the National Movement itself (UNM, the former ruling party) and parties that broke away from it, but also forces that positioned themselves as alternatives to both the UNM and Georgian Dream. These include Mamuka Khazaradze’s Lelo and Giorgi Gakharia’s party, even though Gakharia himself previously served as prime minister for Georgian Dream.

The term then expanded further. Irakli Kobakhidze included not only opposition parties but also non-governmental organisations and media outlets as part of the “collective National Movement”:

“They are all in the same pot… All the radical opposition parties, all these radical NGOs, their radical media,” Kobakhidze said.

According to Georgian Dream’s current narrative, the political differences between these forces are not significant. The ruling party portrays them as different parts of a single network controlled from abroad. This logic brings together parties with different histories, leaders and political platforms under the “collective National Movement”.

The rhetoric has gradually acquired a specific political goal. In 2024, Kobakhidze compared removing the “collective National Movement” from the political system with banning the National Socialists in post-war Germany.

A year later, he said: “This crisis within the collective ‘National Movement’ must deepen, and it will deepen, ultimately leading to the complete destruction of the collective ‘National Movement’. Only then will Georgia develop a healthy democratic system.”

What does the attempt to ban the parties mean? Views

Representatives of the opposition parties themselves see the Georgian Dream lawsuit not as a separate legal dispute but as part of a broader process of restricting political competition.

Their main argument is that the government is using the courts to remove from the political arena forces that remain its electoral competitors.

Giorgi Sioridze, a representative of the Strong Georgia — Lelo alliance, points to the fact that the list of parties facing a ban has changed several times. He says that each new lawsuit restarts the nine-month period for considering the case.

He believes this allows the government both to retain the option of banning the parties and to delay a final decision.

Giga Lemondzhava, a representative of Coalition for Change, sees the party ban as a new stage in what he describes as authoritarian politics. However, he says political struggle cannot be ended simply by cancelling a party’s legal registration.

The National Movement takes a similar position. One of its leaders, Levan Khabeishvili, called on the opposition in a letter sent from prison not to focus entirely on the parties’ legal status: “Don’t get hung up on the issue of banning parties! They have banned the country!”

His message is that accepting the legal framework created by Georgian Dream would make the opposition dependent on an agenda set by the government. Political resistance, he argues, should not depend on a party’s registration.

The case of Giorgi Gakharia’s party is particularly notable. For Georgia took part in the 2024 election, later entered parliament and does not support violent struggle against the government. Given all this, the party’s MP Giorgi Sharashidze questions how the main constitutional grounds cited in the lawsuit apply to them:

“Unconstitutionality, calls for violence, calls to overthrow the government… What does any of that have to do with us? … We even entered parliament.”

Giorgi Gakharia, meanwhile, sees his party’s addition to the “blacklist” as part of a broader process. In his view, the authorities are trying to leave no functioning critical opposition within institutional politics:

“Regardless of whether they ban us or not, we will not back down in the struggle to restore Georgia’s democracy and protect its European and Euro-Atlantic path.”

The Federalists’ case exposes another contradiction. The party did not take part in the 2024 parliamentary election. Its leaders previously belonged to former President Mikheil Saakashvili’s political team, but they have been in sharp conflict with both Saakashvili himself and the UNM, the party he founded, for many years. Despite this, the authorities also regard them as part of the “collective National Movement”.

Party leader Tamar Chergoleishvili says banning a political competitor is unacceptable to her regardless of her attitude towards that competitor:

“Of course, we see all the other parties as competitors, but we want to defeat our competitors on a level playing field, through fair competition, not as a result of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s bans.”

Georgian Dream explains the process very differently.

According to the authorities, the issue is not about eliminating political competitors but protecting the democratic system. Georgian Dream MP Levan Machavariani argues that opposition parties that appear different on the surface are actually parts of the same political network. He says dividing them into “radical”, “semi-radical” and relatively “constructive” forces is artificial and serves as a way for a common political centre to assign them different tasks.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze follows the same logic. He says the government promised voters to “neutralise foreign agents” and is now fulfilling that promise:

“We made a promise to voters that we would neutralise foreign agents in our country, and we are genuinely fulfilling that promise.”

Kobakhidze also uses this argument to explain the ban:

“It is very important that the state make a decision on this issue — a decision that serves the national interest.”

When can democracy ban a political party?

Europe has precedents for banning political parties, but authorities treat such bans as an extreme measure, usually in very different circumstances from those in Georgia. Banning five parties at once would be unprecedented.

Under the standards of the Venice Commission, authorities may justify dissolving a party if it uses violence or advocates overthrowing the democratic constitutional order. A peaceful call to change the political system or constitution does not, in itself, justify a ban.

European practice focuses not on how radical a party’s position is, but on whether its goals and actions pose a real threat to the democratic order and whether sufficient evidence supports that conclusion.

European case law also sets a high threshold. Spain banned Batasuna after authorities established its links to the ETA terrorist organisation. In Turkey, in the Refah Partisi case, the court considered evidence that the party sought to establish a theocratic system and had made statements linked to the use of force.

In Germany, meanwhile, authorities ultimately did not ban the NPD in 2017, even though the Constitutional Court found that the party’s goals were incompatible with the democratic order. However, the court concluded that the party lacked the real ability to achieve those goals.

What Europe says about Georgia’s case

The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has taken a particularly strong position on Georgia.

Even before the 2024 election, a PACE monitoring delegation said Georgian Dream’s calls to ban the opposition threatened political pluralism.

In 2025, PACE described the planned ban as targeting “virtually the entire functioning democratic opposition” and said such a move would effectively create a one-party system in Georgia.

In June 2026, the Assembly made its position even clearer.

Resolution No. 2664 says the initiative to ban “virtually all democratic opposition parties” is unacceptable. It says implementing the initiative would effectively create a one-party dictatorship in Georgia, which would be incompatible with membership in the Council of Europe. The Assembly called on the authorities to withdraw the lawsuit filed with the Constitutional Court.

The European Commission’s 2025 report also describes “serious democratic backsliding” in Georgia and says legislative and institutional changes threaten political pluralism. The report also notes that the ruling party has effectively consolidated control over the legislative and executive branches of government.

What happens if the parties are banned?

Banning the five parties could have consequences far beyond cancelling their names and legal registrations. The issue is what kind of political competition will remain in Georgia ahead of the next parliamentary election in 2028.

If the Constitutional Court upholds Georgian Dream’s lawsuit, all opposition forces that crossed the five per cent threshold in 2024 could disappear from the political arena. According to official Central Election Commission figures, nearly 800,000 people voted for them in total — about a quarter of all voters.

The current legislation also allows the authorities to extend restrictions to people linked to the banned parties. The court can prohibit them from establishing or joining other parties, standing as candidates in elections or holding political office. Authorities may also terminate the mandates of sitting elected MPs.

A new party name would not automatically provide a way around the ban. The law already includes the concept of a “successor party”. If a new political force substantially repeats the goals, activities or membership of a banned party, the court can ban it as well.

Under the Georgian Dream scenario, all of this could effectively leave the country without political parties or politicians representing the current opposition.

The process is not taking place in isolation. In recent years, the government has also adopted several laws that have sharply tightened the legal environment for foreign funding, grants and the activities of NGOs and media outlets.

Meanwhile, anti-government protests continue in Georgia, and the political confrontation between the authorities and their opponents remains highly tense.

The 2028 election is key to understanding the political significance of these developments. If the court upholds the lawsuit and the current restrictions remain in force, Georgia could enter the next parliamentary election with all four opposition forces that crossed the threshold in 2024 legally dissolved. The mechanism for quickly banning possible successor parties would already be in place.

Ban on opposition parties in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan’s corruption whistleblowers: protection on paper and in practice
World.content:
Azerbaijan drafts anti-corruption bill

Azerbaijan has drafted a separate bill aimed at encouraging and protecting people who report corruption. The bill was submitted to the Milli Majlis on 5 October and is due to be discussed by a parliamentary committee on 6 October.

The initiative comes amid continuing complaints that police officers demand money from citizens, while journalists investigating corruption are sentenced to lengthy prison terms. Existing legislation already provides protections for people who report corruption. The key question, therefore, is from whom – and how – the state intends to protect citizens after they report such cases.

Protection provided by law

Article 11-2 of the Law on Combating Corruption prohibits disclosing the identity of a person who reports corruption without their consent, as well as threatening them or their relatives. It also prohibits dismissing an employee because they have filed a complaint, transferring them to another position, making unlawful deductions from their salary or obstructing their career progression.

If an employee provides evidence that retaliatory measures have been taken against them, the burden of disproving the allegation falls on the employer. The law also prohibits assigning a complaint for review to the person against whom it was made or to anyone with an interest in the outcome of the investigation.

Information registered through an internal reporting procedure must be examined within 20 working days, after which the person who submitted it must be informed of the outcome. If a complaint concerns the head of an organisation, the person may approach a higher-ranking official or a specialised anti-corruption body. The obligation to investigate reports and inform complainants of the outcome therefore existed before the new bill was introduced.

However, a 2025 report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) points to significant gaps in the implementation of these safeguards. Azerbaijan has no specialised body, unit or official dedicated exclusively to protecting people who report corruption. The authorities were also unable to provide examples of the provision placing the burden on employers to disprove evidence of retaliation being applied in 2023-2024.

The report also notes that public disclosure through the media and social networks is not recognised as a protected channel for reporting corruption. This gap is particularly significant for people who report wrongdoing to journalists rather than to state bodies.

Alleged $300 bribe demand and claim of violence

On 28 August, Gündəlik Naxçıvan reported that a young driver had been detained. According to the outlet, police officers said the driver was under the influence of alcohol. He denied this and said he was willing to undergo a medical examination at a hospital.

Instead of being given a medical examination, he was allegedly asked to pay 500 manats (about $300):

“They told me: either you pay the money now, or they will take both you and the car away.”

According to the outlet, after the driver refused to pay, additional traffic police officers arrived at the scene. Five or six officers allegedly used force against him. Witnesses said the driver suffered a broken arm and ribs as a result.

The complaint therefore concerns not only an alleged demand for a bribe, but also claims that force was used instead of allowing the driver to undergo a medical examination and challenge the allegation against him.

Threats of drug possession and other criminal charges

On 10 September, Gündəlik Naxçıvan published another complaint from residents of Ordubad. People who had returned from Russia said they were taken from their homes and brought to a police station, where they were tested for drugs in a toilet without a doctor present.

One complainant, who asked to remain anonymous, said his test was negative but that he was nevertheless asked to pay 10,000 manats (about $5,882). He said that after being threatened with arrest and torture, he paid 5,000 manats (about $2,941).

Similar allegations have been made in the past. In a Toplum TV report published on 17 December 2025, Shiraz Guliyev, who had returned from Turkey, said he was asked to pay 300 manats (about $176.50) near the Sadarak customs checkpoint on the grounds that he had allegedly dropped a cigarette butt. Guliyev said he told officers that he did not smoke, but was threatened with arrest on charges of resisting police if he refused to pay.

In June 2025, blogger Mehman Huseynov alleged that officers from Baku’s Khatai district police station No 37 beat five teenagers and released them after receiving money from their parents.

Lawyer Khalid Bagirov told Meydan TV that the problem was not the absence of mechanisms for holding officers accountable, but that those mechanisms were not being effectively applied.

What do the official figures show?

The Main Anti-Corruption Directorate under the Prosecutor General’s Office said it reviewed 5,655 complaints in the first half of 2026. A total of 54 criminal cases involving 102 people were sent to court. Of the calls received through the “161” hotline, 4,062 were registered as reports of corruption-related offences.

The figures show that investigations are being carried out. However, the number of cases sent to court does not indicate how effectively people who report corruption are subsequently protected from pressure or retaliation.

This distinction is particularly important in cases involving complaints against the police. A person who complains about an officer with the power to detain them, take them to a police station and formally record offences is seeking more than the return of money. They also need guarantees that those powers will not be used against them in retaliation. Receiving a complaint and protecting the complainant are two separate tasks.

According to an OECD report assessing the situation in 2023-2024, Azerbaijan has made no significant overall progress in combating corruption since 2022. The system for declaring the assets and interests of public officials was not operational, while gaps also remained in declaration forms and procedures for their electronic submission and verification.

In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Azerbaijan scored 30 out of 100 and ranked 130th out of 182 countries. Despite an eight-point increase compared with the previous year, the score remains low in terms of perceived levels of public-sector corruption.

Arrests of journalists investigating corruption

The authorities’ pledge to protect those who report corruption also contrasts with the situation surrounding the Abzas Media case. On 20 June 2025, seven defendants in the case were sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven years and six months to nine years. They included journalists Ulvi Hasanli, Sevinj Vagifgizi and Hafiz Babali, who had investigated corruption.

The defendants rejected the charges against them. Reporters Without Borders described the sentences as the result of a politically motivated trial aimed at silencing those who expose corruption and injustice.

Against this backdrop, several questions arise: Is a person who reports an alleged demand for a bribe protected from retaliation? Is the alleged offence independently investigated, and are the findings made public? And can a journalist who exposes corruption continue their work without facing the threat of imprisonment?

World.title: Opinion from Yerevan: Baku steps up pressure on Armenia with new tools
World.content:
Opinion on Baku’s tougher rhetoric

Statements by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev should be seen as a “public expression of dissatisfaction with Nikol Pashinyan’s government”, according to political analyst Suren Surenyants.

Speaking at the eighth congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party, Aliyev said, among other things, that the blame should not be placed solely on Armenia’s former leadership.

“It is true that Armenia’s former leaders are war criminals and must be punished, but it was Armenia’s current government that made territorial claims against us and insulted the dignity of the Azerbaijani people with inappropriate and uncivilised statements. We must never forget this,” the president stressed.

Political analyst Suren Surenyants analysed what prompted the recent statements by Aliyev and his aide Hikmet Hajiyev, as well as Azerbaijan’s tougher rhetoric more broadly.

“Baku is effectively signalling that it is dissatisfied with the way Pashinyan is fulfilling his commitments and, if necessary, could use his previous positions and statements as an additional means of exerting pressure,” he said.

‘We would like to make peace not only with the Armenian government, but with the Armenian people’

Against the backdrop of Aliyev’s tough statements, the head of the foreign policy department of the Azerbaijani presidential administration also addressed the peace agenda with Armenia. Speaking at the CAMCA Regional Forum in Baku, he said Azerbaijan intended to build a long-term architecture for peace:

“That is why we always say that we want to make this peace not only with the Armenian government and the country’s prime minister. We want to make peace with the Armenian people. And that is why we continue to expect changes to Armenia’s Constitution. Of course, this is an internal matter, and we fully refrain from interfering in this process.

“We are waiting for just one final step – amendments to Armenia’s Constitution concerning territorial claims against Azerbaijan. After that, I think the final peace agreement will become a reality.”

Baku is demanding amendments to Armenia’s Constitution as a precondition for signing a peace treaty. Azerbaijan argues that the document contains territorial claims. The Constitution itself contains no wording that could give rise to such concerns. However, it refers to the Declaration of Independence, which mentions the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. A draft of Armenia’s new Constitution is currently under discussion. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that it should not contain a reference to the Declaration of Independence. At the same time, he insists that constitutional change is something Armenia itself needs.

Expert commentary

Political analyst Suren Surenyants notes that Armenia is building its entire policy around the peace agenda with Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan, far from softening its rhetoric, has been toughening it in recent months:

“One possible explanation is that Azerbaijan is seeking to consolidate as quickly as possible the political gains resulting from the military advantage it achieved through the war, recognising that the current balance of power will not last forever.”

In his view, this interpretation is also supported by statements from the Azerbaijani president’s aide. In particular, he points to Hikmet Hajiyev’s remarks that a peace treaty will only be signed after Armenia changes its Constitution, despite peace having already been established:

“This is not a contradiction, but a division of labour. One formulation is intended for an international audience, while the other is addressed to Yerevan, reminding it of the need to fulfil its commitments.”

Surenyants also considers the statement about seeking peace not only with the Armenian government but also with the Armenian people noteworthy.

According to him, this means Azerbaijan wants changes in Armenia to acquire “legitimacy enshrined through a referendum and to be made as irreversible as possible”.

The political analyst suggests Baku is in a hurry because the regional balance of power could change, primarily due to the growing Iranian factor:

“If Iran is able to capitalise on its regional influence, a shift in the balance of power in the South Caucasus could limit Baku’s ability to exert pressure on Armenia.”

Surenyants notes that:

Tehran has repeatedly said that any violation of Armenia’s territorial integrity, changes to international borders or alteration of the geopolitical status quo in the region constitute “red lines” for Iran;

Iran is particularly sensitive to the development of transport links through Armenia, viewing them through the prism of its own security and regional influence.

Surenyants argues that the demand for changes to Armenia’s Constitution is taking on additional significance and cannot be seen simply as a “mechanical precondition” for signing a peace treaty.

“Azerbaijan is seeking to achieve its desired outcome within Armenia at both the legal and political levels. And that outcome will not be limited to removing the reference to the Declaration of Independence,” he argues.

The analyst notes that discussions have intensified again in Baku, in particular about the return of Azerbaijanis to “Western Azerbaijan”, by which they mean virtually the entire territory of Armenia. He believes these developments will not end with changes to Armenia’s Constitution and is convinced that Azerbaijan will then present Armenia with a new list of demands:

“Does all this mean that Azerbaijan is preparing for a new military escalation? At present, there is not enough publicly available evidence to draw such a definitive conclusion.”

The political analyst believes Baku has not yet obtained everything it wants from Armenia and is therefore stepping up political pressure. In his assessment, this is driven by concerns that it may become more difficult to secure all its demands in the future:

“And Baku is rushing to get everything it wants while there is a government in Yerevan that regards Baku’s demand for constitutional amendments as part of its own agenda, and before regional developments close the ‘window of opportunity’ for exerting unilateral pressure on Armenia.”

World.title: Russian court fines Abkhaz journalist Nizfa Arshba for violating foreign agent law
World.content:
A court in Vladikavkaz, North Ossetia, Russia, has fined Abkhaz journalist Nizfa Arshba for violating Russia’s foreign agent law. However, no one notified her about the fine. Authorities allegedly sent the notice to an address in Russia where she has never lived.

The court imposed a 30,000 rouble fine [about $353] on 31 August 2026. It ruled that Arshba had “posted material on the social network Facebook without indicating that the material was produced or distributed by a foreign agent, or that it concerned the activities of a foreign agent.”

Nizfa Arshba

Arshba learned about the fine by chance after coming across the information online. The journalist said no one had officially notified her about it.

Opposition journalist Nizfa Arshba, who runs the Telegram channel Aiashara, was added to Russia’s foreign agent register by the Russian Justice Ministry in March 2025, shortly after Abkhazia’s presidential election.

Unlike another Abkhaz journalist, Izida Chania, who also appears on the sanctions list and holds dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, Arshba has only one citizenship — Abkhaz. She has never lived in Russia and has no ties to the country at all.

Under the procedure, Russian citizens, including those listed in the foreign agent register, receive notifications about fines through their personal accounts on the Gosuslugi public services portal. But Nizfa Arshba is neither a Russian citizen nor a resident, so she is not registered on the portal and could not have received notification of the Vladikavkaz court’s decision.

The court’s decision also says that Arshba did not attend the hearing and did not explain why she was absent. At the same time, the court claims that it notified Arshba of the time and place where officials drew up the administrative offence report, as well as the time and place of the hearing. It says authorities sent the notice to her last known place of residence in Russia.

“I would like to know how and by whom my place of residence in Vladikavkaz was assigned to me, given that I have never lived in Russia, never held Russian citizenship and never assumed any obligation to comply with the laws of any foreign state,” Nizfa Arshba wrote on her Telegram channel.

The journalist says she does not intend to pay the fine.

Nizfa Arshba has actively opposed draft laws and Russian-Abkhaz agreements that she believes run counter to Abkhazia’s interests. One example is the controversial bill that would have allowed Russian citizens to build, sell and buy apartments in Abkhazia.

Because of similar positions, two Abkhaz politicians, Kan Kvarчия and Leuan Mikaa, lost their Russian citizenship, while three journalists, including Nizfa Arshba, were added to the foreign agent register.

For Abkhazia’s residents, this label also makes it extremely difficult to travel abroad. Russia remains the most accessible foreign destination for them, and they also have to travel through Russia to reach the wider world. But those labelled foreign agents fear travelling to Russia.

If Arshba violates the foreign agent law again, she could face criminal charges. The local authorities in Abkhazia do not pose any threat to her.

World.title: All four German political foundations halt work in Georgia; ALDE calls for EU sanctions
World.content:
German foundations close in Georgia

German Ambassador to Georgia Barbara Voss said all four German political foundations that had operated in the country for many years have been forced to close because of restrictions introduced by new legislation, including the Law on Grants.

According to the ambassador, worsening relations between Georgia and Germany have put years of cooperation at risk, including ties in education.

Against this backdrop, the European Liberal, Democrat and Reform Party (ALDE) sent a letter to EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas, calling on the European Union to respond with concrete action.

On 30 September, the Konrad Adenauer Foundation closed its office in Tbilisi. The Georgian office of the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which had worked in the country for 20 years, followed. The Heinrich Böll Foundation and Friedrich Ebert Foundation have also closed their offices.

What the German ambassador said

Barbara Voss, who replaced Peter Fischer as Germany’s ambassador to Georgia in August 2026, said that years of cooperation between the two countries had been seriously damaged.

“All four of our political foundations, which have supported Georgia and its people for decades on their path towards European integration, have been forced to suspend their work following a decision by the Georgian government. Two of the four foundations were forced to close their offices just two days ago,” the ambassador said.

Voss also highlighted Ilia State University, which has long-standing academic ties with Germany and is, according to the ambassador, one of Georgia’s most internationally recognised universities.

She said the university is now at risk of closure.

“These developments are also worsening relations between Georgia and the EU. In the coming years, I personally, as ambassador, will work to preserve what can still be preserved,” Voss said.

The diplomat said Germany would continue to meet its commitments in certain areas, including support for civil society, environmental protection and conservation of natural resources.

The German ambassador also spoke about security cooperation between the two countries. She stressed that Berlin and Tbilisi share common interests and face common challenges in this area.

“Russia is trying to destabilise Europe and divide people through disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression,” Voss said.

She said the Georgian population was well aware of the consequences of Russian military aggression. The ambassador noted that 20% of Georgia’s territory is occupied by Russia and said Moscow’s goal was not to maintain a balance of power but to establish dominance.

According to Voss, Germany continues to support Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as its right to determine its own security policy.

“In this context, we will support cooperation with the Georgian Defence Forces within the NATO framework to further strengthen their defence capabilities against potential aggression and contribute to the security of the South Caucasus and Europe,” the German ambassador said.

“Enough! The Georgian Dream regime is silencing independent voices”

“Enough is enough! The Georgian Dream regime is squeezing out independent voices and pushing Georgia further away from Europe.

After more than 20 years in the country, Friedrich-Naumann-Stiftung für die Freiheit has been forced to close its Tbilisi office because it could no longer operate independently.

ALDE Party President Svenja Hahn and European Liberal Forum President Jan-Christoph Oetjen are calling on the EU to act.

Targeted sanctions against those responsible for repression and the systematic undermining of democracy. No more looking the other way. Our joint letter to Kaja Kallas and Marta Kos,” ALDE said in a social media post.

The letter says the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom was forced to close its Tbilisi office, which had operated in the country for more than two decades, after the Georgian authorities rejected its application for foreign funding.

“The Georgian authorities made it clear that the foundation’s activities would only be permitted if they were aligned with their priorities. Under these conditions, FNF concluded that it could no longer carry out its mission as an independent political foundation,” the letter says.

The letter describes this as “another clear example of the growing restrictions on independent civil society and the wider repression of protesters, opposition figures, journalists and independent voices.”

“These developments show how far the Georgian Dream government is moving away from the standards expected of an EU candidate country and send a worrying signal to all those with European aspirations.

What is happening in Georgia matters not only to its citizens, but also to the credibility of the EU’s enlargement policy and its commitment to democracy and fundamental rights,” the letter says.

The authors again called on the EU to “respond with targeted sanctions against those responsible for the repression and systematic undermining of democracy and fundamental freedoms in Georgia”.

“The EU must ensure that those defending democracy and fundamental freedoms are not left without support,” ALDE said.

“We are not concerned about unfair sanctions” – ruling party representative

“We are not particularly concerned about their [the EU’s] incompetent and completely unfounded sanctions packages, introduced year after year or month after month,” parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtchkhalia said in response to ALDE’s call.

“We should not be surprised by such statements from ALDE or the EU’s political establishment. For years, our country has been subjected to direct and unfair attacks from them.

No package of sanctions can force us to abandon the course chosen at the request of our society. That course is peaceful development, progress and prosperity for every citizen and, above all, the peaceful reunification of our country,” Kirtchkhalia said.

News in Georgia

World.title: 13 Azerbaijani citizens repatriated from Syria
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. As a result of the phased and coordinated measures taken by the Government of the Republic of Azerbaijan, 13 Azerbaijani citizens, including six women and seven children, were repatriated from the Syrian Arab Republic to Azerbaijan on October 6, the Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry said.

It was noted that, as a first step, the whereabouts, identities, and Azerbaijani citizenship of the repatriates were established.

Members of a Working Group comprising representatives of government agencies responsible for the repatriation of Azerbaijani citizens who find themselves in crisis situations abroad were dispatched to Syria. Initial medical and psychological examinations of the repatriates were also arranged.

Subsequently, with the relevant coordination provided by the Azerbaijani embassies in Syria and Türkiye, as well as the Consulate General of Azerbaijan in Istanbul, the citizens were provided with certificates of return to Azerbaijan and air tickets, after which they were brought back to the country.

Relevant measures are planned to ensure the social rehabilitation of the repatriates and their reintegration into society.

The Azerbaijani government will continue taking the necessary measures to repatriate Azerbaijani citizens who have become victims of armed conflicts in foreign countries.

World.title: Ancient rock art heritage of Azerbaijan presented in Italy (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: State Committee on Work with Diaspora of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. Azerbaijan’s ancient rock art heritage has been presented in Italy, the State Committee on Work with Diaspora of the Republic of Azerbaijan said.

An international seminar titled “Rediscovering the First Art of Humanity” was held in the Italian city of Cassine.

The seminar was organized by the “SEN1SEN” think tank and the “Palazzo Mandrilli” Gallery, with technical support from the Azerbaijan Diaspora Support Fund under the State Committee on Work with the Diaspora of the Republic of Azerbaijan and the Cassine City Municipality.

The event brought together senior officials from government institutions of various countries, leading European scholars, international experts, museum directors, archaeologists, and specialists in the study, preservation, and management of rock art heritage.

One of the main objectives of the event was to present the Gamigaya rock art complex, which Azerbaijan has proposed for inclusion in the UNESCO World Heritage List, to an international scientific and professional audience.

The exhibition titled “Messages from the Millennia: Gobustan Petroglyphs,” prepared under the guidance of Professor Malahat Farajova, a representative of the Azerbaijan State University of Culture and Arts, presented ancient rock carvings of Gobustan, their historical and cultural significance, as well as Azerbaijan’s rich rock art heritage to an international audience.

The participating scholars and experts shared their views on the role of rock art in human history, modern scientific research in this field, and new findings. An international cooperation memorandum was subsequently signed, outlining future areas of cooperation and development in the field of rock art.

The seminar was significant in terms of bringing Azerbaijan’s rock art heritage to a wider audience through the use of modern digital technologies.

World.title: EIA raises its Brent price forecast by $14 for Q4 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) has raised its forecast for Brent crude oil prices in Q4 2026 amid ongoing disruptions to oil supplies from the Middle East, attacks on oil infrastructure, and a decline in global inventories.

According to the October issue of the Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), the EIA expects Brent crude oil spot price to average $105 per barrel (b) in 4Q26, $14/b higher than in last month’s STEO.

“Although we expect oil production and supplies from the Middle East to increase, we have raised our forecast for the global oil price compared with last month,” the EIA report states.

According to the agency, the attacks on the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia highlight the potential for continued volatility in physical oil flows and oil prices amid ongoing withdrawals of oil inventories globally.

As EIA analysts note, additional upward pressure on crude oil prices stems from extreme tightness in diesel markets that raises demand for crude oil for refiners to meet diesel demand.

The price of Brent reached $114 in September

The Brent crude oil spot price increased to an average of $114 per barrel (b) in September, $23/b higher than in August. The EIA attributes the increase to increased attacks on oil infrastructure and tankers around the

Middle East.

The most notable among these developments were attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, which temporarily halted flows on a crucial bypass used to circumvent the Strait of Hormuz.

According to the EIA’s estimates, before the attacks, this pipeline was shipping more than 5.0 million barrels per day (b/d) of

oil exports via Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu port on the Red Sea.

“The disruption of the pipeline led to the daily Brent spot price reaching as high as $131/b on September 15, as buyers scrambled to secure near-term supplies due to the loss of Saudi exports. Daily prices eased somewhat during the last week of September as the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia was repaired and partially resumed flows as of September 22,” the report states.

Some of the decrease in Red Sea exports has been offset by shifting exports back through the Strait of Hormuz. Ship tracking data from

Vortexa indicates that oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz increased slightly in September as Saudi Arabia increasingly used ship-to-ship transfers along Oman’s coast.

Production disruptions are decreasing

Despite the rise in the number of attacks, the EIA estimates that oil exports from the Middle East increased in September compared with August, while the volume of production curtailments decreased.

“We assess that crude oil production shut-ins averaged 4.8 million b/d in September, down from 5.8 million b/d in

August and down from 10.9 million b/d at the peak in May,” the report states.

In the fourth quarter of 2026, the EIA expects restrictions on oil flows from the Middle East to persist. The average volume of curtailed production is forecast to be 4.5 million barrels per day.

High tanker rates are putting further pressure on prices

The EIA also notes an increase in risks for tankers transiting the region. This has led to higher freight rates and insurance costs, and has also increased the risk premium factored into oil prices.

“High tanker rates, which reached record levels in

September, reflect increasing insurance costs and are putting additional upward pressure on delivered

crude oil prices to refiners,” the EIA notes.

In addition, vessels are forced to take longer routes to avoid conflict zones, which reduces the number of available tankers.

Against this backdrop, the EIA estimates that global oil inventories declined by an average of 1.9 million b/d in the third quarter of 2026 and will fall an additional 0.7 million b/d on average in 4Q26.

EIA expects prices to decline in 2027

Despite raising its short-term forecast, the EIA expects prices to decline gradually.

“Although we raised our crude oil price forecast from last month, we still expect oil prices to generally fall from their early October average,” the forecast states.

The agency expects that alternative routes for oil exports from the Middle East — including pipelines and overland bypass routes, ship-to-ship transfers, and new bypass pipeline capacity in the UAE, which is expected to come online in 2027- will allow for a gradual reduction in the volume of suspended production.

The EIA forecasts that most of the region’s oil production will return to pre-conflict average levels by the end of the second quarter of 2027.

Against this backdrop, the agency expects the average price of Brent to fall to $87 per barrel in the second quarter of 2027 and, as global inventories recover, to $74 per barrel in the fourth quarter of 2027.

At the same time, the EIA warns that the conflict in the Middle East will lead to continued volatility in crude oil flows both through the Strait of Hormuz and through alternative routes, which will likely lead to more volatility in short-term price movements than forecast indicates.

World.title: Athletes drive to make table tennis a smash at national Special Olympics debut
World.content:
The repetitive click-clack of a small white ball paddling back and forth over a net may seem like a simple game of ping pong, but for these three teammates, it could be their ticket to the world stage.

The Bundaberg athletes are gearing up to compete in the Special Olympics Australia in Melbourne later this month, where table tennis is making its competitive debut.

Oscar Quarrell, 16, is diligently working to perfect his pendulum — a serve with a bit of side and back spin.

Oscar Quarrell (right) talks with coach Ha Bui as he prepares to play in his first Special Olympics. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Oscar is one of three from his regional club, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, to be selected as part of the 14-strong Queensland table tennis team.

"I love table tennis because it's something that takes my mind off thinking and gives me a break," he said.

"It's also very fun to do with people that actually enjoy hanging around you."

Celebrating 50 years

The Special Olympics is for people with intellectual disabilities, cognitive delays or autism. It is also an organisation that supports community-based clubs and participation.

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Special Olympics movement in Australia.

Oscar Quarrell, Taylah Sim and Nicholas Jefferson train with coach Ha Bui. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Special Olympics Australia CEO Jamie O'Connor said 850 athletes across 13 sports would compete at the 2026 games.

"Special Olympics provides programs at a grassroots level week in, week out, at a community level," he said.

"But it also has the path that goes through local competitions to state events, to national events, to international events.

"Our Special Olympics is more about participation opportunities than it is about winning gold medals."

Mr O'Connor said that, in addition to the inclusion of table tennis, dance sport would be a demonstration sport for the first time this year.

Oscar Quarrell practises with Taylah Sim. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

"As sport evolves, and the demand for different sports evolves, then we try and provide options for people with intellectual disability and the sports that they want to compete in," he said.

About 60 athletes who are successful in the national games will go on to compete at the Special Olympics World Games in Santiago, Chile, next October.

Trio take on games

As the excitement builds towards the national games alongside his backhand, Oscar was also preparing for a big leap in independence.

"I'm excited to do something different, and it's also the first time I haven't had my parents with me, so they are going to come and watch, but I'm not allowed to speak to them," he said.

Clubmates Taylah and Nicholas will be joining Oscar in Melbourne.

Taylah Sim has been putting in the hours to prepare for her Special Olympics debut. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Taylah has her eyes firmly on the prize, saying she looks forward to winning then going on to compete at the world games.

Nicholas is also hoping to win a medal, having played the game for 13 years.

His mum, Margaret, said table tennis had opened doors for her son and she enjoyed watching the competition.

"They all want to do their best but, at the end of the day, whoever gets first, second or last, they're all rewarded, and they are happy for them," Ms Jefferson said.

"There's cheering, there's no jealousy, they're here to support each other."

Table tennis has opened doors for Nicholas Jefferson. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Queensland table tennis head coach Kim Hammermeister had high hopes for her Queensland team when they competed at the national level for the first time.

"Bundaberg has always been very strong with their school program for people with an intellectual impairment," she said.

Ms Hammermeister said any Special Olympics sport provided opportunities for friendship.

"People with an intellectual impairment can become very isolated, especially after school," she said.

"Of course, the physical benefits of being active are amazing; you can't put a price on that."

World.title: Breaking: Death row inmate Christa Pike wakes after botched execution
World.content:
Death row inmate Christa Pike has woken up and is speaking almost a week after a botched execution attempt at a Tennessee prison.

"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking and continues to receive critical medical care," her attorney said.

"Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented."

Pike, 50, was rushed to hospital following two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital, inside the death chamber at Nashville's Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.

She was sentenced to death in 1996 for the killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer, 19, when Pike was 18 years old.

Her attorneys said Pike's prognosis remained unclear.

Media witnesses recount the moments before the execution of Christa Pike. (AP Photo: George Walker IV)

Court order to preserve evidence

Pike's attorneys are set to go to court as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.

Last week, the head of Tennessee's prison system announced he would step down in the wake of the incident.

The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the attempted execution.

Chancery Court Judge I'Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning, local time, status conference in the case.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Camel team hauls wagon into record books in southern NSW
World.content:
Thirty-two camels in harness pulling a loaded wagon at a heritage festival in southern New South Wales have set an Australian record.

The record-breaking feat at the Good Old Days Festival in Barellan on Saturday was set by a group of cameleers from NSW, Queensland and Victoria.

The team broke the previous record of 22 camels set at the same event in 2024.

The camels were harnessed to an antique wagon loaded with wool bales, which they pulled for multiple laps around the arena as the crowd cheered.

Rodney Sansom and Thirsty the camel led the team. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Cameleer Rodney Sansom, whose camel Thirsty led the team, said one of the biggest challenges was bringing together the animals from four different owners.

"They've got to get used to all the other camels and they've got to get used to all the drivers," he said.

"We've spent years training camels. There's the leaders and the wheelers and we've got young camels in here that we've being getting ready for just this job."

The team practised on stock routes before the festival. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Mr Sansom said key to training the camels was learning to communicate with each other.

"You've got to teach him English … be kind to the camel, show him what you want to do and he will love doing it for you," he said.

US camel ranchers impressed

The record attempt attracted international attention with a delegation from the North American Camel Ranch Owners Association attending the festival.

Doug Baum has combined his love of history and camels with travel. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

The association's education officer Doug Baum said their visit was about sharing international "camel culture".

"The Australian cameleers of modern times … have a love and a respect for this country's history and you are seeing it kept alive at the festival," he said.

Another member of the delegation, Valeri Crenshaw, was impressed by the skill and training of the Australian cameleers.

"These guys are starting with feral camels that have been out running in the bush and we start with camels that were born and bred on farms," she said.

"There's a different level in how you have to build patience and build the relationship with the animal."

Valeri Crenshaw says camels stole her heart. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Ms Crenshaw said she enjoyed spending time with the camel teams, camping on the stock routes in the Riverina and learning to drive the wagon.

"Australia does a very good job of embracing its history and bringing to life how camels started in this country and what they were used for," she said.

Ms Crenshaw grew up riding horses on a cattle ranch in Kansas but camels stole her heart.

"When I got introduced to camels, it knocked me off my feet with joy," she said.

"They're so smart and they're so intuitive … they want to interact and they want to please you."

Valeri Crenshaw said it was a thrill to be able to drive the wagon during practice. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Camel history on show

Mr Baum said camels were a novelty in his home state of Texas, but he enjoyed sharing their role in history, such as how the United States Camel Corps transported military supplies in the 1850s.

"The camel is a curiosity … like a keyhole into greater discovery," he said.

"If I show up on a school campus or at a national park or library with my camels, people are at least intrigued and maybe they'll even learn some history."

The camels waiting to be harnessed to pull the wagon. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Mr Sansom said he was pleased to have been part of the team to make its own Australian camel history.

"I've always said I wish I was around 100 years ago [when camels were used to haul freight], but I'm here now," he said.

"We're making memories as we go."

Rodney Sansom says while he should not have a favourite camel, Thirsty is special. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

A second Australian record fell at the festival with a team of 56 bullocks.

In 2025, a heavy horse record was set at the festival by 62 Clydesdale, Australian draught, Suffolk Punch and Shire horses pulling an antique wagon.

World.title: Live: Wall Street hits new record highs but ASX likely to open flat
World.content:
European markets also performed well overnight with Britain's FTSE and Germany's DAX rising 0.4% and 0.8% respectively.

On Wall Street, the S & P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, rose to new record highs after shares of AI-related companies jumped.



One reason why markets are feeling optimistic is because inflation fears have eased slightly as oil prices stabilised around the $US100 per barrel mark, which is much lower than it has been lately.

Though, given the volatility in geopolitics, that relief could easily turn to 'doom and gloom' at any moment, judging from how the US-Israeli war against Iran has played out in the past few months.

For now, investors are feeling less worried about oil-driven inflation, which led to global bond yields (or government borrowing costs) falling slightly.

Government borrowing costs slip

Long-dated US Treasury yields eased after touching fresh 24-year highs earlier this week, amid a persistent sell-off since late August on inflation and unsustainable debt concerns.

The US 10-year yield fell by 0.04 percentage points to 5.26%, while the 30-year yield dropped 0.03 percentage points to 5.63%.

Bond markets also found some respite after France's unpopular budget triggered a French debt sell-off and fuelled fears of broader stress across the euro zone.

France's 10-year bond yield dipped to 4.7% after surging to its highest since the 2000s last week.

Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in next spring's presidential election, outlined her plans to slash spending if elected in 2027.

Since yesterday evening, the Australian 10-year yield fell 0.06 percentage points to 5.35%.

In currency markets, the euro rose 0.4% to US1.13, stabilising after hitting a 17-month low in the previous session due to concerns about the euro zone's fiscal outlook.

The Australian dollar also fell marginally to 62 euro cents, after hitting a 22-month high against the European currency yesterday.

- with Reuters

World.title: Trump draws backlash for suggesting Iran could 'take out' LA
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's comment that Iran could "take out" a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego has sparked backlash from Californians.

Mr Trump, speaking at a political rally in Nebraska on Monday, said petrol prices were only temporarily high and worth it as part of his war on Iran.

"And again, remember, with the war, it's just artificial. It's a little bit high [but] it's a small price to pay," he told the crowd, referring to rising fuel prices.

"They could take out a city. Let 'em take out Los Angeles, let 'em take out San Diego" he said.

"It's essentially almost over with," Trump went on. "But it's going to end very soon, and it's going to end one way or the other."

Trump has a history of denigrating US cities, especially the largest ones that lean heavily Democratic. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

The White House defended the president's remark, saying the president was stating that US cities would have been threatened by Iran if he had not launched the war.

Mr Trump has shrugged off cost-of-living concerns stemming from the Iran conflict before, and he previously downplayed his concerns about the potential for Iran or its allies to launch an attack on US soil.

Californians condemn Trumps comments

California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat who may run for president in 2028, denounced the Republican president as "deranged and dangerous".

"After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should 'take out' Los Angeles and San Diego," he wrote on X.

One of the Republicans running in a competitive race in a redrawn California district near San Diego, Jim Desmond, distanced himself from the president's remarks.

"I vehemently disagree with President Trump's comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland," he wrote on X.

"No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage."

US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in a competitive race in northern California, said in a statement that Trump's comment was "unhelpful".

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, said in a statement that his comment "could potentially compromise our safety".

Early voting underway in California

The comment in Nebraska, a state the Trump administration won with more than 55 per cent of the vote in the 2024 presidential election, targeted Democratic-run cities in California, a solidly Democratic state the president often criticises.

California's early voting for the November midterm elections started on Monday.

Midterm early voting has kicked off in California. (Reuters: Lucy Nicholson)

The president's Republican Party has hoped to win more races in the state in recent years, including this year's gubernatorial election.

Mr Newsom championed the redrawing of California's congressional map last year to favour Democrats in this year's election after Trump pushed for conservative-led Texas to redraw its map to boost Republicans.

Los Angeles and San Diego rank as the largest and second-largest cities in California by population.

More than 115,000 active-duty service members are also stationed in San Diego.

"My constituents — including many active duty service members, veterans, and their families — are not acceptable collateral damage in Trump's stupid war," US Representative Sara Jacobs, a Democrat, said in a social media post.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Texan company plans to build new outback town for gas workers
World.content:
A Texan company has plans for a new "workforce village", which could house up to 3,000 gas workers in a remote part of the Northern Territory.

Dunmarra Development Land has published plans online, which say thousands of people could be housed at its 600 hectare "petroleum services precinct and workforce village".

It would be located just south of the Dunmarra Wayside Inn in Birdum, about 600 kilometres south of Darwin, and include supermarkets, a medical clinic, airstrip and sporting facilities, with all open for public use.

At full capacity it would provide 23 unit complexes as accommodation for a "rotating workforce", with services provided in the "town centre".

A worker at Tamboran's Beetaloo site, which recently started supplying gas to the energy grid. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Drilling companies and gas industry contractors would also be able to lease commercial lots to base their business operations at the precinct.

The website does not state how much construction would cost or how long it would take to build, but it does say it would not be permanent.

Dunmarra is close to the Beetaloo Basin, a massive gas resource which the industry and NT government say could provide a long-term gas supply for energy markets both domestically and overseas.

The company is owned by Kit Sheffield, a relative and business associate of Bryan Sheffield, an American businessman who invested in Tamboran Resources's project in the Beetaloo, which recently produced its first gas.

"Gas development in the Beetaloo brings drilling, completions, civil and logistics crews to a region with almost no serviced land and no workforce housing," the website said.

"Dunmarra puts the workshop, the bed and the mess in one place, on the highway, with gas and an airstrip at the fence."

If fully built, the development would be one of the biggest settlements in the NT and dwarf pre-existing towns in the area such as Elliott, Daly Waters and remote communities.

Kit Sheffield was contacted for comment.

Development surprises mayor

Barkly Regional Council Mayor Sid Vashist said he was unaware of the plan before he was contacted by the ABC.

Sid Vashist says local government has not been contacted about the plan. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

He said it was important the development supported existing towns in the region like Elliott and did not reinforce the industry's reliance on fly-in fly-out (FIFO) workforces.

"This is literally a huge township that's going to be proposed and created, which could be bigger than Tennant Creek at this stage," Cr Vashist said.

He said it was important to have long-term plans for developments built due to the resources sector to ensure they thrive after the lucrative industry departs.

"Towns like Tennant Creek were built on mines, but when the mining left, the socio-economic profile of the residents in this town reduced quite significantly, which has been a huge challenge," he said.

" We do not want to go through a similar cycle anywhere else in the Northern Territory, and that's a concern for me. "

It is understood no environmental or development applications have been lodged with the NT government.

World.title: Gauff hits out at racist abuse after China Open incident
World.content:
Coco Gauff says she received an "insane" amount of racial abuse on social media after beating local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open.

The ‌American won 7-5, 6-1 on Monday to reach the fourth round but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set.

She raised her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner.

After a video review, the umpire ordered the point to be replayed.

Gauff won the replayed point and held serve ⁠for 5-5 before cruising to victory against her 16-year-old opponent.

De Minaur retires from China Open with injury Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

The two-time major singles champion said she received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match.

"You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff wrote on X in reply to a post containing a racial slur.

"The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane.

"Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."

The WTA has made efforts to ‌tackle ⁠online abuse by introducing an AI-powered system that monitors thousands of players and officials on social media.

A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to over 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts a year earlier.

Gauff explained she was ⁠following the rules when she challenged the point.

Players are allowed to request video reviews of select judgement calls, including claims a distraction may have interfered with play.

Gauff said she spoke to Sun about the ⁠point at the end of the match.

"I apologised for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff wrote.

"I didn't like to see ⁠her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it's like but this is the beginning of an incredible career.

"It was an honour to share the court in front of her home crowd."

World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty ‘Against all odds’: Christa Pike awake and speaking after botched Tennessee execution Updated October 7, 2026 — 8:18am ,first published 8:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nashville: Christa Pike, a Tennessee inmate who survived an attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said. “Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented,” attorneys for Pike said in a statement on Tuesday (US time). Christa Pike survived a double lethal injection and is receiving life-saving care. AP “Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.” The attorneys said they were grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”.



Related Article Graphic content

Death penalty How Christa Pike’s botched Tennessee execution unfolded, minute by minute The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday. A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalised on Tuesday. Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as they attempted to put her to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug didn’t kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered. Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said the development “bodes well for a good recovery”.



But he said it could be weeks or months before anyone knew exactly what her recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try again to execute her. Related Article Updated

Death penalty Christa Pike ‘on a ventilator and unconscious’ after failed execution “She’s still in the ICU,” he said. “She has recovered to a certain degree that she’s able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. “There’s still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well.” Pike’s attorneys are set to go to court on Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.



The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the September 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case. Pike’s attorneys said in their statement that they continued to ask Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute Pike’s sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole. “Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time,” her attorneys said. More to come AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
