World.title: ASX set for flat start, Wall Street closes at record; Paramount completes $158b Warner Bros takeover
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set for flat start, Wall Street closes at record; Paramount completes $158b Warner Bros takeover Stan Choe Updated October 7, 2026 — 8:00am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market has never been higher, even as the list of challenges chipping away at it keeps growing. The S&P 500 climbed 0.6 per cent to a record after topping its prior all-time high set in August. Despite worries about everything from war to high inflation to pressure from the bond market, the index at the heart of many retirement accounts has soared 23 per cent since hitting a bottom in late March. Wall Street’s benchmark index is on track to post a record closing high. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 253 points, or 0.5 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite tacked 0.4 per cent onto its own all-time high set the day before. The record-high stock prices are helping investors feel better about their finances, or at least less bad, when Americans are generally feeling discouraged about keeping up with the fast-rising cost of living. The Australian sharemarket is set for a flat start, with futures at 6.58am AEDT pointing to a loss of 1 point, at the open. The ASX added 0.6 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US69.86¢.



Many of the fears that sent the US stock market to its bottom in March have indeed come true. Oil prices are high because of the war with Iran, which has made inflation worse. Yields have cranked higher in the bond market, which threatens to slow the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. And Americans broadly say they’re feeling more pessimistic about the economy and where it’s heading. Related Article Opinion

Government debt FROGS, not PIIGS, could spark the next global financial crisis Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist But one vital source of support has remained resolute for the US stock market throughout: the relentless ability for companies to make more money. Lamb Weston, which sells frozen fries and other potato products, said on Tuesday that its profit and revenue during its latest quarter topped its projections, for example. The results also beat analysts’ expectations, and its stock rallied 7.5 per cent. CEO Mike Smith said the company continues to deal with unexpected increases in freight and other expenses. But the company nevertheless raised its forecast for an underlying measure of profit for its full fiscal year.



It’s not just potato products proving to be profitable. All kinds of companies are lining up to report soon how much profit they made from July through September, and expectations are high. Delta Air Lines will report its third-quarter results on Friday, with several of the country’s biggest banks headlining the following week. Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to deliver overall growth of nearly 30 per cent in earnings per share from a year earlier, according to FactSet. If they’re correct, it would be the third straight quarter of growth better than 25 per cent. That’s crucial because corporate profits are one of the main levers that set prices for stocks, along with interest rates. At the moment, high bond yields are making investors less willing to pay high prices for investments that aren’t bonds. But the simultaneous strength for corporate profits is allowing the market to stay high and “to win the tug-of-war against yields,” according to strategists at Barclays. To be sure, much hinges on companies actually meeting those expectations for fatter profits. If they fail to do so, stock prices could easily fall off their records. Some critics also point to a possible bubble in stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry after how much they soared in the frenzy around the technology. Overnight, Paramount Skydance closed its $US110 billion ($157.5 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, completing one of the biggest media mergers of all time. The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together under a new name: Skydance. The deal, which followed a tumultuous, roughly yearlong fight, further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players.



AI stocks have been a huge force driving the US market to records, including Nvidia’s 28.3 per cent surge so far this year. That’s roughly double the broad market’s gain. Constellation Energy jumped 12.2 per cent for one of Tuesday’s biggest gains in the S&P 500 because it’s also riding that rising tide. It announced a long-term deal to supply Google with about as much electricity as a new nuclear reactor makes. The boom in AI data centers has made not just electricity more in demand but also construction crews and materials throughout the economy. Elsewhere on Wall Street, Option Care Health soared 32.6 per cent after CD&R and McKesson said they’re buying the provider of infusion services. The two are paying $32.05 for each Option Care Health share, valuing it at roughly $5.8 billion. All told, the S&P 500 rose 44.98 points to 7,818.93. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 253.38 to 51,521.28, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 122.48 to 27,599.79.



Bond yields offered some slack on Tuesday after falling back from their highest levels in years or even decades. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the focal point of the US bond market, eased to 5.28 per cent from 5.31 per cent late Monday. Related Article Exclusive

AI Sneak peek: Government gave AI giant early look at data centre rules It fell after oil prices steadied themselves somewhat. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, dropped to roughly $97 in the morning before pulling back to settle at $100.58. While that was up 0.3 per cent from Monday’s settlement price, it’s still below the nearly $110 it was at a few weeks ago. In stock markets abroad, indexes ticked higher in Europe as yields continue to swing in their bond markets amid concerns about high government debts and tight budgets. In France, tens of thousands of demonstrators marched in support of protests by students demanding more funding for schools. In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 jumped 1.1 per cent, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng climbed 1 per cent, but South Korea’s Kospi dropped 0.9 per cent.

World.title: Vigils mark anniversary of Hamas October 7 attack
World.content:
Vigils mark anniversary of Hamas October 7 attack

Vigils are being held across the country, including at Bondi, to mark the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel when 1200 people were killed.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Vigils to mark October 7 attack on Israel; Paramount, Warner Bros. merge in $158b deal
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has released a statement to mark the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel, when 1200 people were killed and 250 hostages taken. Read the full statement:

Today, we pause to remember the devastation that Hamas unleashed in the terrorist attack in Israel on the 7th of October, 2023.

On this dark anniversary, we remember the 1200 who were taken from the world, the largest loss of Jewish life on any single day since the Holocaust.

We think of everyone who was dragged into captivity, everyone who never returned home to their families, and everyone forever scarred by what they endured.

We think of all who lost loved ones, everyone who suffered, and those who entered that most agonising of vigils, struggling to bear the weight of hope as they waited for news of their loved ones held hostage.

We mourn Australian Galit Carbone. Our hearts are with her family, who live each day with her absence.

We solemnly vow to never forget what the terrorists perpetrated in all their cruelty.

That they chose to target young people at a music festival promoting friends, love and infinite freedom sent a clear message to the world that Hamas stands in opposition to humanity.

Time marches on with an ease denied to the human heart. For so many, no day since has been easy, but anniversaries fall with their own terrible weight. And for many others, what compounds the pain is the approach of the first anniversary of the antisemitic terror attack at Bondi Beach.

These few years have been hard beyond measure, but Australia stands with the Jewish community here and across the world.

We stand against antisemitism and racism in all its forms because it goes against who we are.

We stand against Hamas, which must disarm and play no role in Palestine’s future.

Australia continues to push for the implementation of the Gaza peace plan to end the conflict after such terrible suffering and loss of civilian life.

The Australian Government encourages and welcomes all genuine moves towards a just and lasting peace in the Middle East, underpinned by the State of Israel and the State of Palestine living side by side, within internationally recognised borders in peace and security.

Such a future would be the greatest victory of humanity over hatred. That is the future we must strive for together.

World.title: ‘It’s very emotional’: Axed presenter Sarah Macdonald to return to ABC 702 Sydney
World.content:
Exclusive CultureTV & radioABC ‘It’s very emotional’: Axed presenter Sarah Macdonald to return to ABC 702 Sydney Garry Maddox October 7, 2026 — 7:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Less than two years after her shock axing, the ABC has confirmed that radio presenter Sarah Macdonald is returning to 702 Sydney in a different timeslot. The former Mornings host is taking over Afternoons from next March. It’s the show that James Valentine hosted with warmth and wit for more than two decades, other than during a brief stint on Breakfast, before his diagnosis with oesophageal cancer. Sarah Macdonald is taking over Afternoons on ABC 702 Sydney from next March. Blake Photographic/ABC The much-loved Valentine died in April, with Afternoons co-hosted this year by James O’Loghlin and Kathryn Robinson. The ABC says they will “remain regular voices” on the station. There was an outcry in late 2024 when the popular Macdonald, who had hosted Weekend Nightlife and Evenings before Mornings, revealed that the ABC would not be renewing her contract.



Hamish Macdonald, another popular ABC personality, took over Mornings last year. Related Article Radio ratings ABC Radio Sydney makes comeback after presenter shake-up Since then, Sarah Macdonald has been podcasting, appearing weekly on Mark Levy’s show on 2GB and writing a book that she describes as “sort of a sequel to Holy Cow!”, her 2002 book on India. “James and I were friends and I deeply miss him,” she said of the new role. “I feel really honoured to be stepping into his shoes, his seat, his microphone. It’s very emotional – it’s a lot – and I hope to do him proud.” Macdonald said that when ABC managing director Hugh Marks texted her on April Fools’ Day to ask if she would like to have a chat, she thought it was a friend playing a prank.



“I appreciated that it came from him, really,” she said. “I think that he was getting hassles when he was going out occasionally from the public, so he was interested to find out what was going on and whether I’d consider coming back. “But it’s taken a while to work it all out [and] put my heart back into it.” Former Afternoons host James Valentine. James Alcock Before accepting the new show, Macdonald discussed it with Valentine’s widow, clinical psychologist Joanne Corrigan. “I really needed her blessing,” she said. “She’s not James, of course, but I know what James would say: ‘Well, do you want to do it or not? It’s up to you, kid.’ ”



So does Macdonald still have any bad blood about her axing? She laughed. “I’ll never really completely know what happened,” she said. “I’m just choosing to be really optimistic and hopeful and do the job … I had to come back with an open heart and an open mind and I am.” Macdonald praised “brilliant new station manager” Nick Lowther. “We didn’t have a station manager off and on for quite a while there but Nick is amazing,” she said.



Related Article Vale ‘A room full of love’: Memorial a fitting celebration of James Valentine’s life While ABC management would not comment on whether it had made a mistake axing her and how it felt about Mornings ratings since her departure, Lowther said he was thrilled to welcome her back. “Sarah is one of those broadcasters who builds a genuine, lasting bond with her audience,” he said. “She has an instinct for the conversations people want to have, and a warmth that comes through every time she’s on air.” While Craig Reucassel will continue in Breakfast, Hamish Macdonald on Mornings and Thomas Oriti on Drive next year, the ABC has flagged more announcements about the station’s line-up later in the year. Vigils are being held across the country, including at Bondi, to mark the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel when 1200 people were killed.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Vigils to mark October 7 attack on Israel; Paramount, Warner Bros. merge in $158b deal
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has released a statement to mark the third anniversary of Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel, when 1200 people were killed and 250 hostages taken. Read the full statement:

Today, we pause to remember the devastation that Hamas unleashed in the terrorist attack in Israel on the 7th of October, 2023.

On this dark anniversary, we remember the 1200 who were taken from the world, the largest loss of Jewish life on any single day since the Holocaust.

We think of everyone who was dragged into captivity, everyone who never returned home to their families, and everyone forever scarred by what they endured.

We think of all who lost loved ones, everyone who suffered, and those who entered that most agonising of vigils, struggling to bear the weight of hope as they waited for news of their loved ones held hostage.

We mourn Australian Galit Carbone. Our hearts are with her family, who live each day with her absence.

We solemnly vow to never forget what the terrorists perpetrated in all their cruelty.

That they chose to target young people at a music festival promoting friends, love and infinite freedom sent a clear message to the world that Hamas stands in opposition to humanity.

Time marches on with an ease denied to the human heart. For so many, no day since has been easy, but anniversaries fall with their own terrible weight. And for many others, what compounds the pain is the approach of the first anniversary of the antisemitic terror attack at Bondi Beach.

These few years have been hard beyond measure, but Australia stands with the Jewish community here and across the world.

We stand against antisemitism and racism in all its forms because it goes against who we are.

We stand against Hamas, which must disarm and play no role in Palestine’s future.

Australia continues to push for the implementation of the Gaza peace plan to end the conflict after such terrible suffering and loss of civilian life.

The Australian Government encourages and welcomes all genuine moves towards a just and lasting peace in the Middle East, underpinned by the State of Israel and the State of Palestine living side by side, within internationally recognised borders in peace and security.

Such a future would be the greatest victory of humanity over hatred. That is the future we must strive for together.

World.title: ‘It’s very emotional’: Axed presenter Sarah Macdonald to return to ABC 702 Sydney
World.content:
Exclusive CultureTV & radioABC ‘It’s very emotional’: Axed presenter Sarah Macdonald to return to ABC 702 Sydney Garry Maddox October 7, 2026 — 7:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Less than two years after her shock axing, the ABC has confirmed that radio presenter Sarah Macdonald is returning to 702 Sydney in a different timeslot. The former Mornings host is taking over Afternoons from next March. It’s the show that James Valentine hosted with warmth and wit for more than two decades, other than during a brief stint on Breakfast, before his diagnosis with oesophageal cancer. Sarah Macdonald is taking over Afternoons on ABC 702 Sydney from next March. Blake Photographic/ABC The much-loved Valentine died in April, with Afternoons co-hosted this year by James O’Loghlin and Kathryn Robinson. The ABC says they will “remain regular voices” on the station. There was an outcry in late 2024 when the popular Macdonald, who had hosted Weekend Nightlife and Evenings before Mornings, revealed that the ABC would not be renewing her contract.



Hamish Macdonald, another popular ABC personality, took over Mornings last year. Related Article Radio ratings ABC Radio Sydney makes comeback after presenter shake-up Since then, Sarah Macdonald has been podcasting, appearing weekly on Mark Levy’s show on 2GB and writing a book that she describes as “sort of a sequel to Holy Cow!”, her 2002 book on India. “James and I were friends and I deeply miss him,” she said of the new role. “I feel really honoured to be stepping into his shoes, his seat, his microphone. It’s very emotional – it’s a lot – and I hope to do him proud.” Macdonald said that when ABC managing director Hugh Marks texted her on April Fools’ Day to ask if she would like to have a chat, she thought it was a friend playing a prank.



“I appreciated that it came from him, really,” she said. “I think that he was getting hassles when he was going out occasionally from the public, so he was interested to find out what was going on and whether I’d consider coming back. “But it’s taken a while to work it all out [and] put my heart back into it.” Former Afternoons host James Valentine. James Alcock Before accepting the new show, Macdonald discussed it with Valentine’s widow, clinical psychologist Joanne Corrigan. “I really needed her blessing,” she said. “She’s not James, of course, but I know what James would say: ‘Well, do you want to do it or not? It’s up to you, kid.’ ”



So does Macdonald still have any bad blood about her axing? She laughed. “I’ll never really completely know what happened,” she said. “I’m just choosing to be really optimistic and hopeful and do the job … I had to come back with an open heart and an open mind and I am.” Macdonald praised “brilliant new station manager” Nick Lowther. “We didn’t have a station manager off and on for quite a while there but Nick is amazing,” she said.



Related Article Vale ‘A room full of love’: Memorial a fitting celebration of James Valentine’s life While ABC management would not comment on whether it had made a mistake axing her and how it felt about Mornings ratings since her departure, Lowther said he was thrilled to welcome her back. “Sarah is one of those broadcasters who builds a genuine, lasting bond with her audience,” he said. “She has an instinct for the conversations people want to have, and a warmth that comes through every time she’s on air.” While Craig Reucassel will continue in Breakfast, Hamish Macdonald on Mornings and Thomas Oriti on Drive next year, the ABC has flagged more announcements about the station’s line-up later in the year. World.title: National unveils 47-point small business plan
David Tamihere will not face a retrial over the murders of Heidi Paakkonen and Sven Höglin
World.content:
David Tamihere will not face a retrial over the 1989 murders of Swedish backpackers Heidi Paakkonen and Urban Höglin.

Tamihere's convictions were earlier this year quashed by the Supreme Court, which said it was up to Crown prosecutors to decide whether to hold another trial.

On Wednesday, in the High Court at Auckland, Crown prosecutor Claire Patterson told the court there was no longer sufficient evidence to proceed with a further prosecution.

Justice Simon Mount discharged Tamihere on the two charges of murder and said he was free to go.

Tamihere, who is now in his 70s, quickly left the court.

Patterson said the Crown solicitor had concluded that there was no longer sufficient evidence to support Tamihere being retried.

"It would rely substantially on visual identification and observation evidence, allegedly placing Mr Tamihere and a woman resembling Ms Paakkonen at Crosby's Clearing on the Coromandel Peninsula at a relevant time. That evidence has always been and would be strongly disputed by Mr Tamihere.

"Some of that evidence is no longer available to the Crown because the witnesses who would give it are no longer available."

Other evidence would not be admissible at a retrial following amendments to evidential admissibility rules since the first trial, Patterson said.

"As a result of the passage of time, some 36 years, significant pieces of evidence that the Crown [adduced] in the 1990 trial are no longer available, or if available, will likely be subject to reliability challenge. The conclusion is therefore that the evidential test for prosecution is no longer met. As I have said, if the evidential test for prosecution is not met, then a prosecution cannot proceed, irrespective of the public interest analysis considered," Patterson said.

Tamihere's lawyer, Murray Gibson, told the court that based on the evidence and counsel's submissions, the Crown was required to withdraw the charges.

"This speaks for itself. Their moral and legal obligation was clearly to dismiss the charges."

Höglin, 23, and Paakkonen, 21, were last seen in Thames in 1989. Their disappearance and the subsequent trial was one of the country's highest profile crimes.

Many aspects remain a mystery.

Höglin's body was found in 1991, after Tamihere had been convicted, but Paakkonen's body has never been found.

At the time the couple went missing, Tamihere had been living in the bush in the Coromandel for about three years.

Much of the Crown's original case was circumstantial. It included evidence that Tamihere had been seen driving around the Coromandel region in the couple's ute.

Tamihere admitted dumping or selling their possessions but maintained he had never met them.

The Crown's case also relied on testimony from former inmate Roberto Conchie Harris, who said Tamihere told him he killed the Swedes. However Harris was convicted of perjury over evidence in 2017.

Tamihere first appealed his convictions in 1992, after Höglin's body was found wearing a watch that a prosecution witness had initially said he had seen at Tamihere's house.

The body was also 70km away from where the Crown first suspected he had been killed.

That appeal was unsuccessful but the 2017 perjury conviction of Harris prompted a new round of appeals from Tamihere.

In 2024, the Court of Appeal declined to quash the convictions, saying despite the problems with some crown evidence, there was still enough to safely say Tamihere was guilty.

The Supreme Court released its decision in March that finally quashed the convictions.

It said Harris's evidence meant the trial was fundamentally unfair, and that there had been a "radical recasting" of the Crown case since the original trial.

That effectively meant the case had never truly been tested by a jury.

World.title: Explainer: What is the 'purple vote' and why is it shrinking?
World.content:
Explainer - You'll see a lot of red and blue, pink and green signs leading up to Election Day - but purple might be the colour to keep a close eye on.

One month out from the election, one thing is becoming clear - voters are turning away from Labour and National as minor parties reap the rewards.

The "purple vote" has been dropping in recent elections and polling shows it might reach a new low this year.

What is the 'purple vote' anyway?

It's just a way of describing the combined vote for National (who favour blue) and Labour (who favour red).

Election results over the past 10 years and polling for this year's election are showing a steady decline in their overall share of the pie as smaller parties like the Greens and New Zealand First take bigger slices.

"People are switching off from the so-called major parties," RNZ's political editor Jo Moir said after the latest poll numbers came in Tuesday.

"There's a broader trend away from major political parties around the world," said analyst Lara Greaves, an associate professor in politics at Victoria University of Wellington and a senior research fellow in statistics.

What do the last few elections tell us?

The purple vote has been steadily declining since the 2005 election, with a bit of a shift upwards in the 2017 election.

In 2005, Labour and National combined took 80.2 percent of the party vote, but by 2014 that had fallen to 72.17 percent.

In the 2017 general election, the purple vote rose back up to 81.3 percent, in an election which saw NZ First and the Greens fall under 8 percent and ACT getting only 0.5 percent of the party votes.

But after 2017, it started to fall again, and by the 2023 election the purple vote only managed 64.97 percent.

That was the lowest purple vote since the 1996 election, the first under MMP, when only 62 percent of the party vote went to National and Labour, and NZ First, the Alliance Party and ACT all finished strongly.

Greaves said that first MMP election saw a shift away from Labour and National, "and then people kind of went back to them, which was kind of interesting".

MMP "kind of rewards us as voters from moving away from the major parties," Greaves said.

Audio player for " Political editor Jo Moir analyses latest RNZ poll " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1776776%2Fexplainer-what-is-the-purple-vote-and-why-is-it-shrinking

Political editor Jo Moir analyses latest RNZ poll Morning Report Download MP3 11m

"We don't have to worry as much about a wasted vote, although some people still do."

After 30 years, many voters have never known the old first-past-the-post system of voting, she noted, and tend to vote more strategically.

What do the polls tell us about this year?

The polls if anything show an even sharper drop could be possible on November 7.

Reid Research polling dating back to 2021 shows a steady downward trajectory for the combined purple vote.

The latest RNZ-Reid poll released this week had Labour and National getting just 56.7 percent of the party vote, which if repeated on Election Day would be by far the lowest result for the two in MMP's history.

Other polls this season have generally showed similar trends. The latest 1News-Verian Poll released Tuesday night showed National at 29 percent and Labour at 28 percent.

Moir called the 56.7 percent for the purple vote in the latest RNZ-Reid poll "jawdropping".

"That is down from 61.3 in August in our poll then and it is down from 64.9 at the 2023 election."

It might ultimately lead to a change in how "major" and "minor" parties are defined, Greaves said.

"You know, when you start to get minor parties solidly in the teens, and the major parties heading into the 20s, it's like at what point are they no longer a major party? And at what point do they have less of the cards?"

If a major party did dip below 20 percent in the party vote, "that would be shocking to me, but stranger things have happened," she said.

It's all a sign that the purple vote is "just continuing to slide away, people are switching off from the so-called major parties and it's creating all sorts of weird things," such as the talk about strategic voting to engineer potential overhangs, Moir said.

Politicians worldwide have ridden a wave against business as usual. BILL PUGLIANO / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP

Are voters just perpetually dissatisfied now with the status quo?

It's hardly a New Zealand phenomenon to see minor parties romping ahead of the established players in polls and a growing anti-incumbent movement.

In Britain, Nigel Farage's Reform UK has been leading many polls for months, while in Australia Pauline Hanson's One Nation has also seen a resurgence.

And it's hard not to note that the steeper decline in the purple vote began in 2017, around the time Donald Trump first assumed the US presidency and a general wider shift in global politics began happening.

So many normal political processes have become unsettled in the past 10 years, Greaves said.

"There is this argument that people are turning to the minor parties because the major parties haven't fixed anything.

"It is this genuine swing towards more radical change or more action or someone a bit different because the major parties have held power for so long and they haven't actually helped our lives improve so much more than where they were, say, 20, 30 years ago."

In the end, voters may decide to try something new like the novelty of the Opportunity party or give established smaller parties a go.

The latest RNZ-Reid poll also found 53 percent of people responding said they think the country is on the wrong track.

World.title: Fire near Queenstown surges to cover 1200 hectares as winds fuel flames
World.content:
A bush fire on the shores of Lake Wakatipu, near Queenstown, has surged to cover 1200 hectares as winds fuel the flames.

The blaze, which has been burning since Tuesday morning, was not contained or controlled when firefighters suspended operations on Tuesday night.

Firefighting resumed at Walter Peak at Wednesday morning, both in the air and on the ground.

Assistant District Commander Nic McQuillan said on Tuesday night strong nor-westerly winds had fueled the fire, which had escalated in the McKinlays Creek area.

"There are areas where the fire will burn itself out, but we are expecting it to still be going quite strongly first thing in the morning," he said on Tuesday night.

The fire at Lake Wakatipu as seen on Wednesday morning. SUPPLIED

Four helicopters equipped with monsoon buckets were cooling hotspots and dampening the fire perimeter on Wednesday morning, with a fifth helicopter used as an aerial platform to direct the air attack.

While overnight conditions had been favourable, the fire had continued to grow and is now estimated at approximately 1200 hectares, McQuillan said.

The size is likely to increase if the fire becomes more active due to weather conditions.

A Fire and Emergency spokesperson said there were 11 firefighters on the ground, with additional crews arriving throughout the day. It expected up to 25 firefighters to be on the ground.

The geography of McKinlays Creek was a ravine, causing it to act like a chimney, funnelling wind and fire upwards, making it difficult for firefighters to access the area, McQuillan had said.

"The wind funnels up it and draws the fire with it - essentially the smoke and the fire is drawn up the valley and out the top of the mountains, which makes it very hot and impressive in terms of what we're seeing.

"Helicopter operations have been hindered by the amount of smoke being generated and the fact that the McKinlays Creek area is acting like a chimney, which means that we can only get into the bottom part of it."

The fire on Tuesday. FENZ

"Conditions on the fireground are benign at the moment but are expected to become more challenging during the morning as the wind is forecast to strengthen."

McQuillan said the protection of Walter Peak Station homestead and farm stock remain the priority.

Queenstown's mayor John Glover said the blaze was "confronting".

"It's very large, very visible, and the fact that we haven't been able to contain it is top of mind for everyone involved in the response."

Glover said it was normal for high country stations in the area to have burns this time of year to renew land for Spring - but these could get out of control.

"It's a real stark reminder of the fact that our hillsides can be dry and if we get a wild fire it can spread quite easily."

Glover understood the historic Walter Peak homestead had not been damaged, which he was relieved about.

He advised locals to keep boats away from the area, which was across the lake from the central city.

Members of the public on the lake are reminded to stay at least 500 metres offshore to keep clear of where our helicopters are operating.

This exclusion zone will be monitored by the Harbourmaster and Coastguard throughout the day to ensure public and firefighter safety, the FENZ spokesperson said.

Smoke conditions may worsen in some areas on the opposite side of the lake during the day.

Residents affected by smoke are advised to keep windows and doors closed and limit exposure where possible.

World.title: Aid versus Defence: parties clash on foreign policy spending priorities
World.content:
The Labour Party has promised to increase New Zealand's foreign aid spending as fiscal conditions allow, while National plans to slash it.

But both parties have said they would prioritise the Pacific - Labour to shift spending towards climate resilience, and National to "protect it" from cuts.

Labour foreign affairs spokesperson Vanushi Walters said that the Pacific would remain a priority for the aid programme, which it would raise as close as possible to a target of 0.7 percent of gross national income, or around $3 billion.

This is in line with a target set for wealthy countries by the OECD, which has reported plummeting aid levels globally as the US and Europe pull back.

Walters stopped short of making any year-by-year promises.

"We know that that is a significant commitment, which is why we've said it's a horizon commitment," she said.

"I'm not saying that we would take steps to that toward that in the next year... we are firmly focused on addressing the cost of living for New Zealanders here."

The government raised aid spending slightly this year to $1.2 billion in Budget 2026, funded by a $162.5 million underspend in 2024.

In nominal terms, the current government has run a three-year aid budget (a triennium) comparable to Labour's most recent term - around $3 billion.

Additionally, $110m in aid spending for the Indo-Pacific was set aside for the next triennium. Pacific Islands countries receive roughly two thirds of the total aid budget.

Aid 'not a priority' for current government - Treasury

In contrast to Labour, National has pledged to divert aid spending - outside of that allocated to the Pacific region - to fund bowel screening and medicines at home.

This election policy carved out $431.2m in IDC and admin costs, a ten percent cut overall, over the next three years. It would also seek a further $45.6m in savings from departmental costs within MFAT.

The party nevertheless promised that the Pacific "will be fully protected, reflecting the importance of our closest neighbours and strongest interests." It did not say whether this differentiated bilateral aid direct to the Pacific from multilateral aid - to the UN, for example - that would impact the region.

Examples of "wasteful" aid spending provided by the party included "smart agriculture systems in Latin America and the Caribbean, workshops with indigenous farmers in Patagonia, and installing livestock emissions equipment at universities in South Africa," among other things.

National leader and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told reporters today that it's "just not right" that aid money is being spent in areas that don't serve New Zealand's national interest.

"I think this is a very sensible tradeoff," he said, adding that like economies such as the UK and Canada have made very similar choices.

"We're going to be more choiceful, a little more intentional about how we deploy a billion dollars worth of aid budget each and every year."

But the foreign minister, NZ First's Winston Peters, called it "both desperate and dangerous" and said it would jeopardise international relationships.

Meanwhile, National will push ahead with the government's current defence plans. Budget 2026 upped the defence budget by $3.5 billion this year, with a government commitment to increase defence spending to 2 percent of GDP - $12b - over eight years.

Advice to Finance Minister Nicola Willlis from Treasury ahead of Budget 2026, released last month, emphasised that defence was a key priority for the government this year, while foreign affairs, and thus aid spending, was not.

Treasury officials advised Willis to disregard the 0.7 percent OECD standard for aid entirely.

"We disagree with the approach of providing spending uplifts in line with GNI, as this would create fiscal pressure... spending should be justified in terms of its value-for-money, outputs, and outcomes."

A separate document revealed that MFAT had tried for the absolute maximum aid spend possible ahead of the budget. The original bid for aid was $740.35 million over the next four years, which was whittled down to just $238.50 million - 68 percent less.

"If investment in Pacific resilience is a high priority we would recommend funding is focused on more responsive and targeted initiatives (including where outside of IDC), or defence spending," officials told Willis.

No 'ad infinitum' defence spend - Labour

Vanushi Walters said that Labour was concerned New Zealand's external priorities would drift towards "militarisation" under the status quo.

She said Labour supported a tempered increase in defence spending, coupled with a shift in focus towards areas like disaster relief.

"I do think that regional security requires that, but certainly not at the cost of development and aid."

"We will not shift one eye from that focus on development and climate. We must keep that horizon objective front of mind so that it doesn't become solely an objective of increasing defence funding."

Vanushi Walters VNP / Phil Smith

Walters said aid and defence would be regarded as equal priorities.

"We cannot get pulled into this idea that you have to spend two or three percent of your budget on defence. I think that defeats the purpose of our spend in the Pacific, which is really ultimately to protect the Pacific's interests."

"Pacific leaders are telling us that is about energy resilience, that is about climate, that is about about development and infrastructure."

World.title: EatClub dining discount app launches with more than 250 venues signed up
World.content:
A new app lets restaurants offer discounts of up to 50 percent to fill empty tables, with more than 250 venues signed up for its New Zealand launch.

Restaurant discount app EatClub, part-owned by British chef Marco Pierre White, has launched in Auckland and Wellington, promising diners' savings of up to 50 percent when venues have spare tables.

More than 250 restaurants and cafes have joined the platform here, including eight Michelin-starred venues and names such as The French Cafe, Cassia, Cibo, KOL, Atelier and Dockside.

Restaurants can post a live offer whenever they want to bring in more customers, choosing the discount, time and number of tables available.

Diners claim an offer through the app and receive a straight percentage off everything they order.

EatClub chief executive and co-founder Pan Koutlakis said the system could respond quickly to a quiet spell or a last-minute cancellation.

"A restaurant in Sydney can have a cancelled booking, post an offer and have someone sitting in their restaurant in the next 20 or 25 minutes. It's that live and that dynamic."

Customers pay using an EatClub digital card held in their phone's wallet, which is linked to their usual debit or credit card.

The discount is applied automatically when they pay, so there is no need to show a voucher or tell restaurant staff they are using a deal.

Koutlakis said the app was designed to help restaurants make better use of quieter periods without cutting menu prices for everybody or changing the dining experience.

Venues could schedule offers for traditionally slow times, such as late afternoon during the week, or put one up in real time if bad weather kept customers at home.

He said high-end restaurants had also been receptive to the idea, despite the risk that discounting could be seen as denting their image.

"This is actually something that our co-founder Marco Pierre White says often: the only thing that really devalues your brand is an empty restaurant."

White, a shareholder and adviser to EatClub, has been involved since before the product launched.

The platform already operates in Australia and the United Kingdom, where it says it has more than three million users and 10,000 restaurants.

It plans to expand into other New Zealand cities in the coming months.

World.title: Lake Wakatipu bush fire has grown, firefighters expect further increase due to weather
World.content:
A huge vegetation fire on the southern shores of Lake Wakatipu has grown larger overnight and is likely to increase further due to weather conditions.

The blaze, which has been burning since Tuesday morning, was not contained or controlled when firefighters suspended operations on Tuesday night.

Assistant District Commander Nic McQuillan said firefighting resumed on Wednesday morning with air and ground operations.

Four helicopters with monsoon buckets were cooling hotspots and dampening the perimeter with a fifth helicopter being used as an aerial platform to direct the air attack, McQuillan said.

There were 11 firefighters on the ground and additional crews would arrive during the day to bring the numbers up to 25, McQuillan said.

Protection of Walter Peak Station homestead and farm stock remain priority, McQuillan said.

"While overnight conditions were relatively favourable, the fire has continued to grow and is now estimated at approximately 1200 hectares. The size is likely to increase if the fire becomes more active due to weather conditions."

McQuillan said people on the lake should stay at least 500m offshore to keep clear of helicopters.

The exclusion zone was monitored by Harbourmaster and Coastguard to ensure safety for the public and firefighters.

"Smoke conditions may worsen in some areas on the opposite side of the lake during the day. Residents affected by smoke are advised to keep windows and doors closed and limit exposure where possible."

The fire was not contained or controlled when firefighters suspended operations on Tuesday night. Supplied / Tom Kelly

Earlier, Walter Peak tour operator RealNZ said people had been evacuated and experiences were cancelled.

McQuillan said the most likely cause of the fire was a burn off that reignited a week later.

"This burn off was out, but when the conditions are right, they'll reignite by themselves. If you are intending to have a burn off or you are intending to have an outdoor fire, make sure it is fully extinguished.

"It's not just a case of let it burn itself out and walk away, put it out, make sure it's wet."

He said the upcoming El Niño weather pattern, which is likely to bring more frequent and stronger winds, made this even more critical.

"The wind is a guaranteed factor in the El Niño coming up, and that's a hugely contributing factor to how fire grows and develops and the speed it travels.

World.title: Why Takanini is key for Indian representation in Parliament
World.content:
Audio player for " Takanini emerges as a key electorate to watch " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1775168%2Fwhy-takanini-is-key-for-indian-representation-in-parliament

Takanini emerges as a key electorate to watch Morning Report Download MP3 5m

The result of the election battle for Takanini in South Auckland has the potential to be something of a turning point for Indian political representation in New Zealand.

The Labour Party has selected Kharag Singh, an Indian Sikh and local supermarket owner, to run against sitting National MP Rima Nakhle, who won the seat off Labour's Neru Leavasa by a hefty margin in 2023.

The electorate has one of the highest percentages of Indian households in the country, and so the vote will truly test whether this cohort can collectively unite behind a candidate aligned with a recognisable heritage.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406233692112

Why is the contest interesting?

Of the six Indian-origin lawmakers in Parliament's 172-year history, only two have won electorate seats.

Gaurav Sharma won the Hamilton West electorate in 2020, with Priyanca Radhakrishnan taking Maungakiekie the same year.

However, the 2020 election is widely considered to be an aberration, since Dame Jacinda Ardern's Labour won an outright majority of 64 seats - a first in the MMP era.

Otherwise, Radhakrishnan and four more Kiwi Indian MPs entered Parliament via the party list, largely because Indian-origin candidates tended to stand in electorates that traditionally didn't favour their parties, whether they were standing for National, Labour or New Zealand First.

That's why Singh's nomination for Takanini was interesting, said Ravi Bajpai, former editor of Indian Weekender and now editor of news portal Awaaz.

"Over the last few years, Labour politicians have been quite visible in the Takanini electorate, not just in election years," Bajpai said.

"So, there's surely the realisation that people of Indian origin have a heavy influence in this South Auckland seat.

"The question is: Will this cohort rally behind a political candidate of Indian origin as Indian New Zealanders aren't known to vote en masse on ethnic affinity."

Campaign hoardings for Labour candidate Kharag Singh and other political parties sit on the side of a road in the South Auckland electorate of Takanini ahead of the November election. RNZ / Blessen Tom

However, there were signs this might be changing, Bajpai said.

"The local body elections in Papatoetoe last year, and the rerun this year, have demonstrated [that] it is possible to rally Indian New Zealanders as a voting block if the candidate is enterprising enough," he said.

"In fielding Kharag Singh in Takanini, Labour must have had that calculation in mind."

Bajpai was referring to the 2025 local government elections in which four Kiwi Indians running under the Papatoetoe Ōtara Action Team banner won the Papatoetoe subdivision of the Ōtara-Papatoetoe Local Board, beating four strong Labour-affiliated candidates, including former Labour MP Ashraf Choudhary.

After the Manukau District Court ordered a re-election after voting irregularities were discovered, three of the four won again when a new election was held in April this year.

Indian influence in Takanini is reflected in the fact that roughly a quarter of voters in the electorate identify as having Indian ethnicity, which alongside Mount Roskill, is among the highest proportion in the country.

Created before the 2020 election in response to rapid population growth in South Auckland, Takanini drew voters from the Labour stronghold of Manurewa and National-leaning Botany and Papakura.

This makes it a marginal seat from the outset.

A campaign hoarding for National candidate Rima Nakhle sits on the side of a road in the South Auckland electorate of Takanini ahead of the November election. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Venkat Raman, editor of Indian Newslink, warns against making any predictions based on ethnicity alone.

He noted that Takanini shifted from being a large Labour victory in 2020 to a decisive National victory three years later, making it a highly volatile swing seat.

"[The] general elections held in 2020 and 2023 were considerably swept by respective Labour and National waves," he said.

"With the territory redrawn, Takanini accounts for the single largest population of people of Indian origin.

"While it would be presumptuous [for] the entire population to vote for the same candidate, voters will certainly evaluate several factors before deciding to cast their vote."

Several locals RNZ spoke to said household income, occupation, migration history, home ownership, law and order, and access to public services stood out as influential issues that may produce varied voting choices within the same broad ethnicity.

Rima Nakhle is the National Party candidate for the Takanini electorate in the 2026 election. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Who's standing and what happened in previous elections?

The above concerns should give Nakhle some confidence.

Nakhle is the first New Zealand lawmaker of Lebanese descent and someone who is very visible in the electorate.

That she comes from the influential and wealthy Nakhle family doesn't hurt either.

She is married to Roger Nakhle, son of Elias and Henriette Nakhle, who established the family's large-scale property development business in South Auckland decades ago.

National Business Review estimated the family fortune to be $200 million in 2018.

Calling the past three years an "absolute privilege", the first-term MP enjoyed being able to help a lot of people during her tenure.

She highlighted the ruling coalition's efforts in reducing crime, which seems to have become less of an election issue.

"I meet people regularly who say, 'Thank you for making us feel safe again'," Nakhle said.

She was proud to have been a member of the justice select committee responsible for banning displays of gang insignia in public, reinstating the three-strikes regime and making stalking illegal.

Nakhle acknowledged voter concerns on rising living costs but said Prime Minister Christpher Luxon was focused on it.

"The government has taken several steps and is taking some more with the ultimate goal of growing the economy," she said.

"So, life can be a little more affordable for my neighbours in Takanini [but] that will take some time.

"The average person in my electorate doesn't feel the impact just yet."

Kharag Singh, Labour's Takanini electorate candidate for the 2026 general election. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Singh similarly highlighted the current "cost of living crisis" ahead of the 7 November election.

"As my leader Chris Hipkins has said, this is a cost-of-living election," Singh said.

"In Takanini, my focus will be on growing infrastructure and improving public services."

Singh wanted to reassure the community on law and order should labour win the election, saying "Labour is never soft on crime".

"We had a very successful circuit-breaker programme then [for young repeat offenders] which was showing good results," he said.

"Our focus is always on the causes of crime, one of which is poverty," he said.

"That's why we will have a wrap-around system to deal with crime in New Zealand, including more police on the beat."

Singh stood for Labour against Luxon in Botany in 2023.

Meanwhile, Nakhle defeated Labour MP Neru Leavasa in Takanini by more than 8000 votes.

Leavasa had previously defeated Nakhle in Takanini's first-ever election in 2020 by more than 7000 votes.

Interestingly, Leavasa has switched places with Singh and is up against Luxon in Botany this time.

Other candidates in Takanini electorate include Paul Nooroa Teio from NZ Loyal, Lynley Tulloch from the Animal Justice Party and Elliott Ikilei from New Zealand First.

Ikilei is a former New Conservative leader and has been associated with Hobson's Pledge. His party secured 3 percent of the party vote at the 2023 election.

Tulloch stood in the 2023 election as well and gathered 736 votes. His party vote was 0.2 percent.

Similarly, the NZ Loyal party vote was 0.33 percent three years ago.

Considering similar voting patterns this year, none of these three candidates have a realistic chance of making much of a dent in either the left or right voting blocs.

What do the locals say?

Some issues for voters in Takanini are nationally relevant such as the struggling healthcare sector, which some claim is in "crisis".

Prabhjot Kaur, a teacher at Sikh Heritage School, said healthcare services seemed to be "worst" these days.

"My husband had kidney stones recently and it took us over a month to see a specialist," she said.

"He suffered severe pain and survived on Panadol while we waited for our turn."

Colleague Jagtar Kaur, who has lived in South Auckland for 22 years, wanted Punjabi to be part of the local school curriculum.

"At least schools in Takanini where the majority of the Punjabi community lives, Punjabi language can be an elective subject so that our children remain attached to our language and culture," she said.

"We do whatever we can at the Sikh Heritage School, but weekends classes are not enough."

Jaspreet Singh is the editor of NZ Punjabi News. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Jaspreet Singh, editor of NZ Punjabi News, who is based in the electorate, argued for traffic to be better managed in Takanini.

"Over the years, Takanini has had one of the fastest increases in population across electorates, but the road infrastructure hasn't grown accordingly," Jaspreet said.

"Our roads are always jammed, no matter weekends or off-peak."

He also wanted the next government to consider changing the parent resident visa settings.

"The new hybrid model put in place this week for the parent resident visa category hasn't met the community demand, as some parents will have to wait years to get a chance to apply," he said.

Daljit Singh is a spokesperson for the Supreme Sikh Society of New Zealand. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Is there an election issue that is relevant to this electorate in particular?

Daljit Singh, a spokesperson for the Supreme Sikh Society, highlighted another issue of concern to the Indian community in the lead-up to elections.

"Our nagar kirtans (Sikh religious processions) were disrupted, and there were deeply concerning calls advocating violence against migrant communities and places of worship," Daljit said.

"We understand, respect and value the fundamental right to freedom of speech in New Zealand. However, freedom of speech must be exercised responsibly and should never be used to justify threats, hatred, intimidation or incitement to violence against any individual or community.

"People of Indian heritage have been part of New Zealand's diverse society for more than a century and have made significant contributions to the country's social, cultural and economic development.

"It is therefore deeply concerning to see an increase in anti-Indian and anti-migrant rhetoric in recent years. We hope that New Zealand continues to be a country where every community feels safe, respected, included and valued.

"I would commend the Indian Sikh communities for the patience, dignity and restraint they have demonstrated, as well as their continued commitment to building bridges, fostering understanding and strengthening relationships with people from all communities across New Zealand."

National MP Mark Mitchell RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Ethnic Communities Minister Mark Mitchell has repeatedly said freedom of speech comes with responsibility.

In June, Mitchell labelled social media comments to "purge" Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims from New Zealand as the "actions of a scared bully" and "cowardly social media attacks" designed to tear New Zealand's social fabric.

The minister also said such remarks were assessed by the police against the thresholds set out in the Human Rights Act.

In general, political parties on both sides of the aisle have adopted mixed positions on calls for the government to amend hate speech legislation.

The National Party did not support legislating against hate speech, while ACT believed more enforcement of existing legislation was needed.

The Greens said the party was open to extending hate speech legislation. Te Pāti Māori also appeared to broadly support legislative reform.

Labour said it was in the process of developing and refining its ethnic and social cohesion policies and would release them in due course.

In the end, it will boil down to money in people's back pocket, Jaspreet added.

More so, as the electorate is immigrant heavy, of younger age and rapidly growing, has low home ownership, and is highly exposed to cost-of-living pressures, the local journalist said.

"Inflation or cost of living is the biggest issue, above all," he said.

"The Punjabi community here is well connected to the one in Australia and they always compare how the authorities there have put in measures to ease price rise," he said.

World.title: Aussies dealt major injury blow ahead of first South Africa Test
World.content:
Cameron Green has been ruled out of the first Test against South Africa in Durban after succumbing to an abdominal strain.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald said Green failed to overcome the injury, which he suffered in the final one-day international (ODI) played in Potchefstroom last week.

McDonald said it was "highly unlikely" Green would bowl later in the series, should he prove his fitness for the remaining two Tests.

The injury blow is likely to leave Australia with a choice to make between Cooper Connolly or Nic Maddinson at number five in the batting order for the first Test, which begins on Friday night, AEST.

Travis Head is expected to remain as opener, with Alex Carey to bat at six.

Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Green appeared to be finding some rhythm with the bat, having scored a century against Bangladesh in Darwin in August.

"He is progressing pretty well, all things considered … he is still here for a reason, so there is some light at the end of the tunnel," McDonald said

"It will just be a matter of going through the rehab. He has a pretty demanding week as he reintroduced some activities.

"It's a bit of an unknown, but there is still optimism that he will take part in the series at some stage."

Green had been managing a shoulder injury that stopped him bowling in the white-ball matches against the Proteas.

His planned bowling return in the final ODI was aborted due to the abdominal injury.

"We would be solely focused on getting him to return as a batter. We wouldn't be putting that demand on him to return as a bowler," McDonald said.

"That would be too high-risk, is the information I have."

Maddinson has not played a Test for Australia since 2016 but was a surprise addition to the squad last week when Josh Inglis suffered a fractured finger.

Australia is also weighing up whether a dry Durban surface pushes them towards picking Connolly, with an expectation the Kingsmead wicket will turn later in the match.

Matt Kuhnemann is also on the tour as a second spinner, but it would appear unlikely Australia will opt to play him ahead of one of the three frontline quicks.

Green's injury also increases the chances of Beau Webster holding his spot as a fourth seamer, after he played in the last three Tests batting at number seven.

AAP

World.title: Geelong scores major coup with Matildas-Colombia clash
World.content:
The Matildas will return to Victoria this year, with Geelong's Kardinia Park named as the venue for the second leg of a two-match series against Colombia.

The Victorian government today announced the December 2 fixture, two years after 30,000 fans packed out the regional stadium to see the "Tillies" beat Chinese Taipei 6-0.

The announcement is a major coup for Geelong, which will be the only Victorian city to host the Matildas this year.

The national team last played in Victoria in May 2025.

"This blockbuster clash will drive visitation across the Geelong region, support local businesses and showcase Victoria's unmatched ability to host world-class sporting events," Visit Victoria chief executive Brendan McClements said.

Football Australia deputy chief executive Heather Garriock said Victorians' support of the Matildas was "always outstanding".

"We're delighted to bring the CommBank Matildas back to Victoria for what promises to be a special occasion for football fans, as our FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 preparations intensify," Ms Garriock said.

The first leg of the Colombia series will be played at Canberra Stadium on November 28, with the games expected to serve as a valuable test ahead of the World Cup in Brazil in June.

Both Australia and Colombia have already qualified for the World Cup.

Matildas fans were out in force in 2023, and will be raring to go in Brazil (AAP Image)

The Matildas finished fourth in the 2023 World Cup, and earlier this year were runners up in the AFC Women's Asian Cup.

Ms Garriock, who is also Football Australia's executive director of football, in August said the Colombia series would be an opportunity to give younger talent a chance to impress.

"We sat down with (coach) Joe (Montemurro) some 12 months ago when he started in the Matildas position, and we asked him what his ideal preparation was in the lead-up to the Women's World Cup," Ms Garriock said.

"It was very evident that different styles of play were important to him, but also trying to blood some of the next generation as well.

"We've seen that (younger players getting an opportunity) at the recent World Cup in the US with (Socceroos coach) Tony Popovic as well."

World.title: Kostecki loses engineer to bike accident as he goes for Bathurst record
World.content:
Supercars star Brodie Kostecki can surpass Australian motor racing legends Peter Brock and Allan Moffat with a Bathurst record this weekend, but will do it without the support of his engineer.

Kostecki has claimed pole position at the previous three Bathurst 1000s, trying the record for most consecutive poles for the great race with Moffat (1970-72) and Brock (1977-79).

Should the West Australian be the fastest in Saturday's top-10 shootout, he will become the first driver to secure four consecutive poles for the great race.

Kostecki is the only driver to secure pole position at Bathurst in the Gen3 era which began in 2024, and he put the number 17 Dick Johnson Racing entry on pole position for the last Supercars round at The Bend.

However, there will be a change on the pit wall for Kostecki, with his engineer George Commins not attending Mount Panorama this weekend.

Dick Johnson Racing announced that Commins, who was Kostecki's engineer for this Bathurst triumph in 2024 with Erebus Motorsport, had been injured in a mountain biking accident.

"Car 17 race engineer George Commins will miss the Repco Bathurst 1000 after sustaining injuries in a mountain biking accident prior to the race weekend," the team said in a statement.

"Team manager Tom Moore will take over race engineer duties for Brodie Kostecki and Todd Hazelwood at Mount Panorama while George recuperates at home."

Moore is no stranger to the engineering role, or Kostecki. The pair have been working in the same team since 2021. Moore was the race engineer for Kostecki's then-teammate Will Brown at Erebus.

Kostecki has been very good in qualifying this season, with six pole positions from 28 races.

His shootout laps at Mount Panorama for the past three years have been excellent, with Kostecki claiming pole position by margins of 0.483, 0.131 and 0.176 seconds.

Qualifying for the Bathurst 1000 will be held on Friday afternoon. That will set the grid for positions 11 to 27.

The top 10 from Friday will participate in Saturday's top-10 shootout to determine the grid from pole to 10th.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

World.title: Jannik Sinner to miss rest of tennis season with knee injury
World.content:
World number one Jannik Sinner will not compete again in 2026 after opting to continue his recovery ‌from a knee injury that has kept him out of action ‌since his ⁠triumphant Wimbledon campaign in July.

"Me, together with the doctors, have decided that I need a course of treatment for my knee, which means that the 2026 season is officially over," Sinner said in a video message on Instagram.

" I also need to think about my long-term career so I will do everything possible to get back 100 per cent. "

Sinner has not played since beating Alexander Zverev in the All England Club final on July 12, with the 25-year-old missing the North American hardcourt swing, the US Open as well as the ongoing slate of tournaments in Asia.

He will now miss the European indoor hardcourt swing as well as the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin, where he won the title in the last two years.

Sinner's team said in a statement that he would follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee.

"The decision has been made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary time to recover before beginning preparations for 2027."

Sinner's absence could open the door for Zverev to finish the year at the top of the world rankings.

The German world number two has cut the gap to Sinner after winning the French Open and US Open titles.

World.title: Zach Merrett staying 'open-minded' after high-profile AFL move to Hawks
World.content:
Boom AFL recruit Zach Merrett is open-minded over what role he will play at Hawthorn under coach Sam Mitchell.

More than a year after the bombshell revelation that the Hawks were trying to lure Merrett from Essendon, a deal was finally struck for the former Bombers captain when the trade period opened on Monday.

Essendon will receive the number 15 and 25 picks in this year's national draft, as well as Hawthorn's 2028 second-round selection.

The bitter rivals were unable to reach a deal for Merrett in trade talks a year ago.

Merrett would obviously boost Hawthorn's midfield, but he noted on Tuesday in a club interview that he could also play in defence or across half-forward.

"It is funny that Gia and I are back together," he said of former Essendon assistant coach Daniel Giansiracusa, who is now at the Hawks.

"We worked for three years on trying to be the most flexible player in the competition, being able to play a number of different roles.

"I have no preconceived ideas with Sam. We're going to be pretty open-minded, to what that could look like.

Loading Instagram content

"There are already so many incredible players out there for the Hawks, so wherever I fit in, I will make sure I make that work — whether that's back, forward, mid, or wing, or whatever it looks like."

Merrett has toured Hawthorn's Dingley headquarters and met with captain Jai Newcombe.

"It's been a bit overwhelming, the last 24 hours," Merrett said.

"To see the whole facility and to get so many incredible messages, I feel extremely welcomed, and so is my family."

Last Thursday Merrett became the third player to win Essendon's best and fairest award seven times, alongside Dick Reynolds and Bill Hutchison.

"It was a really hard decision, it was probably something I weighed up for six to nine months," Merrett said of the move.

"It felt like Hawthorn was going to be the best place for me and my family, moving forward, to keep achieving, to achieve out of footy.

"I also have so much respect and love for Essendon as well, so it is a unique feeling, a little bit.

"But I'm keen to move forward, get stuck into work."

Hawthorn, whose season ended with an epic preliminary final loss to premiers Brisbane, are also expected to recruit key forward Ben King from Gold Coast.
